rule_name: Agency Sunset Rule Mandate (Executive Order 14270, "Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy")
agency: White House / OMB (directs EPA, DOE, DOI, FERC, NRC, Army Corps of Engineers, BLM, BOEM)
status: In effect, partly implemented: FERC and NRC sunset rules are in force (first lapses due Dec. 5, 2026 and Jan. 8, 2027 unless extended); DOE withdrew its direct final rule July 9, 2026, and its identical proposal is pending; no EPA sunset rule in the Federal Register as of Sept. 2026.
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- this is a new process mandate targeting energy-related regulations under statutes including the Federal Power Act, Natural Gas Act, Atomic Energy Act, Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, Endangered Species Act, and appliance efficiency law; EPA and the Army Corps were to name their own covered statutes to OMB.
what_changed: Directs covered agencies (EPA, DOE, FERC, NRC, DOI bureaus, Army Corps, BLM, BOEM) to issue a 'sunset rule', effective by September 30, 2025, inserting a 'Conditional Sunset Date' into covered existing regulations -- one year after the sunset rule's effective date, unless the agency affirmatively extends it (to a date no more than 5 years out). All new energy-related regulations must include a sunset date no more than 5 years out. **If an agency does not act to extend a regulation before its sunset date, the regulation automatically expires and is removed from the Code of Federal Regulations -- no further rulemaking is required for the expiration itself, though the order says the agency will first offer the public a chance to comment on the rule's costs and benefits.** Agencies missed the September 30, 2025 deadline and applied the order narrowly. FERC issued a direct final rule on October 21, 2025, effective December 5, 2025, giving a set of its regulations a December 5, 2026 sunset date; it rescinded the sunset for one provision (non-mandatory smart-grid guidance) after an adverse comment. NRC issued its direct final rule on December 3, 2025, effective January 8, 2026, with a January 8, 2027 sunset date. NRC said the vast majority of its regulations fell outside the order because they protect public health and safety or the common defense, form part of its statutory permitting regime, or implement other statutes, so it applied sunsets mainly to unused or outdated provisions such as interpretation sections. After six comment submissions raised significant adverse comments, NRC withdrew the sunset for its aircraft impact assessment requirement for reactors (10 CFR 50.150) on January 8, 2026, then reinstated it through a final rule effective April 8, 2026. In June 2026 NRC opened the promised public comment period on the costs and benefits of the regulations due to lapse January 8, 2027. DOE published a direct final rule and an identical proposed rule on May 29, 2026, setting a one-year sunset on 21 parts of Title 10 of the CFR and a five-year sunset on seven more (covering access to classified information, the Human Reliability Program and worker safety), while leaving out nuclear-safety rules tied to Price-Anderson indemnification; its list does not include DOE's appliance efficiency standards. Adverse comments followed: the Institute for Policy Integrity said the process 'bypasses both meaningful public input and true consideration of whether the sunsets comport with statutory mandates or improve overall public welfare,' and 14 state attorneys general wrote that the proposal 'effectively repeals hundreds of regulations.' DOE withdrew the direct final rule on July 9, 2026, and said it would respond to the comments in any final action on the proposed rule, which remains pending. In a June 2026 oil and gas leasing proposal, BLM declined to add a sunset date, saying those rules rest mainly on the Mineral Leasing Act rather than the Federal Land Policy and Management Act.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed EO 14270 personally on April 9, 2025, as one of three deregulatory orders issued that day (alongside the 'Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations' memorandum, tracked separately in this database).

corporate_beneficiaries: Energy producers and regulated industries broadly across the covered statutes -- a structural mandate rather than a single-sector rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Structural risk to energy, nuclear and environmental protections: the order flips the normal default so covered rules lapse automatically unless an agency affirmatively renews them, with no further rulemaking needed for the lapse itself. As implemented so far, its reach is narrower than its text. NRC and FERC applied sunsets mainly to unused, outdated or procedural provisions, though NRC's list includes its aircraft impact assessment requirement for reactors. DOE's pending proposal, which 14 state attorneys general said would effectively repeal hundreds of regulations, including rules on access to nuclear facilities and information and nuclear waste storage, would put 28 parts of its rules on a sunset clock. No sunset rule has appeared for EPA's pollution standards, DOE's list leaves out appliance efficiency standards, and BLM declined to sunset its oil and gas leasing rules.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: Counts are TAP's, taken from the agencies' Federal Register documents; no agency, GAO or outside estimate of health, mortality or dollar effects was found, and none is claimed here. The 'hundreds of regulations' characterization is the state attorneys general's. Real impact depends on which provisions agencies let lapse at the first sunset dates, on DOE's final action, and on whether EPA, Interior bureaus and the Army Corps issue sunset rules; the order's requirement that new covered rules carry sunset dates of no more than five years is not captured in these counts.

confidence_note: Strong 'process is the harm' entry, similar to EO 14192 but energy-specific and more severe in mechanism -- automatic expiration by default, rather than requiring agencies to affirmatively act to repeal. Worth noting that NRC and FERC applied sunsets mainly to unused, outdated or procedural provisions (NRC said most of its rules were outside the order's scope), DOE withdrew its direct final rule after adverse comments, and BLM declined to sunset its oil and gas leasing rules: the mechanism is structurally risky, but outcomes so far are narrow and uneven. NRC did, however, reinstate a sunset on its aircraft impact assessment requirement over adverse comments.
pull_quote: The sunset process 'bypasses both meaningful public input and true consideration of whether the sunsets comport with statutory mandates,' the Institute for Policy Integrity told DOE, which withdrew its direct final rule in July 2026.

section_summaries.what_changed: Agencies must give existing energy rules automatic expiration dates; unless renewed, they lapse. FERC and NRC applied it narrowly; DOE withdrew its direct final rule after adverse comments.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: The order makes covered energy rules lapse unless renewed, but agencies have aimed it mostly at minor or unused rules; the first lapses are due Dec. 2026 (FERC) and Jan. 2027 (NRC).
section_summaries.confidence_note: A structurally risky mechanism with a narrow, uneven rollout: NRC and FERC sunset mostly unused rules, DOE withdrew its direct final rule, and BLM left its leasing rules out.

rule_name: NEPA Categorical Exclusions and Clean Water Act Nationwide-Permit Exploration for AI Data Center Construction (Executive Order 14318 and the AI Action Plan)
agency: CEQ / EPA / U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
status: Weakened (not fully repealed)
date_of_action: 2025-07-23 (EO 14318 and the AI Action Plan issued); implementation ongoing through 2026
original_rule_summary: Before this action, large infrastructure projects including data centers were generally subject to standard environmental review: NEPA environmental assessments or full environmental impact statements for actions with significant federal involvement, individualized Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting (with public input) for construction affecting wetlands or waterways, and standard Clean Air Act permitting -- including public comment periods -- for facilities' air emissions, without any blanket exemption specific to AI or data-center infrastructure.
what_changed: On July 23, 2025, Trump signed three executive orders implementing his 'Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan': EO 14318, 'Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure'; 'Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government'; and 'Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack.' EO 14318 applies to data-center projects with at least $500 million in capital expenditures or more than 100 megawatts of incremental power load (or projects otherwise designated by the Secretaries of Defense, Interior, Commerce, or Energy) and directs the Council on Environmental Quality to coordinate with agencies to identify or create new NEPA categorical exclusions for data-center-related construction found to customarily have less-than-significant environmental effects -- allowing qualifying projects to skip the standard environmental assessment or full environmental impact statement process. The order also presumes that federal financial assistance covering less than 50% of a project's total cost does not constitute the level of federal control that would otherwise trigger full NEPA review. Separately, the AI Action Plan directs the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to 'explore the need' for a nationwide Clean Water Act Section 404 permit specific to data centers -- a blanket permitting mechanism that would let qualifying projects avoid the individualized water-quality review a project-specific permit requires. The EPA separately proposed allowing data centers to obtain air-pollution permits without the standard public-comment process. More than 230 environmental and public-interest groups asked Congress to impose a temporary moratorium on new data-center approvals and construction until federal rules addressed energy use, water needs, local impacts, and emissions. The Southern Environmental Law Center -- leading a coalition of nearly 200 environmental, health, and community groups -- filed comments opposing the EPA's no-public-comment air-permit proposal. Seven Senate Democrats, in a letter led by Sen. Adam Schiff, questioned the administration over the potential Clean Water Act nationwide permit, warning it could let data centers avoid individualized scrutiny of their water-quality impacts. As an example of the underlying pressure driving these fights, **conservation groups in South Carolina separately criticized a state permit allowing a Google data center to draw 1.5 million gallons of water per day, arguing it prioritized tech-industry water demand over local needs** -- illustrative of the water-use concerns the proposed federal permitting changes would make harder to individually review. NEPA itself, signed into law by President Nixon in 1970 and often described as the U.S.'s foundational environmental statute (sometimes called the environmental 'Magna Carta'), requires federal agencies proposing actions like roads, bridges, or energy projects to study their environmental effects before proceeding; a White House Council on Environmental Quality spokeswoman defended the AI Action Plan's approach as 'meaningful NEPA reform to reduce the delays in federal permitting, unleashing the ability for America to strengthen its AI and manufacturing leadership' (AP/ABC News, July 29, 2025).

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed EO 14318 and unveiled the broader AI Action Plan on July 23, 2025, directing CEQ, EPA, and the Army Corps of Engineers to streamline environmental review and permitting specifically for AI data-center infrastructure.

corporate_beneficiaries: Large-scale AI data-center developers and hyperscale cloud companies broadly, per the EO's own stated purpose of accelerating this class of infrastructure
Google, named specifically in South Carolina reporting over a state permit allowing 1.5 million gallons/day of water use for a data center amid the same broader permitting-easing push

estimated_health_impact.summary: Environmental and public-health groups warn that exempting AI data centers from individualized NEPA, Clean Water Act, and Clean Air Act review removes public input and case-by-case scrutiny over local air emissions, water withdrawals, and wetland/waterway impacts at a moment of rapid data-center buildout, though no single quantified national health/mortality estimate specific to this policy was identified in sourcing reviewed.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: This entry documents a policy that removes or streamlines standard environmental review mechanisms rather than a rule with an existing quantified health-impact estimate (e.g. a premature-mortality figure) -- no such single figure specific to this action was identified in sourcing reviewed. The Google South Carolina water-use figure is a specific, illustrative state-level permit example cited by critics of the broader trend, not a measured national consequence of EO 14318 itself. Re-verify once CEQ's new categorical exclusions and any Army Corps nationwide CWA permit are finalized, since both remain in a proposal/exploration stage as of the sourcing reviewed.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the executive orders' existence, their specific terms (thresholds, categorical-exclusion directive, CWA nationwide-permit exploration directive), and the environmental groups' and Senate Democrats' documented objections -- corroborated across multiple law-firm client alerts (Sidley, Paul Hastings, Hunton, DLA Piper, Arnold & Porter, Allen Matkins) analyzing the same official White House text, plus Carbon Credits, PBS NewsHour, and Sen. Schiff's own office for the advocacy/opposition side. MODERATE confidence that these mechanisms have been finalized and are actually reducing review in practice -- both the CEQ categorical exclusions and the Army Corps nationwide CWA permit were, per sourcing reviewed, still in a proposal/exploration stage rather than fully implemented as of the reporting reviewed for this entry. AP/ABC News reporting is a corroborating source for the same underlying AI Action Plan/NEPA story, adding NEPA's own background and CEQ's on-record defense of the reform rather than describing a separate action.
short_summary: Trump's July 2025 AI Action Plan exempts qualifying AI data centers from standard NEPA/Clean Water Act review.

section_summaries.what_changed: Trump's July 2025 AI Action Plan and EO 14318 direct CEQ to create new NEPA categorical exclusions for AI data centers and the Army Corps to explore a nationwide Clean Water Act permit for them, while EPA proposed skipping public comment on their air permits.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: 230+ environmental/public-interest groups sought a congressional moratorium on new data-center approvals; no national health/mortality figure specific to this policy exists yet, but critics point to cases like a Google South Carolina facility's 1.5-million-gallon daily water permit as illustrative of the local impacts individualized review would otherwise catch.
section_summaries.confidence_note: The executive orders' terms and the organized opposition are well-corroborated; whether the streamlined review mechanisms have actually been finalized and applied remains to be verified.

rule_name: Reopening of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain and National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska to oil and gas leasing, and a new five-year offshore leasing draft program (2026-2031)
agency: Department of the Interior (Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management)
status: ANWR and NPR-A leasing limits rescinded (Oct.-Nov. 2025); June 2026 ANWR sale drew $3.74M from two bidders as suits remain pending; the 2026-2031 offshore program is still a draft, its next proposal pending as of Sept. 2026
date_of_action: 2025-10-23 (ANWR Coastal Plain reopened) through 2026-06-05 (ANWR lease sale results); NPR-A final rule published 2025-11-17; five-year OCS leasing draft program released 2025-11-20, comment period closed 2026-01-23
original_rule_summary: The Biden administration had left the Arctic Refuge's 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain under a 2024 Record of Decision limiting leasing to a small fraction of the area Trump's first-term program allowed, and had suspended Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority's (AIDEA) leases from a 2021 sale. A separate 2024 rule protected roughly 13 million acres of ecologically sensitive 'Special Areas' within the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska by creating a regulatory presumption against oil and gas activity there unless operators could show minimal or no adverse effect on surface resources. The Biden administration's 2024 five-year Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) oil and gas leasing program scheduled no new lease sales in federal waters through 2029, the first such plan in the program's history to include zero new sales.
what_changed: On October 23, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum rescinded the Biden-era Record of Decision on the Arctic Refuge and reinstated the maximum-leasing 2020 program, reopening the entire 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing and lifting the suspension on AIDEA's 2021 leases. On November 17, 2025, Interior published a final rule in the Federal Register rescinding the 2024 National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska rule, removing the presumption against drilling across roughly 13 million acres of 'Special Areas' and reverting to weaker 1977-era standards; Burgum said the change would 'unlock Alaska's energy potential.' On November 20, 2025, Interior released a draft five-year OCS leasing program for 2026-2031 proposing as many as 34 lease sales -- the most aggressive offering in decades -- across 21 of 27 planning areas, including six sales off California, new drilling at least 100 miles off Florida, and 21 Alaska sales spanning Cook Inlet, the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, and a newly designated 'High Arctic' area over 200 miles offshore. Interior had already dropped the Atlantic coast from the plan about three weeks before the draft's release, after Republicans in the region pressed to keep rigs away from their shores, so the draft schedules no Atlantic sales. The 60-day public comment period ran November 24, 2025 through January 23, 2026. On December 11, 2025, Trump signed a Congressional Review Act resolution (H.J. Res. 131, Public Law 119-52) nullifying the Biden administration's December 2024 Coastal Plain Record of Decision. On March 18, 2026, the first National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska lease sale since 2019 -- one of five the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act mandates there over 10 years -- drew a record $163 million in high bids from 11 companies, with ConocoPhillips and Repsol the most prominent bidders, on more than 1.3 million of the nearly 5.5 million acres offered; BLM accepted bids on tracts around Teshekpuk Lake even though U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason had two days earlier issued an injunction reinstating a right-of-way agreement that bars development there, and the sale's inclusion of long-protected land is the subject of two lawsuits by Native and environmental groups. **A June 2026 BLM lease sale in the Arctic Refuge, held under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's mandate of at least four Arctic Refuge sales through 2035 and while three separate but parallel lawsuits -- originally filed in 2020, with at least two amended in January 2026 to challenge the October 2025 decision -- remained pending (brought by NRDC/Center for Biological Diversity/Friends of the Earth, the Gwich'in Steering Committee, and the Native Village of Venetie Tribal Government), drew just nine bids on five of the 58 tracts offered -- 72,049 of the 688,829 acres put up for sale -- with high bids totaling $3.74 million, and only AIDEA and Anchorage-based HEX Energy LLC bidding; HEX, a Cook Inlet gas producer, has never operated on the North Slope, and AIDEA had done no exploration work on the leases it has held since 2021.** On July 8, 2026, the Justice Department settled suits by the State of Alaska and AIDEA over the Biden-era Coastal Plain limits, conceding that the 2024 program violated the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. As of late September 2026, BOEM's program page still lists the offshore program's next step, the Proposed Program (2nd Analysis and Proposal), as pending, though a Secretary's Order issued with the draft directed BOEM to have the new program in place by October 2026. Separately, a non-oil-and-gas Alaska extraction project -- the Donlin Gold mine, distinct from this entry's ANWR/NPR-A leasing actions -- received fast-track federal permitting coverage (FAST-41) on October 27, 2025 under the same broader administration push; the companion Donlin Gold entry covers that project's distinct legal mechanism and its own unresolved tailings-dam spill-risk court finding.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Signed the October 2025 ANWR rescission and the November 2025 NPR-A rule, and Interior released the five-year OCS leasing draft program under his direction, implementing Trump's Executive Orders 14153 and 14154 (both signed his first day in office, Jan. 20, 2025), the latter directing agencies to maximize domestic energy development.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA, a state-owned development corporation) and HEX Energy LLC
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: The only two bidders at the June 2026 ANWR Coastal Plain lease sale; AIDEA also had its 2021 leases -- suspended under the Biden administration -- reinstated by the October 2025 rescission.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Oil and gas developers with interests in the newly reopened National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska Special Areas (including ConocoPhillips and Repsol, the prominent bidders at the record March 2026 NPR-A sale) and OCS planning areas (California, Gulf of Mexico, Alaska, Florida)
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: The NPR-A rule removes the presumption against drilling on ~13 million acres, and the draft five-year OCS program would open the largest number of new lease sales in decades if finalized.

estimated_health_impact.summary: The harm documented here is risk, not a realized event: the Gwich'in, whose subsistence and way of life depend on the Porcupine caribou herd that calves on the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain, and North Slope communities such as Nuiqsut near NPR-A development, face exposure of the land and wildlife they rely on as the entire 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain is reopened to leasing and about 13 million acres of NPR-A Special Areas lose their presumption against drilling, with the offshore draft proposing 34 more sales. Denning polar bears, caribou and migratory birds lose protected habitat. No modeled human mortality figure exists. Financially, the June 2026 Arctic Refuge sale raised $3.74 million, half of it for Alaska, while the March 2026 NPR-A sale drew a record $163 million, so the revenue case differs sharply between the two areas.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No oil spill or direct human-health incident has occurred under these actions as of September 2026; the harm is exposure and risk (polar bear denning habitat, the Porcupine caribou herd, migratory birds, and, offshore, walrus and bowhead and beluga whales, per Defenders of Wildlife, the Center for Biological Diversity, the Gwich'in Steering Committee and other opponents) rather than a realized event, and No agency or group estimate of a human health effect was found. The Arctic Refuge sale's weak results are cited by opponents as evidence the expansion lacks industry demand, but that characterization is contested (BLM and North Slope Inupiat groups called the sale a success) and the record NPR-A sale, where the prominent bidders already operate, drew strong demand. The offshore program is a draft: the Atlantic was excluded before its release, the next proposal is still pending, and final scope could differ.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the ANWR and NPR-A actions (BLM's and DOI's own press releases, corroborated by Reuters, AP, and Earthjustice) and on the June 2026 lease-sale results (BLM's official bid recap and Alaska Beacon). HIGH confidence on the five-year OCS draft program's proposed scope (Interior's November 20, 2025 release and BOEM's program page give the 34-sale/21-of-27-planning-area figures; PBS/AP and NRDC report the same plan), though its status is a draft, not a finalized program -- treat any acreage/sale-count figure as proposed, not final, pending Interior's final program. The litigation challenging the ANWR decision (three separate suits) was pending, not resolved, as of the sources reviewed.
pull_quote: Interior Secretary Burgum said reopening the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska's protected Special Areas would ‘unlock Alaska's energy potential’; the reserve's March 2026 sale drew a record $163 million, while the Arctic Refuge's June 2026 sale drew just $3.74 million from two bidders.

section_summaries.what_changed: Interior reopened ANWR's 1.56M-acre Coastal Plain and stripped protections from 13M NPR-A acres (2025), and proposed 34 offshore lease sales; a June 2026 ANWR sale drew just $3.74M from two bidders.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Gwich'in who rely on the Porcupine caribou herd and North Slope villages like Nuiqsut face habitat risk as millions of Arctic acres open to leasing; no spill or health harm has occurred yet.
section_summaries.confidence_note: ANWR/NPR-A actions and sale results rest on DOI/BLM records, a public law and multiple outlets; the offshore program is still a draft, so its final scope needs a recheck.

rule_name: ATF zero-tolerance dealer-license revocation policy and gun-show sales background-check rule (Biden-era gun trafficking enforcement framework)
agency: ATF (Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives) / DOJ
status: In effect: zero-tolerance dealer policy ended April 2025 and at least 23 revoked dealers relicensed; ATF's May 2026 proposal to largely repeal the 2024 gun-show dealer rule is not final, but a federal court vacated the whole rule in June 2026 and refused DOJ's bid to narrow that Aug. 13
date_of_action: 2025 through 2026-07 (ongoing rollback, per ProPublica's reporting period)
original_rule_summary: Under Biden-era policy, ATF pursued a 'zero-tolerance' approach to federal firearms licensees who knowingly violated gun laws, revoking dealer licenses for serious violations, and pursued gun-trafficking referrals for prosecution at a higher rate, with a rule addressing the so-called 'gun show loophole' around private/unlicensed sales.
what_changed: The Trump administration reversed the ATF's zero-tolerance dealer-license enforcement policy, inviting dealers who had lost their licenses under Biden to reapply; **nearly a dozen previously revoked gun shops had been relicensed and were selling firearms again as of July 2026, with at least 23 stores receiving new licenses after resubmitting applications**. ProPublica found that dealer license revocations fell to 56 in 2025, down 69% from the year before. ATF referrals for common gun-trafficking charges fell 15% in 2025 from 2024, and DOJ declined 30% more ATF trafficking referrals than the year prior, per a ProPublica analysis. rule_name: Presidential proclamations reducing Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments by ~90%
agency: Department of the Interior / Executive Office of the President
status: In effect since September 11, 2026, when land cut from both monuments opened to new mining claims. Conservation groups moved September 2 to reopen their 2017 lawsuit, arguing the Antiquities Act lets presidents create monuments but not shrink them; no ruling yet.
date_of_action: 2026-07-13 (executive orders/proclamations signed) through 2026-09-11 (effective date)
original_rule_summary: Bears Ears National Monument (established 2016, roughly 1.36 million acres) and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument (established 1996, roughly 1.87 million acres) had federal Antiquities Act protection preventing most commercial development, including oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral extraction, within their boundaries. Bears Ears in particular was designated to protect land sacred to multiple Native American tribes. This is not the first attempt to shrink these monuments -- Trump previously reduced them substantially in his first term, a move Biden reversed in 2021.
what_changed: On July 13, 2026, Trump signed a pair of executive orders/proclamations in the Oval Office, surrounded by Utah's full congressional delegation, Gov. Spencer Cox, and state House Speaker Mike Schultz, **reducing Bears Ears National Monument from approximately 1.36 million acres to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante from approximately 1.87 million acres to about 182,000 acres -- a combined reduction of nearly 3 million acres, roughly 90% of both monuments' prior size**. The proclamations take effect 60 days after signing, on September 11, 2026. The move is part of Trump's broader push to expand oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral development on public lands following his early-2025 declaration of a national energy emergency, and follows a similar, smaller reduction attempt in Trump's first term that Biden reversed in 2021. Tribal representatives condemned the move as opening previously protected land -- including sites sacred to multiple Native American tribes -- to extraction industry development. One day after the signing, a mining company filed seven claims within the old Bears Ears boundaries, ahead of the September 11 date the proclamations set for new claims; the proclamations say such early filings vest no rights. On September 2, 2026, conservation groups including the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and the Natural Resources Defense Council, represented by Earthjustice, moved in federal court in Washington, D.C. to reopen their 2017 lawsuit, arguing the Antiquities Act gives presidents the power to establish monuments but not to shrink or undo them. Once the land opened on September 11, claimants moved quickly: the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, an advocacy group tracking San Juan County recorder filings, counted 16 claims recorded by noon that day and 72 by September 28 -- more than triple the 20 filed in the same lands during the entire 2018-2021 first reduction -- from Land Survey Advisors LLC (36), Kimmerle Mining (33) and George W. Schultz (3), in places including the headwaters of the Dark Canyon Wilderness and just outside Natural Bridges National Monument. The Grand Canyon Trust, another advocacy group, said the entire White Canyon region surrounding Natural Bridges, where uranium deposits lie, was cut from the monument.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Personally signed both proclamations in the Oval Office, with Utah's congressional delegation and state officials present, framing the move as part of the administration's broader public-lands energy-development agenda.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral extraction companies with interests in the affected Utah public lands
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Nearly 3 million acres previously under Antiquities Act monument protection became available for new mining claims and mineral leasing on September 11, 2026, under the reduced monument boundaries.

rule_name: Environmental and historic-preservation law waivers for border barrier construction in Big Bend National Park
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- waived for a specific project area, not a nationwide rule change; on October 2, 2026 a federal court blocked construction in the Big Bend sector and, according to Marfa Public Radio, suspended the waivers there while the lawsuit proceeds
date_of_action: 2026-06 (initial waiver) through 2026-07-27 (subsequent waiver by Secretary Mullin extending the project area)
original_rule_summary: A body of federal environmental and preservation statutes -- including the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, National Park Service Organic Act, Clean Water Act, Historic Preservation Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Migratory Bird Conservation Act, Archaeological Resources Protection Act, Paleontological Resources Protection Act, and Federal Caves Protection Act -- that normally require environmental review, habitat/species protection, and preservation safeguards before construction affecting protected federal land.
what_changed:
**DHS invoked its statutory waiver authority under Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (as amended by the REAL ID Act) to bypass the above laws and authorize construction of border barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and sensors through Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park -- protected federal and state land; the Center for Biological Diversity called it the first time a broad slate of environmental laws had been waived in a national park.** DHS had already awarded a $1.7 billion contract in May 2026 explicitly described as 'for border wall through Big Bend.' A subsequent waiver signed by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took effect July 27, 2026, extending the covered project area across the Border Patrol's Big Bend and Del Rio sectors.

Update 2026-10-05: Bulldozers were seen clearing land inside Big Bend National Park in August 2026, drawing bipartisan calls to stop; activity in the park was then paused, a pause that expired September 30, and the first border wall panels in the Big Bend sector went up in mid-September. On October 2, 2026, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction blocking construction of the wall and related infrastructure across the roughly 500-mile Big Bend sector, including the national park, ruling that the plaintiffs were "likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit" and likely to suffer "serious, irreparable harm" without an injunction. According to Marfa Public Radio, the order also suspended the Big Bend sector waivers while it remains in effect.

primary_proponent.name: Markwayne Mullin
primary_proponent.note: Signed the July 27, 2026 waiver extending the project area to the full Big Bend and Del Rio sectors; the initial June 2026 waiver was issued under DHS during the same border-infrastructure push.

corporate_beneficiaries: Contractor(s) awarded the $1.7 billion border-construction contract for the Big Bend project (specific firm not identified in reporting reviewed)

estimated_health_impact.summary: The waivers let construction on protected national park and state park land skip the environmental review, endangered-species protection, water-quality safeguards, and archaeological/paleontological/historic-preservation review that would otherwise apply; land inside the national park was cleared in August 2026 before a federal court temporarily halted construction in October.

The lawsuit (Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and a river guide) argues the waivers exceed DHS's authority; on October 2, 2026 the court granted a preliminary injunction halting construction and, according to Marfa Public Radio, suspending the Big Bend sector waivers pending a ruling on the merits, so the waivers' legality is still unresolved.

rule_name: CFPB overdraft-fee cap rule (Regulation Z / Regulation E updates for large-bank overdraft services)
status: Fully Repealed (CRA Disapproval)
date_of_action: 2025-03-27 (Senate vote) through 2025-05-09 (Trump signature)
original_rule_summary: Finalized by the CFPB on December 12, 2024, the rule closed what the agency called an 'overdraft loophole' in the Truth in Lending Act for banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets. It required those institutions to either cap overdraft fees at $5, cap fees at a level justified by their own cost data, or treat overdraft lines as consumer credit subject to standard lending disclosures (APR, terms) under Regulation Z. The rule was scheduled to take effect October 1, 2025. The CFPB estimated it would **save consumers up to $5 billion a year in fees, or about $225 per year for the roughly 23 million households that pay overdraft fees annually**.
what_changed: Congressional Republicans moved to kill the rule under the Congressional Review Act (CRA) before it could take effect. The Senate voted 52-48 on March 27, 2025 to pass a CRA joint resolution disapproving the rule. The House followed with a 217-211 vote on April 9, 2025. President Trump signed the resolution into law on May 9, 2025, formally nullifying the rule. Because it used the CRA rather than a normal rulemaking repeal, the disapproval also bars the CFPB from issuing any 'substantially similar' overdraft rule in the future without new statutory authorization from Congress -- a broader and more durable rollback than a simple rule withdrawal would have been.

primary_proponent.name: Senate and House Republican leadership (CRA joint resolution sponsors)
primary_proponent.role: Introduced and passed the CRA disapproval resolution in both chambers
primary_proponent.note: President Trump signed the resolution May 9, 2025, formally enacting the repeal; the CFPB itself, under acting leadership installed by the Trump administration, did not defend the rule during the CRA process.

corporate_beneficiaries: Banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets, the institutions the rule would have covered (broadly; no specific institution named in reporting reviewed)

estimated_health_impact.summary: The repeal preserves banks' ability to charge overdraft fees above the $5/cost-based cap the CFPB rule would have imposed on large institutions, at the direct expense of the consumer savings the rule was designed to produce -- roughly $5 billion a year industry-wide, or about $225 per year for a household that regularly overdrafts.

Both figures are the interested party's own projection (CFPB's for the rule, OMB's against it), not an independent third-party estimate; no post-repeal empirical study of actual fee revenue or consumer cost was identified in reporting reviewed.

rule_name: CFPB Payday Lending Underwriting Rollback
status: Fully Repealed (ability-to-repay provisions; final rule July 2020, effective Oct. 20, 2020). The surviving payment-withdrawal limits took effect March 30, 2025, but CFPB said it would not prioritize penalties under them; a planned rule to reconsider them had not been proposed as of Sept. 2026.
date_of_action: 2019-02-06 (proposed); 2020-07-07 (finalized)
original_rule_summary: 2017 CFPB rule (under Director Richard Cordray) requiring payday and short-term title lenders to verify a borrower's actual ability to repay a loan before issuing it -- an underwriting requirement developed over 5 years of CFPB research, aimed at preventing debt-trap cycles from loans with APRs often exceeding 390%.
what_changed: **The Trump-era CFPB proposed and later finalized removal of the ability-to-repay ('underwriting') provisions, while leaving in place separate provisions restricting how lenders can debit a borrower's bank account.** Acting Director Mick Mulvaney delayed the 2017 rule before it could take effect, and on February 6, 2019 the CFPB under Director Kathy Kraninger formally proposed dropping the underwriting provisions. A senior CFPB official, speaking to reporters on condition of anonymity, said the decision stemmed from a concern that there was not enough evidence that payday lending was unfair and abusive enough to require the rule -- even though the 2017 rule rested on five years of CFPB research and had declared lending without a reasonable ability-to-repay determination an unfair and abusive practice. In that 2019 proposal, the bureau estimated that dropping the underwriting requirements would raise payday lenders' annual revenue by about $3.4-3.6 billion and vehicle-title lenders' by about $3.9-4.1 billion. The CFPB finalized the rescission on July 7, 2020 (published July 22, 2020; effective October 20, 2020); the final rule itself acknowledged studies suggesting that the repeat borrowing the 2017 rule had limited could lead to overdraft and NSF fees, involuntary checking-account closures, financial instability, and effects on stress and related health measures. The surviving payment provisions -- which bar a lender from trying again to withdraw money from a borrower's account after two consecutive attempts fail for insufficient funds, unless the borrower gives new authorization -- were held up by industry litigation and finally took effect on March 30, 2025. Two days earlier, on March 28, 2025, the CFPB announced it would not prioritize enforcement or supervision actions over penalties or fines under those provisions. CFPB's 2026 regulatory agenda (released July 6, 2026) then designated the remaining provisions of the 2017 rule, including their compliance dates, for a further rulemaking, categorized as deregulatory under Executive Order 14192, with a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking anticipated for July 2026. As of late September 2026, no such proposal had been published in the Federal Register, so the payment provisions remain in effect on paper.

primary_proponent.name: Mick Mulvaney
primary_proponent.note: Initiated the delay and rollback process starting in 2018; publicly called the CFPB a 'sick, sad joke' and had proposed abolishing it as a congressman. Documented as having accepted campaign donations from payday lenders; during his tenure the CFPB dropped its lawsuit against four tribe-owned payday lenders and ended its investigation of installment lender World Acceptance Corporation. The 2019 proposal and 2020 final rule were issued under his successor, Kathy Kraninger.

corporate_beneficiaries: Payday and short-term title lenders, including Select Management Resources, Advance America, and Check Into Cash, several of which donated to Trump's inaugural committee

estimated_health_impact.summary: Payday and car-title borrowers lost the requirement, before it ever took effect, that lenders check they could repay before lending, leaving open the repeat-borrowing debt trap the 2017 rule was built to stop; CFPB had found that more than 80% of payday loans are rolled over or followed by another loan within two weeks. CFPB's own 2020 final rule acknowledged studies suggesting such reborrowing can bring overdraft and NSF fees, involuntary account closures, financial instability, and effects on stress and related health measures. In money terms, CFPB's 2019 proposal estimated that dropping the underwriting requirements would add about $3.4-3.6 billion a year to payday lenders' revenue and $3.9-4.1 billion to vehicle-title lenders' -- roughly $7 billion a year, largely borrower fees, that the 2017 rule would have kept from lenders. The account-debiting limits that survived took effect in March 2025, but the CFPB said it would not prioritize enforcement actions seeking penalties or fines under them.

The health linkage comes from studies CFPB cited generally, not a rule-specific quantified health or mortality estimate. Does not capture the effect of CFPB's 2025 decision not to prioritize penalties or fines under the surviving payment provisions.

rule_name: Public Lands Order 7923 -- 20-year mineral withdrawal creating a 10-mile no-drilling buffer around Chaco Culture National Historical Park
status: Proposed Repeal -- draft environmental assessment published, public comment closed July 29, 2026; no final decision announced as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-03-31 (BLM formally proposes revocation) through 2026-07-29 (public comment period closes); final decision pending
original_rule_summary: In June 2023, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland finalized a 20-year mineral withdrawal barring new oil, gas, coal, and uranium leasing on roughly 336,000 acres of federal land within a 10-mile buffer of Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in New Mexico containing more than 7,500 known historic and 145 cultural properties sacred to multiple tribal nations. The withdrawal followed two and a half years of assessment, 150 days of public comment, and eight public meetings.
what_changed: **On March 31, 2026, BLM formally proposed revoking the 20-year withdrawal, opening a seven-day online public scoping period for an environmental review -- far shorter than the original withdrawal's 150-day comment process.** BLM published a 140-page draft environmental assessment roughly three months later, after gathering about 70,000 comments during the scoping window, and opened a 14-day comment period (closing July 29, 2026) rather than holding public hearings. The agency is weighing three options: leave the withdrawal in place, shrink the buffer from 10 miles to 5 miles, or revoke it entirely and reopen all ~336,000-338,690 acres to leasing; BLM's own draft EA estimates full revocation could yield the equivalent of more than 2.2 million barrels of oil over 20 years, opening the door to up to 14 new wells. New Mexico's congressional delegation (Sens. Heinrich and Lujan, Reps. Leger Fernandez, Stansbury, and Vasquez) publicly objected to the compressed timeline and to Secretary Burgum's unfulfilled commitment to individual tribal consultation meetings, citing polling showing over 70% of New Mexico voters oppose the reversal. Tribal reaction is not unanimous: the Chaco Heritage Tribal Association, representing five tribal nations, opposes the revocation -- Laguna Pueblo tribal historic preservation officer Richard Smith Sr. said 'when an agency asks tribes for knowledge and then builds its decision without it, the injury is not administrative' -- while Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren supports rescinding the buffer, since many Navajo allottees hold mineral rights and stand to gain drilling royalties inside the buffer zone; some Navajo landowners had blocked access to Chaco in 2023 to prevent Haaland from attending the withdrawal's celebration. No final decision had been announced as of mid-September 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: BLM, under Burgum, proposed and is administering the revocation review; New Mexico's delegation says Burgum committed to individual tribal consultation meetings that have not been fully carried out.

corporate_beneficiaries: Oil and gas companies holding or seeking leases within the 10-mile Chaco buffer, and Navajo allottees with mineral rights inside the withdrawal area who stand to gain drilling royalties if it is revoked or shrunk

estimated_health_impact.summary: Revoking or shrinking the buffer would reopen land adjacent to a UNESCO World Heritage Site containing thousands of documented cultural and archaeological properties to oil and gas leasing, a cultural-heritage and tribal-sovereignty harm rather than a direct public-health standard rollback; the administration's own draft analysis quantifies the extraction upside but not any offsetting cost.

rule_name: Clean Power Plan repeal and replacement with the Affordable Clean Energy (ACE) Rule
status: Fully Repealed and replaced
original_rule_summary: 2015 Obama-era EPA rule setting the first-ever national carbon dioxide emission limits for existing power plants, aimed at cutting power-sector greenhouse gas emissions roughly 32% below 2005 levels by 2030.
what_changed: EPA repealed the Clean Power Plan outright and replaced it with the much weaker Affordable Clean Energy Rule, which set no binding numeric emissions targets and instead directed states to require only modest efficiency upgrades ('heat rate improvements') at individual coal plants, explicitly rejecting the prior rule's system-wide approach of shifting generation toward cleaner sources. Update: EPA also rescinded the 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding in February 2026, targeting motor-vehicle GHG standards specifically rather than this entry's power-plant rule -- see the separately-tracked "endangerment-finding-rescission-trump2" entry for full detail (litigation status, EPA's cost claims, National Academies' rebuttal). Noted here only as broader legal-context for the regulatory environment this rule now sits in, not as a second rollback of the ACE Rule itself.

rule_name: U.S. Financial Regulators' Participation in Climate-Related Financial Risk Oversight (NGFS Membership and FSOC's Climate-Risk Committees)
agency: Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, Treasury Department (Federal Insurance Office), Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC), FHFA
status: Fully Repealed
original_rule_summary: The Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) is a global coalition of financial regulators that develops shared climate-risk scenarios and analysis to help member institutions assess how climate change threatens financial stability; U.S. members included the Federal Reserve, the OCC, the FDIC, Treasury's Federal Insurance Office, and FHFA. Separately, FSOC -- the interagency body chaired by the Treasury Secretary that monitors systemic financial risk -- maintained two dedicated bodies, the Climate-related Financial Risk Committee (CFRC, staff-level) and the Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC, outside experts), created to inform FSOC's assessment of climate change as a threat to U.S. financial stability.
what_changed: Starting just before Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, U.S. federal regulators left the NGFS one after another: the Federal Reserve Board announced its withdrawal January 17, 2025, saying NGFS's work had 'increasingly broadened in scope, covering a wider range of issues that are outside of the Board's statutory mandate'; the FDIC followed January 21, saying 'the work of NGFS is not within the FDIC's authorities and mandate'; Treasury's Federal Insurance Office withdrew January 30, saying NGFS's initiatives were 'inconsistent with this Administration's priorities to grow the U.S. economy and American jobs'; and the OCC withdrew February 11, with Acting Comptroller Rodney Hood saying participation 'extends well beyond the OCC's statutory responsibilities.' Then, **at its September 10, 2025 meeting, FSOC -- chaired by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent -- voted unanimously to rescind the charters of both CFRC and CFRAC outright, eliminating the interagency body's dedicated climate-risk monitoring infrastructure entirely.** According to the meeting minutes, Bessent introduced the vote 'in recognition of the fact that the Council does not consider climate change a financial stability risk or relevant to the Council's work,' and said rescinding the charters would let the Council 'better focus its attention and resources on core financial stability issues.' Days later, FHFA Director William Pulte announced on September 19, 2025 that FHFA was withdrawing from the NGFS too, and FHFA said September 25 it had completed the withdrawal, with Pulte stating 'Biden drove housing costs up with politicized nonsense that prioritized climate activists over American families.' Congressional Democrats pushed back on the committees' rescission: 46 House members, led by Reps. Juan Vargas and Sean Casten, sent Bessent an October 24, 2025 letter demanding answers on the committees' disbandment and urging the Council to reconsider, and Senate Banking Committee Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren cited the rescission in a December 10, 2025 letter to Bessent faulting FSOC's retreat from its mission. Separately, in a letter released December 11, 2025, Bessent called more broadly for loosening FSOC's general oversight function -- beyond the climate-specific committees already rescinded -- saying 'too often in the past, efforts to safeguard the financial system have resulted in burdensome and often duplicative regulations,' without detailing specific proposed changes to FSOC's designation authority or other tools. CBS News reported the call came amid mounting financial-stability concerns critics cited as reasons for caution rather than deregulation, including potential AI-related stock-valuation risk and recent bankruptcies of Tricolor Holdings, First Brands, and Renovo Home Partners. Oscar Valdés Viera of Americans for Financial Reform said 'what you're removing is the smoke alarm for the entire financial system,' and Sen. Elizabeth Warren said loosening safeguards 'just as cracks are emerging in the financial system and yellow lights are flashing across our economy is especially reckless.' Treasury and the White House did not respond to CBS News's requests for comment. In March 2026, a GAO review of the banking agencies' NGFS membership found the Fed, OCC and FDIC had cited changed agency priorities and their statutory mandates in withdrawing, had spent only staff time on the network, and, according to agency officials, had never adopted NGFS recommendations or shared nonpublic supervisory data.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Bessent
primary_proponent.note: Directed and chaired the September 10, 2025 FSOC vote to dissolve both climate-risk committees. The earlier NGFS withdrawals were agency-level decisions not attributed to Bessent personally: the Federal Reserve's (January 17, 2025, three days before the inauguration), the FDIC's (January 21), Treasury's Federal Insurance Office's (January 30) and the OCC's (February 11). They reflect the same policy shift he later directed at FSOC.

estimated_health_impact.summary: No direct health or mortality pathway is documented: these were monitoring and coordination bodies, not rules governing any industry's conduct or emissions. What was lost is regulators' shared capacity to track how climate-driven disasters -- $746.7 billion in U.S. billion-dollar weather and climate disaster losses from 2020 to 2024 -- could spill into insurance, housing and credit markets that households depend on: FSOC's staff committee, which drew staff from all 15 Council members to pool climate data and scenario analysis; its outside-expert advisory committee; and U.S. regulators' seats in the NGFS's shared climate-scenario work. Bessent said the Council does not consider climate change a financial-stability risk. On the savings side, GAO found NGFS membership had cost the banking agencies only staff time.

figures.source: NOAA NCEI billion-dollar disaster data, as cited in the October 24, 2025 letter from Reps. Vargas, Casten and 44 colleagues

figures.metric: Cost of U.S. banking agencies' NGFS membership (what withdrawal saved)
figures.value: Staff time only; no funding provided to NGFS

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No agency, GAO or independent estimate quantifies harm from losing these monitoring bodies; the $746.7 billion figure measures total disaster losses the committees were tracking, not damage caused by their removal. GAO described the banking agencies' participation and reasons for leaving but did not assess what supervisory capacity was lost. The harm, if any, would show up as unanticipated climate-driven stress in insurance, mortgage or bank markets, which no one has modeled for this rollback.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of withdrawals and the FSOC vote -- each NGFS exit is documented in the withdrawing agency's own release, and the vote in Treasury's FSOC meeting readout and minutes, with Reuters and the Congressional letters confirming the committees were dissolved; GAO's March 2026 review confirms the three banking agencies' exits. This entry combines several formally separate agency-level actions (a series of NGFS withdrawals plus one FSOC vote) under one entry because they represent a single policy shift on the same subject matter; treat each action's date carefully if citing this entry, since they were not simultaneous. Bessent's broader December 11, 2025 call to loosen FSOC's general oversight function is HIGH confidence, directly sourced to CBS News's own dedicated report, including the named critics' quotes (Valdés Viera, Warren) and the specific bankruptcies cited as context. This is a distinct, broader move than the climate-committee rescission this entry otherwise documents -- included here as a related development by the same chair of the same body, not as the same specific action.

status: Delayed/Paused (deadline extension finalized 2026-02-10) + Proposed Repeal (broader weakening proposed 2026-04-09, not yet finalized)

original_rule_summary: EPA's 2024 'Legacy CCR Rule' extended federal coal ash monitoring, cleanup, and closure requirements to hundreds of older, previously-unregulated coal ash disposal sites -- 'legacy' impoundments and 'CCR Management Units' (CCRMUs) -- covering roughly half of all coal ash waste ever generated in the US, following a 2015 rule that only covered active sites. EPA identified over 1,000 dumpsites across 42 states requiring monitoring, closure, or remediation.
what_changed: In a Feb. 10, 2026 final rule, EPA extended deadlines for ~110 coal-fired generating units and 189 disposal sites: the deadline to begin closing older coal-ash dump sites (CCR management units) moved from May 2029 to February 2032, and groundwater monitoring from May 2028 to February 2031 -- a roughly 3-year delay -- while the facility evaluations meant to find those sites were pushed back one year. Separately, on April 9, 2026, EPA proposed a much broader rule that would exempt the majority of these dumpsites from federal oversight entirely, alter the definition of 'beneficial use,' and let permit authorities make site-specific determinations on groundwater monitoring points and cleanup levels.

corporate_beneficiaries: Owners of coal-fired power plants and disposal sites, who EPA's own final rule estimates will save $8.1-30 million per year from the deadline extension alone

rule_name: Corporate Transparency Act Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting Rule
status: Finalized -- interim final rule in effect since March 21, 2025 exempting domestic companies from reporting
date_of_action: 2025-03-02 (non-enforcement announced) through 2025-03-21 (interim final rule published)
original_rule_summary: The Corporate Transparency Act, enacted in 2021 with an implementing rule that took effect in 2024, required roughly 32 million U.S. companies to report their true beneficial owners to the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), aimed at preventing anonymous shell companies from being used for money laundering, terrorism financing, and sanctions evasion.
what_changed: On March 2, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Treasury would not enforce any penalties or fines against U.S. citizens or domestic reporting companies (or their beneficial owners) under the CTA, and would narrow the rule's scope to foreign reporting companies only. FinCEN's March 21, 2025 interim final rule formalized this: it exempted all domestic entities and their beneficial owners from reporting entirely, and removed any requirement for foreign entities to report their U.S. beneficial owners. The change reduced the number of companies required to report from roughly 32 million to under 12,000 -- more than 99% of previously-covered entities exempted. **NOTUS reported the rollback came despite documented evidence that Mexican drug cartels and Chinese money launderers have used anonymous U.S. shell companies to launder fentanyl-trafficking proceeds, cutting against the administration's own stated anti-fentanyl priorities.** A subsequent GAO report found Treasury's expanded exemptions created gaps in the beneficial-ownership information the CTA was designed to collect.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Bessent
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the non-enforcement decision on March 2, 2025, calling it 'a victory for common sense' and framing it as part of the administration's agenda to reduce regulatory burdens on small businesses.

corporate_beneficiaries: Domestic shell-company formation and registered-agent industry, broadly -- no single named company or trade group was identified as the driver in sourcing reviewed

estimated_health_impact.summary: Not a direct health-impact rule -- the CTA is a financial-transparency/anti-money-laundering measure. Its rollback is estimated instead by the scale of exempted reporting (over 99% of previously-covered companies) and a GAO-documented information gap; NOTUS's reporting links that gap to law-enforcement concerns that cartels and money launderers exploit anonymous shell companies to hide fentanyl-trafficking proceeds, a public-safety rather than a direct-health harm.

rule_name: Deregulatory Fast-Track Memo ("Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations")
agency: White House / OMB (directs all executive departments and agencies)
status: Fully Enacted (in effect, ongoing)
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- builds on Executive Order 14219 ('Ensuring Lawful Governance...'), issued Feb. 19, 2025, which had directed agencies to identify 'unlawful and potentially unlawful' regulations within a 60-day review period.
what_changed: This Presidential Memorandum instructs agencies to repeal regulations they determine are 'facially unlawful' without going through the normal notice-and-comment rulemaking process, by invoking the Administrative Procedure Act's 'good cause' exception (normally reserved for genuine emergencies). It targets regulations agencies believe conflict with 10 specific recent Supreme Court decisions, including Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024, overturning Chevron deference), West Virginia v. EPA (2022, establishing the 'major questions doctrine'), and Sackett v. EPA (2023, narrowing WOTUS). Within 30 days after the review period, agencies must submit a one-page summary to OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) for each regulation identified as unlawful, then move to repeal.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Issued the memorandum personally on April 9, 2025, the same day as EO 14270 (the sunset rule mandate, tracked separately) and an EO on showerhead water pressure standards.

corporate_beneficiaries: Regulated industries broadly across all sectors where agencies determine a rule is 'unlawful' under the cited Supreme Court decisions -- a cross-cutting structural mandate rather than a sector-specific rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Severe systemic risk by design: **bypassing notice-and-comment eliminates the primary formal mechanism by which public health advocates, toxicologists, affected communities, and other stakeholders can submit evidence or objections before a rule is repealed**. This is a procedural harm distinct from any single rule's substantive content -- it changes how rules can be undone, not just which rules.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health impact figure exists for the memo itself, since it is a process mechanism enabling repeal of other rules, not a rule targeting a specific pollutant or practice. Its harm is best argued as procedural (loss of public input) rather than via a body-count claim. Downstream rules repealed under its authority may have their own quantified figures in other entries of this tracker.

confidence_note: Strong 'process is the harm' entry, similar in category to EO 14192 and the sunset rule mandate. The specific mechanism here -- invoking APA 'good cause' to skip notice-and-comment based on an agency's own legal judgment that a rule is 'unlawful' -- is a distinct and arguably more aggressive procedural shortcut than either of the other two structural entries, since it removes public input entirely rather than just accelerating repeal volume or adding expiration dates. rule_name: Dodd-Frank Asset Threshold Amendment (Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act / S.2155)
status: Fully Repealed (legislative rollback of Dodd-Frank provisions)
original_rule_summary: Post-2008 Dodd-Frank Act (2010) required banks with $50 billion or more in assets to undergo enhanced Federal Reserve oversight: company-run stress tests, enhanced liquidity requirements, resolution plans ('living wills'), and heightened supervision, on the theory that failures at this scale posed systemic risk.
what_changed: S.2155 raised the asset threshold for enhanced prudential standards from $50 billion to $250 billion, exempting all but the largest US banks. Banks with $50-100B in assets were exempted immediately; banks with $100-250B were exempted after 18 months (with Federal Reserve discretion to re-impose standards). This was the most significant legislative rollback of Dodd-Frank since its passage.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Primary Senate sponsor and drafter was Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID), Senate Banking Committee Chair. Passed Senate 67-31 (bipartisan) and House 258-159.

corporate_beneficiaries: Regional and super-regional banks with $50-250B in assets, including Comerica, Zions, BB&T, SunTrust, Fifth Third, and Silicon Valley Bank

estimated_health_impact.summary: Indirect/systemic: increases financial system volatility risk, which correlates with mental health and economic-stability harms during downturns rather than a direct physical health pathway. This is not purely theoretical -- **the Roosevelt Institute directly traces mechanisms of the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapse to the stress-test and liquidity exemptions this law created for banks in the $50-250B range**.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No formal quantified mortality/illness estimate exists for this rollback, as is typical for financial (rather than environmental/health) regulation -- the strength of this entry is the documented causal chain to an actual bank failure (SVB, 2023), not a modeled health figure.

confidence_note: This is legislation, not a unilateral executive rollback -- note the mechanism is different from most other entries in this tracker. Strongest framing: cite the direct causal chain to the Silicon Valley Bank collapse as a real-world materialized harm, rather than an abstract 'increases risk' claim. rule_name: DOE cancellation of clean energy manufacturing/project grants, including admitted targeting by state political identity
status: Ongoing -- a federal court has ruled part of the cancellations illegal (Mehta's January 2026 order and the June 2026 settlement together restored 18 awards worth $109.7 million), two further coalition suits remained pending as of August 2026, and the broader rollback (223 projects, $82.9B) continues per a July 2026 BlueGreen Alliance analysis.
date_of_action: 2025 (grant cancellations begin) through 2026-07 (court admission and BlueGreen Alliance analysis)
original_rule_summary: Biden-era clean energy incentives -- including manufacturing and project grants funded through the Inflation Reduction Act and related programs -- had been awarded or were pending to hundreds of clean energy and manufacturing projects nationwide, including in Republican- and Democratic-leaning states alike, based on standard DOE project-merit review criteria.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0371): the earliest documented wave in this pattern, predating the political-targeting revelation by over a year. On May 28, 2025, DOE announced it was terminating $3.7 billion across 24 clean energy and decarbonization grants funded by the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law, nearly 70% of them signed between Election Day 2024 and Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration; Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated at the time the projects 'failed to advance the energy needs of the American people, were not economically viable and would not generate a positive return on investment of taxpayer dollars' -- the same merit-based rationale this entry's later DOE court-filing admission (below) directly contradicts. The 24 cancellations included $500 million for a Heidelberg Materials carbon-capture project at a cement plant in Mitchell, Indiana, $330 million for an ExxonMobil clean-hydrogen project, $540 million for Calpine, and $375 million for an Eastman Chemical plastics-recycling project; Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla wrote Wright condemning the cancellations, including $845 million cut from California projects specifically, and called for reinstatement. A September 2025 Washington Post follow-up on the Heidelberg cancellation's local impact in Mitchell -- describing the same May 2025 award, not a separate later cancellation -- found industry figures warning the loss ceded carbon-capture-cement leadership to China and Europe. A July 14, 2026 analysis by the labor-and-environmental coalition BlueGreen Alliance found that **223 clean energy manufacturing and project awards, representing $82.9 billion in investment and 111,765 projected jobs, have been delayed or canceled during Trump's second term**, attributing the rollback to Trump's tax and spending law (which repealed or curtailed Biden-era clean energy incentives) and other administration actions reducing federal support for renewable energy and electric vehicles. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0634): on October 2, 2025 -- nine months before the July 2026 court-filing admission below -- OMB Director Russ Vought announced DOE would terminate roughly $8 billion in previously-approved energy funding, targeting projects in the 16 states that voted for Harris; per a House Appropriations Committee Democrats tally, the terminations hit 136 congressional districts, 108 held by Democrats and 28 by Republicans. Vought's own on-record justification at the time was explicitly partisan -- he called the funding 'Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda' -- even as DOE simultaneously offered the same merit-based framing ('did not adequately advance the nation's energy needs, were not economically viable') that this entry's later court-filing admission contradicts; Vought's October 2025 quote is itself a contemporaneous on-record statement of the same political motive, predating and reinforcing the July 2026 court admission rather than being a separate incident. The $8 billion October 2025 figure and the $7.6 billion July 2026 court-admitted figure are not confirmed to describe the identical set of cancellations -- both target the same 16 Harris-voting states, but no source reviewed reconciles the two totals; treat them as two separately-sourced measurements of the same underlying targeting campaign, not necessarily the same dollar total. Update 2026-09-03: two specific court wins for terminated grantees, both predating this entry's prior 2026-07-27 verification but not previously named here, are now documented -- in January 2026, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ordered DOE to reinstate 7 awards worth $27.6 million to Saint Paul, Minnesota-area plaintiffs; on June 12, 2026, a federal court settlement (a separate but related suit led by a coalition including the American Institute of Chemical Engineers) required DOE to reinstate 11 more awards worth $82.1 million to grantees in New York, Oregon, Connecticut, Minnesota, and Colorado, with DOE agreeing not to contest that a 'primary reason' for the terminations was the awardee being in a 'Blue State.' Two further, more sweeping cases were reported still pending as of August 2026: one from a coalition of states including California and New York, and a separate one from the University of California system. FactCheck.org published an August 2026 analysis ('Wright's Hairsplitting Statements About Canceled Energy Grants in Blue States') concluding Secretary Wright's public merit-based framing does not hold up against DOE's own court admissions -- consistent with, and reinforcing, this entry's existing framing. Separately, in court filings unsealed around July 25, 2026, federal lawyers acknowledged that the Department of Energy canceled $7.6 billion in grants for clean energy projects specifically located in the 16 states that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election -- an admission that the cancellations were based 'solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state,' contradicting Energy Secretary Chris Wright's repeated public statements that the projects were canceled because they failed to adequately advance national energy needs or represented poor investments. DOE's own lawyers acknowledged using keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy, and COVID-19 to screen projects for cancellation. A federal court has since ruled that the administration illegally blocked billions of dollars in clean energy grants to Democratic-leaning states.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: Publicly and repeatedly stated the grant cancellations were based on projects' merits and national energy needs -- a claim DOE's own lawyers subsequently contradicted in court filings, acknowledging the cancellations were based on the political identity of the recipient state. OMB Director Russ Vought, who announced the October 2025 $8 billion round of terminations, is the more directly on-record source for the actual political motive -- he called the funding 'Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda' at the same time Wright and DOE offered the merit-based framing.

corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Clean energy manufacturing and project cancellations reduce competing capacity and investment in renewable energy and electric vehicle manufacturing, indirectly benefiting incumbent fossil-fuel-aligned energy interests, consistent with this tracker's related entry on offshore wind/coal taxpayer-funded rollbacks.

A federal court has ruled the administration illegally blocked billions in grants to Democratic-leaning states, and a court order and a settlement have so far required DOE to reinstate 18 awards worth $109.7 million.

rule_name: Biden-era pause on new LNG export authorizations (imposed January 2024, pending DOE review of climate and economic impacts)
status: Fully Repealed (pause ended; serial export authorizations issued, including CP2 LNG's final authorization)
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (pause ended) through 2025-10-22 (CP2 LNG final export authorization)
original_rule_summary: In January 2024, the Biden administration paused DOE approval of new LNG export authorizations to non-Free Trade Agreement countries, pending a review of the climate, economic, and national security impacts of continued LNG export expansion -- affecting several proposed Gulf Coast terminals, including Venture Global's CP2 LNG project in Cameron Parish, Louisiana.
what_changed: President Trump ended the Biden-era LNG export pause on his first day in office (January 20, 2025). DOE, under Secretary Chris Wright, subsequently issued a series of LNG export authorizations, including a conditional authorization for CP2 LNG in March 2025, followed by FERC's approval of the facility's siting and construction in May 2025, and DOE's final non-FTA export authorization for CP2 LNG on October 22, 2025, permitting exports of up to 3.96 billion cubic feet per day. Assistant Secretary of the Office of Fossil Energy Kyle Haustveit said finalizing the authorization would 'enable secure and reliable American energy access for our allies.' DOE stated **the Trump administration has authorized more than 13.8 Bcf/d of LNG exports in total since ending the pause, exceeding the export volume of the world's second-largest LNG supplier**. The same week as CP2's final authorization, Trump administration officials and Qatar sent a joint letter pressuring the European Union to roll back new EU climate and human-rights due-diligence rules, arguing they threaten LNG imports and 'European economic stability' -- a related but separate diplomatic pressure campaign not itself a U.S. domestic regulatory action, and not otherwise documented in this entry.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright, Secretary of Energy
primary_proponent.note: Signed the CP2 LNG final export authorization under President Trump's direction to end the Biden-era LNG export pause; Assistant Secretary Kyle Haustveit is the specific official quoted on the authorization's rationale.

corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Direct beneficiary of the CP2 LNG project's final export authorization, the specific action this entry documents

estimated_health_impact.summary: CP2 LNG, once constructed, is projected to be among the most polluting LNG facilities in the U.S., with lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions exceeding the annual output of dozens of coal-fired power plants, at a time the administration is simultaneously pressuring the EU to weaken its own climate rules to preserve U.S. LNG export markets.
