rule_name: Federal funding and purchase directives for coal-fired power plants -- not a rule rollback in the traditional sense, but a taxpayer-funded market intervention keeping existing coal plants open, restarting a closed one, and backing new ones
agency: Department of Energy / Department of Defense
status: In effect. Executive Order 14386 tells the Pentagon to seek coal power deals. DOE's $525M coal program is fully committed ($175M in February 2026, $350M in June, incl. two planned new plants); a separate $500M in Defense Production Act funds backs 12 coal-plant projects and an Oakland coal terminal.
original_rule_summary: Absent federal intervention, aging coal-fired power plants face economic pressure to retire as they compete against lower-cost natural gas and renewable generation; no specific prior rule is being rolled back here, but this entry documents a market-distorting subsidy analogous in effect to other entries in this tracker that redirect public funds toward favored, less-competitive industries.
what_changed: On February 11, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14386, which directs the Secretary of War, in coordination with the Secretary of Energy, to "seek to procure power from the United States coal generation fleet" through long-term power purchase agreements serving military installations; Trump said "we're going to be buying a lot of coal through the military now," without specifying a volume. At the same event Trump said the Energy Department would "issue funds" to keep coal plants open, and minutes later DOE announced $175 million for six projects to upgrade and extend the life of seven coal-fired plants in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky. Those awards are part of a $525 million DOE coal program that DOE said would draw on unobligated Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funds, including two carbon-capture programs. On June 4, 2026, DOE selected four more projects for up to $350 million, completing the $525 million: planned new coal-fired plants in Anchorage, Alaska and Mt. Storm, West Virginia (2,850 MW combined), a retrofit of a 510-MW coal plant in Guayama, Puerto Rico, and recommissioning a 205-MW Cumberland, Maryland coal facility that shut in 2024. Separately from that program, DOE announced the same day up to $500 million in Defense Production Act Title III funds: up to $425 million for twelve projects to "expand and reinvigorate America's coal fleet" at 13 existing coal plants in Wisconsin, Arizona, North Dakota, Kentucky, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Indiana, Arkansas, Tennessee and West Virginia (federal shares from $19 million to $90.6 million, the largest for East Kentucky Power Cooperative), and up to $75 million for the West Gateway Terminal, a rail-served marine export terminal in Oakland, California, that DOE says will add West Coast export capacity for American coal producers. The administration frames the effort as grid reliability and affordability amid rising electricity demand, and the Defense Production Act awards as national security.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump / Department of Energy
primary_proponent.role: President (executive order directing Pentagon coal power purchases) and DOE (coal program funding)
primary_proponent.note: DOE's announcement of the February awards is titled 'Keeping Affordable Reliable Power Online for Americans,' emphasizing grid reliability and electricity costs rather than climate or emissions considerations.

corporate_beneficiaries: Owners/operators of the coal-fired plants selected for DOE's $525 million coal program (six upgrade projects in February 2026, four build, retrofit or restart projects in June 2026)

Utilities and cooperatives selected for DOE's separate $425 million in Defense Production Act coal-plant awards (June 2026), among them Duke Energy, American Electric Power subsidiaries Southwestern Electric Power Company and Wheeling Power, Alliant Energy, Oklahoma Gas and Electric, Hallador Power and East Kentucky Power Cooperative

The broader U.S. coal-fired generation industry, which benefits from a potential new federal purchaser (the Pentagon, which the order directs to seek long-term coal power deals) and a signal of continued federal support extending plant operational life

estimated_health_impact.summary: Extending the operational life of aging coal plants -- rather than allowing planned retirements to proceed -- means **continued emissions (including particulate matter and greenhouse gases) from generation sources that would otherwise be phased out on market timelines, at direct taxpayer expense** rather than through market competition. DOE's June 2026 coal-program selections go further, backing two planned new coal plants and the restart of a closed one.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: DOE's stated rationale (grid reliability amid rising electricity demand, and national security for the Defense Production Act awards) is a genuine and non-trivial policy consideration independent of any environmental effect; this entry does not evaluate whether the reliability justification is sound, only documents the subsidy's existence, scale, and stated purpose.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- Executive Order 14386 (Pentagon coal power purchases) is confirmed by its White House text; the $175 million for six projects in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky, and the $525 million total program, are confirmed by DOE's own announcement, and The Hill corroborates the $175 million for six projects in those four states. Re-verified 2026-10-06: corrected the state list (four states, not five, with no Virginia project), clarified that the executive order covers Pentagon purchases while the DOE funding came from an existing program, and added DOE's June 2026 $350 million selections and its separate $500 million Defense Production Act selections, both confirmed on DOE's site; no Pentagon coal power deal found in news searches.

rule_name: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review requirements for advanced nuclear reactor authorization, siting, construction, operation, and decommissioning
status: Finalized (categorical exclusion effective immediately upon Federal Register notice, no advance public participation); DOE has since invoked it for at least five test-reactor projects, April to June 2026.
date_of_action: 2026-02-02 (Federal Register notice, effective immediately)
original_rule_summary: Under NEPA, DOE actions authorizing, siting, constructing, operating, reauthorizing, or decommissioning nuclear reactors generally required environmental review, including a written, public assessment of the project's environmental impacts and the possible consequences of a nuclear accident.
what_changed: **DOE announced a new categorical exclusion (CatEx) in the Federal Register on February 2, 2026, effective immediately with no advance public participation, excluding the authorization, siting, construction, operation, reauthorization, and decommissioning of advanced nuclear reactors from major NEPA environmental-review requirements.** DOE cited the inherent safety features and passive safety systems of advanced reactor designs as justification for the categorical exclusion. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, joined by the attorneys general of Washington, New York, New Mexico, Maryland and Massachusetts, opposed the exemption in a comment letter announced March 5, 2026, arguing the policy is illegal under both NEPA and the Administrative Procedure Act. DOE's own listing of determinations shows it has since applied the exclusion to at least five projects between April 14 and June 15, 2026, including Aalo Atomics' Aalo-X critical assembly and Deployable Energy's Unity zero-power test at Idaho National Laboratory, Valar Atomics' Ward250 research reactor in Utah, and Oklo's Groves-1 zero-power reactor facility. Valar's Ward250 reached zero-power fueled criticality on June 18, according to the American Nuclear Society.

primary_proponent.name: U.S. Department of Energy
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency issuing the categorical exclusion
primary_proponent.note: DOE's stated justification rests on advanced reactor designs' inherent safety features rather than a case-by-case environmental review finding.

corporate_beneficiaries: Advanced nuclear reactor developers seeking faster authorization, siting, and construction timelines without individualized environmental impact review
DOE-funded and DOE-partnered advanced reactor demonstration projects

estimated_health_impact.summary: California AG Bonta's coalition argues the exemption shifts environmental review of a future advanced reactor from a public-facing review to a purely internal DOE examination, for reactors it calls 'new and without an established track record,' some of which use 'novel and unproven technologies.' The review being skipped, NPR reports, typically required a written, public assessment of the possible consequences of a nuclear accident.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: DOE frames the exclusion as appropriately calibrated to advanced reactors' passive safety systems, which differ mechanically from the large light-water reactor designs NEPA's existing review framework was built around; no independent safety-agency (e.g., NRC) finding on the CatEx's substantive safety adequacy was identified in sourcing reviewed, and the projects DOE has excluded so far are zero-power critical assemblies and small research or test reactors, not commercial power plants.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the categorical exclusion, its effective date, and DOE's stated justification are confirmed by DOE's own Federal Register notice, reported by NPR (the same NPR story was carried by Houston Public Media, Georgia Public Broadcasting, and KPBS, so those are not independent confirmations). California AG Bonta's formal opposition is confirmed via his office's own press release. Re-verified 2026-10-06: NPR, the California AG release and DOE's notice page still say what the entry says; DOE's own B5.26 determinations listing shows the exclusion applied to five projects from April 14 to June 15, 2026; no court challenge to the exclusion was found.

rule_name: DOE Section 504 New Construction Accessibility Requirements (Rescinding New Construction Requirements Related to Nondiscrimination in Federally Assisted Programs or Activities)
status: Proposed Repeal (issued as a 'direct final rule'; effective date delayed multiple times amid opposition, not yet in effect)
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (rule published in the Federal Register) through 2026-03-09 (most recently reported delayed effective date)
original_rule_summary: Since the 1970s, DOE's implementing regulations for Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 have required that new construction and significant alterations to buildings receiving DOE federal funding -- including at state and local governments, universities, and private entities -- be built or renovated to be accessible to people with disabilities, mirroring the broader civil-rights mandate that recipients of federal funds not discriminate on the basis of disability.
what_changed: On May 16, 2025, DOE published a 'direct final rule' -- a fast-track mechanism agencies use when they expect no significant opposition, which skips standard notice-and-comment rulemaking -- **rescinding these new-construction accessibility requirements entirely, meaning new and renovated buildings receiving DOE funding would no longer be required to meet accessibility standards**. Mother Jones reported the rescission was published quietly with no public input sought in advance. Disability-rights advocates, including the Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF) and the Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies, along with California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office, filed formal 'significant adverse comment' objections -- the specific procedural mechanism that forces a direct final rule into standard notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than taking effect automatically. Those objections, plus continued advocacy pressure, appear to have contributed to DOE repeatedly pushing back the rule's effective date: originally set for July 15, 2025, then delayed to September 12, 2025, then to December 10, 2025, and most recently to March 9, 2026, per Federal Register notices. A law professor quoted by Mother Jones characterized the DOE action as part of a broader pattern of civil-rights rollbacks, and reporting noted the DOE rescission could be a template for similar rollbacks across more than 80 other sets of agency-specific Section 504 regulations government-wide, since each federal agency maintains its own implementing regulations for the statute.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: No specific DOE official is named on record as personally directing the rescission; it is presented in agency filings as an institutional DOE action. Wright is included as the department's accountable head, not as a documented personal driver of this specific rule.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Removing new-construction accessibility requirements for DOE-funded buildings would allow newly built or renovated facilities receiving federal energy funding to be built without accessibility features, affecting building access for people with mobility, sensory, or other disabilities at an unspecified but potentially large number of state, local, university, and private facilities that receive DOE funding.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed provides a quantified estimate of either the dollar cost/savings to funding recipients or the number of disabled individuals or facilities affected -- reporting characterizes the scope only qualitatively ('thousands of buildings,' per Facilities Dive) without a specific figure on either side of the ledger. This entry states that gap explicitly rather than presenting a manufactured figure.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core procedural facts: the direct-final-rule publication date, the specific mechanism used, the formal adverse comments filed by DREDF and California's AG, and the sequence of effective-date delays are all documented directly in Federal Register notices, independently confirmable at federalregister.gov. MODERATE confidence on the rule's ultimate fate -- as of the most recently reported delay (March 9, 2026), the rule had not been formally withdrawn, but repeated delays in the face of adverse comments leave its final disposition genuinely unresolved as of this entry's most recent verification.

rule_name: DOJ Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title III technical-assistance guidance documents
status: Fully Repealed (guidance withdrawn, not replaced)
original_rule_summary: The withdrawn documents were DOJ technical-assistance guidance -- not regulations themselves, but the department's official interpretive explanations of how businesses must comply with ADA Title III (public accommodations). They included a 10-part manual issued in 2005 explaining ADA compliance for business owners generally, plus documents giving specific guidance for hotels/lodging, gas stations, and retail establishments, including COVID-era accommodation guidance.
what_changed: **On March 19, 2025, DOJ's Civil Rights Division formally withdrew 11 ADA Title III technical-assistance guidance documents, citing President Trump's January 20, 2025 memorandum 'Delivering Emergency Price Relief for American Families and Defeating the Cost-of-Living Crisis' as the basis for reducing regulatory-compliance burdens on businesses.** The withdrawal removes DOJ's official interpretive guidance on ADA compliance for hotels, retailers, gas stations, and other public accommodations, leaving businesses to interpret the underlying statute themselves without DOJ's practical compliance explanations.

primary_proponent.name: Mac Warner
primary_proponent.role: Deputy Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Rights Division
primary_proponent.note: Announced the withdrawal in a public statement, framing it as reducing business compliance costs: 'Putting money back into the pockets of business owners helps everyone by allowing those businesses to pass on cost savings to consumers and bolster the economy.'

corporate_beneficiaries: Hotel/lodging industry
Retail and gas-station businesses subject to ADA Title III public-accommodation compliance

estimated_health_impact.summary: Disability-rights advocates warn the withdrawal, by removing DOJ's practical compliance guidance without rescinding the underlying ADA statute, increases the risk that businesses under-comply with accessibility requirements, potentially reducing physical access to public accommodations for people with disabilities and increasing reliance on private litigation rather than proactive compliance to enforce access.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified figure for reduced accessibility, increased litigation volume, or any documented health/safety harm was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's creation -- the impact described by advocates is a risk/framing claim, not yet a measured outcome. The underlying ADA statute and its accessibility requirements remain in force; only DOJ's interpretive guidance explaining compliance was withdrawn.

confidence_note: The withdrawal itself and Mac Warner's quoted rationale are corroborated across Disability Scoop, U.S. News, PhysiciansWeekly, and the ADA Title III legal-industry trade press (adatitleiii.com); the projected accessibility-harm impact is advocacy framing, not yet an independently measured outcome, and should be cited as such.

rule_name: ATF classification of forced-reset triggers (FRTs) as machine guns under the National Firearms Act
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- DOJ ended federal FRT enforcement via a May 2025 litigation settlement, not rulemaking. A multistate challenge was voluntarily dismissed in April 2026 after ATF withheld returns from states that ban FRTs; returns proceeded elsewhere.
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (DOJ-Rare Breed Triggers settlement announced; signed 2025-05-13); 15 states and D.C. sued to challenge it 2025-06-09 and voluntarily dismissed that suit 2026-04-23 after ATF withheld returns from states banning FRTs
original_rule_summary: Starting in 2021, ATF classified certain forced-reset triggers (FRTs) -- aftermarket devices that use a semi-automatic rifle's own cycling action to reset the trigger, enabling rates of fire of hundreds of rounds per minute without full-auto conversion -- as illegal machine guns under the National Firearms Act, and pursued seizure and enforcement actions against manufacturers (including Rare Breed Triggers) and owners nationwide.
what_changed: A Texas federal court (Judge Reed O'Connor, N.D. Tex.) ruled on July 23, 2024, in National Association for Gun Rights v. Garland, that ATF had exceeded its statutory authority in classifying FRTs as machine guns, applying the Supreme Court's June 2024 bump-stock decision in Garland v. Cargill; the government appealed to the Fifth Circuit. Following Trump's February 7, 2025 executive order on Second Amendment rights, Attorney General Pam Bondi created a Second Amendment Task Force on April 8, 2025; after its review, the government stated in the settlement agreement that 'continuing the Litigation ... is not in the public interest.' The agreement, signed May 13 and announced by DOJ on May 16, 2025, resolved the Texas case, DOJ's Eastern District of New York suit against Rare Breed Triggers, and a Utah forfeiture case. DOJ agreed not to enforce federal machine-gun law against possessing or transferring FRTs that work as the Texas court described and are not designed for handguns, and agreed, 'to the extent practicable,' to return FRTs it had seized or taken by voluntary surrender to owners who requested them by September 30, 2025. **ATF had identified at least 11,884 such devices in its possession as of August 2024, according to the states' later lawsuit, and the agreement on its face had no carve-out for owners in states that ban FRTs or for people barred from having guns.** Rare Breed agreed not to develop, design, or market FRTs for handguns, to seek patent-infringement injunctions against other FRT makers at its own expense, and to promote safe use; the United States agreed to consider filing statements supporting those patent suits. On June 9, 2025, 15 states (led by New Jersey, Maryland, and Delaware) and Washington, D.C. sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland; California joined in an amended complaint on July 7. The states argued that returning the devices, including into states where they remain banned, would cause 'irreversible' harms by threatening public safety and driving up law-enforcement and health care costs, and cited ATF's own finding that more than 60 FRTs had previously been shipped to people legally barred from possessing firearms. In a June 26, 2025 sworn declaration, ATF committed not to return FRTs into states where they are illegal (owners there could have a device sent to them or a third party in a state where it is legal, or abandon it for destruction), to run a background check on everyone requesting a return, and to withhold devices tied to criminal cases. After Judge Paula Xinis signaled doubt that the states had standing, they withdrew their preliminary-injunction motion on July 11, 2025, and dropped Rare Breed and the other private defendants later that month. On April 23, 2026, the states voluntarily dismissed the case without prejudice, saying ATF was nearing completion of the returns and had kept those commitments, and reserving the right to sue again; the court closed the case on April 28, 2026. The settlement does not override state bans: ATF's June 2025 declaration listed 17 states plus D.C. where it understood FRT possession to be illegal. On August 31, 2026, DOJ, appearing for ATF, filed a statement of interest in the consolidated Rare Breed patent litigation in the Eastern District of Texas, arguing that because the settlement does not bind other FRT makers, the public interest 'should be weighed heavily' in favor of Rare Breed's bid for a preliminary injunction against them, while taking no position on the other injunction factors; it repeated a January 2026 statement filed in a Tennessee case before consolidation.

primary_proponent.name: Pam Bondi
primary_proponent.note: Bondi created DOJ's Second Amendment Task Force on April 8, 2025, under Trump's February 2025 executive order; after its review, the government stated in the May 2025 nationwide settlement that continuing the FRT litigation 'is not in the public interest.'

estimated_health_impact.summary: Forced-reset triggers, which the states say let a semi-automatic rifle fire 800 to 900 rounds per minute, are no longer subject to federal machine-gun enforcement, so they can be sold without machine-gun restrictions or a background check, and ATF has been returning the devices it seized (at least 11,884 were in its hands as of August 2024) to owners who asked for them. A multistate lawsuit got ATF to withhold returns from states that ban FRTs and to background-check recipients, which narrows but does not remove the risk. For each device returned, the 16 to 24 ATF staff-hours spent retrieving it are undone.

rule_name: Department of Labor's July 2025 Deregulatory Agenda -- 60+ (DOL's own count: 63) Proposed Rule Repeals/Rewrites Spanning Wage, Safety, and Anti-Retaliation Standards Across OSHA, the Wage and Hour Division, and MSHA (an omnibus regulatory agenda, not a single rule)
status: Proposed Repeal (mixed stages) -- the flagship home-care wage/overtime rule was formally proposed July 2, 2025, its public comment period closed September 2, 2025, and as of the most recent reporting reviewed (mid-2026) no final rule had been issued, though WHD paused enforcement against third-party home care agencies on July 25, 2025 pending the rulemaking; the other 60+ proposed changes remain at earlier, individually-varying stages of notice-and-comment rulemaking with no comprehensive public tracker of each one's status found in sourcing reviewed for this entry
date_of_action: 2025-07-01/02 (agenda unveiled; flagship home-care rule formally proposed) through the most recent status reviewed for this entry (2026-07)
original_rule_summary: The rules targeted by this package predate the current administration and were issued independently of one another, including (among others): the Wage and Hour Division's 2013 Home Care Rule, which extended Fair Labor Standards Act minimum-wage and overtime protections to home care workers who had previously been exempt as "companionship services" providers; an OSHA/construction standard requiring adequate lighting in active work areas; MSHA mine-safety requirements; and anti-retaliation and transportation-safety protections for migrant farmworkers. This entry treats them together because DOL itself packaged and announced them together as one deregulatory agenda, not because they share a single underlying rule.
what_changed: On July 1-2, 2025, the Department of Labor under Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer unveiled a deregulatory agenda proposing to repeal or rewrite more than 60 workplace rules (DOL's own count: 63), framed by the administration as eliminating "obsolete" and burdensome regulations. The package spans multiple DOL sub-agencies and touches wage protections, workplace-safety standards, and anti-retaliation safeguards across a wide range of industries. Its most consequential and best-documented single component is **a proposal to rescind the Wage and Hour Division's 2013 Home Care Rule, which extended federal minimum-wage and overtime protections to an estimated 2 million home care workers providing in-home services to seniors and people with disabilities**. DOL formally proposed rescinding the rule on July 2, 2025, and on July 25, 2025 the Wage and Hour Division announced it would stop enforcing the rule's protections against third-party home care agencies even before any final rule issued -- pausing enforcement while the rulemaking proceeded, though the pause does not affect home care workers' ability to sue their employers directly for back wages, overtime, and liquidated damages. The public comment period on the home-care rule proposal closed September 2, 2025, and as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this entry (mid-2026), no final rule had been issued; the 2013 rule remains legally in effect, though practically less enforced. Other components of the same 60+-rule package, per contemporaneous reporting, include eliminating a standard requiring lighting in active construction work areas, reducing mine-safety regulatory requirements, weakening anti-retaliation and transportation protections for migrant farmworkers, and a proposal to remove OSHA's jurisdiction over certain live-entertainment and motorsports venues (reporting cited NASCAR and SeaWorld as examples). AFL-CIO occupational safety and health director Rebecca Reindel publicly criticized the package, saying workers are "at very great risk of dying on the job already" and that the rollback "is only going to make the problem worse." Each proposed rule change must independently complete notice-and-comment rulemaking before taking effect, so the package's ultimate scope and timeline depend on dozens of separate, individually-contested rulemaking processes rather than one administrative action. Chavez-DeRemer, who announced the agenda, resigned as Labor Secretary in April 2026 amid a personal-conduct investigation unrelated to this rulemaking; Keith Sonderling has served as Acting Secretary since and was nominated in June 2026 to hold the position permanently.

primary_proponent.name: Lori Chavez-DeRemer
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Labor (at time of the July 2025 announcement; resigned April 2026 for reasons unrelated to this rulemaking, succeeded by Acting Secretary Keith Sonderling)
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced and framed the deregulatory agenda as eliminating "obsolete" and burdensome regulations.

corporate_beneficiaries: Home care agencies and other third-party employers of home care workers, relieved of FLSA minimum-wage/overtime enforcement risk while the 2013 rule goes unenforced pending the rulemaking
Mine operators, under the package's proposed mine-safety regulatory reductions
Live-entertainment and motorsports venues (reporting cited NASCAR and SeaWorld as examples), under the proposal to remove them from OSHA's jurisdiction

estimated_health_impact.summary: The package's most quantifiable component -- proposing to rescind wage/overtime protections for an estimated 2 million home care workers -- has already been enforcement-paused since July 2025, even before any final rule issues. The other 60+ proposed rule changes (construction lighting, mine safety, farmworker anti-retaliation) carry plausible but not yet independently quantified safety risk; DOL's own cost-benefit analysis of the package's flagship component did not attempt to quantify it either.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: DOL's own Regulatory Impact Analysis for the home-care rule rescission was under 5 pages and included no dollar-figure estimates of regulatory-familiarization costs, hiring-cost changes, or wage transfers from workers to employers, per EPI's formal public comment on the proposal -- meaning even the agency's own analysis does not quantify the financial or health impact of its highest-profile component. No dedicated mortality/injury estimate specific to the construction-lighting, mine-safety, or farmworker-protection components was found in sourcing reviewed for this entry; those effects are documented qualitatively (industry critics warning of increased injury risk) rather than quantified, and should be revisited if a quantified estimate is later published.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the agenda's existence, scope (60+/63 rules), and the flagship home-care rule's timeline (proposed July 2, 2025; enforcement paused July 25, 2025; comment period closed September 2, 2025; no final rule as of mid-2026) -- corroborated across AP, CBS News, PBS NewsHour, Insurance Journal, and EPI's own policy tracking and formal rulemaking comments. LOWER confidence on the individual status of most of the other 59+ proposed rule changes (construction lighting, mine safety, farmworker protections, OSHA/entertainment jurisdiction) -- no comprehensive, dated tracker of each one's individual rulemaking stage was found in sourcing reviewed; this entry documents them as announced proposals, not confirmed outcomes, and should be rechecked or split into dedicated entries if any of them individually finalizes.
short_summary: DOL proposed repealing/rewriting 60+ workplace rules in July 2025, including stripping ~2M home care workers of minimum-wage/overtime protections.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: The clearest quantified harm is ~2 million home care workers losing wage/overtime protections; the other 59+ rules (construction lighting, mine safety, farmworker anti-retaliation) lack a quantified safety estimate in sourcing reviewed.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well-corroborated on the agenda's scope and the home-care rule's timeline; the other rules' individual statuses are not comprehensively tracked in available sourcing.

rule_name: Improving Protections for Workers in Temporary Agricultural Employment in the United States (H-2A Farmworker Protection Rule, 2024)
status: Fully Repealed (enforcement suspended June 20, 2025; formal rescission published in the Federal Register July 2, 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-06-20 (enforcement suspension announced) through 2025-07-02 (formal rescission published)
original_rule_summary: Finalized by the Biden administration in 2024, the rule extended new protections to workers on H-2A temporary agricultural visas (about 400,000 admitted annually as of 2025, roughly 15% of average U.S. crop-farm employment): the right to engage in 'concerted activity' with coworkers to improve working conditions, anti-retaliation protections barring employers from firing or disciplining workers for organizing, defined progressive-discipline/termination standards, and wage-disclosure and payment requirements.
what_changed: On June 20, 2025, DOL's Wage and Hour Division announced it would suspend all enforcement of the rule nationwide, directing field staff to revert to the pre-rule H-2A labor-certification process in effect before the rule's June 27, 2024 effective date. DOL cited a preliminary federal court injunction -- covering Georgia, Kansas, South Carolina, Arkansas, Florida, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia -- and said the resulting patchwork of enforceability across states created legal uncertainty for agricultural employers, framing the suspension as offering clarity rather than a policy reversal. DOL followed the nationwide non-enforcement announcement with a formal rescission of the rule itself, published in the Federal Register on July 2, 2025, eliminating the underlying protections entirely rather than merely pausing their enforcement pending litigation.

primary_proponent.name: Lori Chavez-DeRemer
primary_proponent.note: The Wage and Hour Division's June 20, 2025 field-assistance bulletin and the July 2, 2025 Federal Register rescission were issued as institutional DOL actions; no more specific individual official is named in sourcing reviewed as personally directing the decision beyond the department's own leadership.

corporate_beneficiaries: Agricultural employers using the H-2A visa program, particularly in the 17 states covered by the preliminary injunction, who are relieved of the rule's organizing-protection and progressive-discipline compliance obligations

estimated_health_impact.summary: Rescinding the rule **removes anti-retaliation protections for a workforce of roughly 400,000 H-2A visa holders annually, most of whom cannot easily change employers under the visa's structure and are therefore especially vulnerable to retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions or attempting to organize** -- a labor-safety and workplace-power dynamic rather than a directly quantified health-mortality risk.

figures.metric: H-2A workers admitted annually, scope of workforce losing the rule's protections
figures.source: USDA Economic Research Service / industry reporting, cited in coverage of the H-2A program

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed provides a dollar cost/savings figure for this specific rescission (e.g., an agency compliance-cost estimate) or a quantified injury/fatality-risk figure specific to the loss of anti-retaliation protections -- this entry states that gap explicitly rather than presenting a manufactured figure. The worker-protection figures above describe the scope of the affected population, not a modeled harm estimate.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core procedural facts: the June 20, 2025 enforcement-suspension announcement and the July 2, 2025 Federal Register rescission are both documented in DOL's own public records (a Wage and Hour Division field-assistance bulletin and the Federal Register notice itself), independently confirmed by EPI, Law360, and multiple employment-law-firm client alerts describing the same dates and mechanism. MODERATE confidence on the practical labor-safety impact, since no source reviewed quantifies actual retaliation incidents before or after the rule's brief effective period (June 2024-June 2025); the harm is presented as a removed legal protection for a documented vulnerable workforce, not as a proven increase in retaliation incidents.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: Removes anti-retaliation protections for roughly 400,000 H-2A workers annually; no dollar-cost or injury-rate figure was found for this specific rescission.
section_summaries.confidence_note: The procedural facts are well-documented in DOL's own public records; the practical labor-safety impact is not independently quantified in sourcing reviewed.

rule_name: Overtime Salary Threshold Expansion Rescission
agency: Department of Labor (Wage and Hour Division)
status: Complete (effective May 15, 2026)
date_of_action: 2026-05-14 (announced) / 2026-05-15 (effective)
original_rule_summary: In April 2024, the Biden administration's DOL finalized a rule raising the Fair Labor Standards Act white-collar overtime exemption salary threshold in two phases: to $844/week ($43,888/year) effective July 1, 2024, and to $1,128/week ($58,656/year) effective January 1, 2025, with automatic updates every three years thereafter. The highly-compensated-employee exemption threshold was set to rise to $151,164/year. The rule was projected to make roughly 4.3 million additional salaried workers newly eligible for overtime pay.
what_changed: Two federal district courts in Texas -- the Eastern District in November 2024 and the Northern District in December 2024 -- struck down the 2024 rule before its second scheduled increase took effect, vacating it on the grounds that DOL had over-weighted salary level relative to job duties in defining the exemption. The Trump DOL declined to continue defending the rule on appeal and withdrew the government's appeals; the Fifth Circuit dismissed the two appeals on May 5 and May 7, 2026 without ruling on the merits. On May 14, 2026, DOL announced a technical amendment, published in the Federal Register and effective on May 15, 2026, formally removing the 2024 rule from the Code of Federal Regulations and reinstating the salary thresholds set during Trump's first term in 2019: $684/week ($35,568/year) for the standard exemption and $107,432/year for highly compensated employees. In practice this formalized what had already been happening since the district court rulings, since DOL's Wage and Hour Division had been enforcing the 2019 thresholds since the 2024 rule was vacated.

primary_proponent.name: Andrew Rogers
primary_proponent.role: Administrator, DOL Wage and Hour Division
primary_proponent.note: Signed and publicly announced the technical amendment, framing it as ensuring the exemption's 'duties, salary basis, and salary level requirements' are 'clearly framed' -- i.e., restoring duties-based analysis over the salary-level test the 2024 rule relied on more heavily.

corporate_beneficiaries: Employers across all sectors who would otherwise have had to reclassify salaried employees between roughly $35,568 and $58,656/year as overtime-eligible, or raise their salaries above the new threshold to preserve exempt status -- disproportionately affecting labor-intensive, lower-margin industries such as retail, hospitality, and food service where many managerial-title but modestly-paid positions cluster in that salary band.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Not a health-impact rule; the relevant harm is economic -- **lost overtime eligibility and pay for millions of salaried workers who would have qualified for time-and-a-half compensation under the rescinded 2024 threshold**.

figures.source: DOL Wage and Hour Division news release, May 14, 2026; Federal Register 2026-09839

figures.source: DOL Wage and Hour Division news release, May 14, 2026; Ogletree legal alert

figures.metric: Share of full-time salaried workers currently eligible for overtime by salary alone
figures.source: Sen. Whitehouse press release; Sen. Sanders' office fact sheet on the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026

estimated_health_impact.caveat: The rationale behind the rescission is the one two federal judges accepted when vacating the rule, which DOL's amendment implements as a technical correction rather than arguing it anew: that Congress intended the white-collar exemption to turn primarily on job duties rather than a compensation test, and that the 2024 rule's salary jump effectively substituted a bright-line pay threshold for that duties analysis. The Fifth Circuit, upholding the 2019 rule in 2024, held that DOL may use salary level as a proxy for exempt status, while warning that a proxy which frequently yields different results than the duties Congress chose goes beyond the agency's power. Critics, including the bill's Senate sponsors, argue the rescission simply strips overtime protection from workers who would have newly qualified, and point out that the reinstated $684/week ($35,568/year) threshold is the level set in 2019. Both sides agree the practical effect since late 2024 has been the same: employers have been operating under the 2019 thresholds since the district court rulings, so this technical amendment formalizes an already-realized status quo rather than changing day-to-day practice by itself.

confidence_note: High confidence throughout. The rescission, its effective date, and both salary threshold figures are drawn directly from DOL's own May 14, 2026 news release and corroborated by multiple independent legal-alert summaries (Foley Hoag, Ogletree). The 4.3-million-worker figure originates from DOL's own 2024 rule impact projections, cited secondhand via a Senate office fact sheet; treated as a solid but administration-sourced estimate rather than an independently audited figure. Re-verified 2026-10-05: the Federal Register text confirms the amendment was published and took effect May 15, 2026 (announced May 14), signed by Wage and Hour Administrator Andrew B. Rogers, and that the Fifth Circuit dismissed the two appeals on May 5 and May 7, 2026, from vacatur orders issued by the Eastern District of Texas (November 2024) and the Northern District of Texas (December 2024); no later DOL rulemaking on the salary threshold found. DOL's own news release now blocks automated fetching; Rogers' quote is confirmed via an HRCI summary.
pull_quote: Today, only about 8% of full-time salaried workers are eligible for overtime by salary alone, down from roughly 63% in 1975, according to Sen. Whitehouse's office and Sen. Sanders' office.

section_summaries.what_changed: DOL formally rescinded the 2024 overtime rule after courts vacated it, reverting to 2019's lower salary thresholds for overtime exemption.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Not a health rule -- the harm is economic: millions of salaried workers lose overtime eligibility and pay under the reinstated lower threshold.
section_summaries.confidence_note: High confidence throughout, drawn from DOL's own release; the 4.3-million-worker figure is DOL's own but cited secondhand via a Senate fact sheet.

rule_name: FAST-41 Fast-Track Permitting Designation for the Donlin Gold Mine, Alongside an Unresolved Court Finding That Federal Reviewers Never Analyzed a Tailings-Dam Failure Spill Risk
agency: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers / Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- FAST-41 designation granted while the underlying Supplemental EIS ordered by a federal court remains in progress
date_of_action: 2025-06-10 (federal court remand order) through 2025-10-27 (FAST-41 designation) and ongoing into 2026 (Supplemental EIS)
original_rule_summary: Before this action, the Donlin Gold mine -- a proposed 34-million-ounce gold mine in southwestern Alaska requiring a 471-foot tailings dam to contain mining waste -- had received its federal permits in 2018 through the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' standard environmental review process under the Clean Water Act, without the accelerated FAST-41 interagency-coordination track applied here, and without having been required to specifically analyze the consequences of a large-scale tailings-dam failure spill.
what_changed: On June 10, 2025, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled that **the Army Corps of Engineers had erred in its 2018 permitting review by failing to analyze the potential impacts of a large spill from a possible failure of Donlin Gold's planned 471-foot tailings dam**, remanding the matter back to the Corps; the Corps began a Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement in response, with federal reviewers only beginning to examine large-spill effects as of early 2026 reporting. Despite that unresolved court-ordered environmental gap, the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council granted the Donlin Gold project FAST-41 coverage on October 27, 2025 -- a fast-track interagency permitting-coordination designation -- citing Trump's executive order on 'Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production,' under which the project's roughly 34-million-ounce gold reserve was named. Donlin Gold's own environmental and permitting manager told reporters the FAST-41 designation would likely not actually accelerate the mine's timeline, but gave the company more confidence in reaching a final investment decision by 2027. The designation is part of a broader Trump administration push adding roughly 10 mineral projects nationally (including Perpetua Resources' Stibnite Gold antimony project) to the federal permitting dashboard. Donlin is planned in partnership with Native corporations holding the land and mineral rights, and proponents emphasize jobs, shareholder payments, and village-service funding; but Alaska Native residents in the region, per an AP feature published August 2025, describe the land and the Kuskokwim River watershed in explicitly spiritual and religious terms tied to subsistence salmon fishing, illustrating the community division the fast-tracked review timeline runs alongside without having resolved. This project and its FAST-41 designation are distinct from, though thematically related to, this database's separate anwr-npra-offshore-leasing-expansion-2025-2026.json entry, which covers Arctic oil-and-gas lease sales under a different legal mechanism (statutory reopening of ANWR/NPRA to leasing) rather than FAST-41 critical-minerals fast-tracking.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: His executive order on 'Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production' was the stated basis for Donlin Gold's FAST-41 fast-track permitting designation.

corporate_beneficiaries: NOVAGOLD Resources and Barrick Gold (Donlin Gold's private-investor partners)
Native corporations holding the land and mineral rights in partnership with the project

estimated_health_impact.summary: A federal court found regulators never analyzed the consequences of a large spill from the mine's planned 471-foot tailings dam before the project's original 2018 permits issued; that analysis remains incomplete even as the project received an expedited federal permitting designation, leaving the potential scale of harm to the Kuskokwim River watershed and downstream subsistence salmon fisheries unquantified as of this entry's creation.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified estimate of the actual health/environmental harm from a potential dam failure was identified in sourcing reviewed -- the Supplemental EIS examining that question was only beginning as of early 2026 reporting, so the scale of at-risk harm remains unquantified rather than merely uncited. Donlin's own permitting manager stated FAST-41 likely would not accelerate the timeline in practice, a claim that tempers (without resolving) the concern that fast-track designation might rush past the pending spill-risk analysis.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the court ruling, the FAST-41 designation and its stated executive-order basis, and the Supplemental EIS -- corroborated across Alaska Public Media, Anchorage Daily News, Alaska Beacon, the Permitting Council's own press release, and the Department of the Interior. HIGH confidence on the AP feature's reporting of Alaska Native community reaction, corroborated by wire syndication across CBC, Washington Post, and Religion News Service. MODERATE confidence that the FAST-41 designation itself will materially accelerate the project, given the company's own on-record statement that it likely will not -- this entry documents the designation and the unresolved spill-risk question as the core accountability facts, not a claim that harm is imminent.

rule_name: DOT Safety Rule Rollback Package (30+ Actions Across FHWA, NHTSA, FMCSA, FAA, and PHMSA)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- mix of scrapped, delayed, and enforcement-gutted actions across multiple sub-agencies, not one single rule
date_of_action: 2025-07 through 2025-11 (individual actions dated July-September 2025; ProPublica investigation compiling all 30 published 2025-11-29)
original_rule_summary: A set of 30+ distinct DOT safety rules and enforcement practices spanning multiple sub-agencies: subway/bus driver hours-of-service limits, a motorcycle helmet safety mandate, truck speed limiters, school bus child-restraint crash-protection requirements, aircraft cockpit barrier requirements, freight-train emergency oxygen masks for hazmat crews, heavy-truck side underride guards, seat belt warning systems, automatic emergency braking mandates for trucks and cars, and two pipeline safety proposals (CO2 pipelines and methane-emissions detection), plus the enforcement infrastructure (vehicle-defect investigations, trucking/bus company enforcement cases, pipeline enforcement, PHMSA penalty schedules) that gives those rules teeth.
what_changed: ProPublica identified 30 regulatory actions under Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that current and former DOT officials and safety advocates said conflict with the agency's public-safety mission. Scrapped outright: subway/bus driver hours-of-service limits, the motorcycle helmet mandate, the truck speed-limiter requirement, school bus child-restraint crash-protection rules, and two pipeline safety proposals. Delayed: the aircraft cockpit barrier requirement, freight-train emergency oxygen masks, heavy-truck side underride guards, seat belt warning systems, a pedestrian-protection vehicle safety rating update, and automatic emergency braking mandates. Alongside the rule actions, enforcement collapsed: vehicle safety defect investigations down 50%, enforcement cases against trucking/bus companies down 83%, pipeline enforcement cases down 58%, and PHMSA penalties per violation dropped roughly 98% (from about $475,000 per 30 days to about $8,000 per 30 days). PHMSA Deputy Administrator Ben Kochman, a former director of the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America, personally signed 23 deregulatory proposals -- more than the entire four-year Biden administration total -- including a proposal to triple the property-damage threshold that triggers pipeline incident reporting and questioning drug/alcohol testing requirements for pipeline workers. PHMSA Chief Counsel Keith Coyle previously fought pipeline safety regulations as an industry lawyer through 2023. ProPublica identified 32 total DOT appointees with industry ties, 11 of whom held recent disclosed investments of $12-52 million in transportation/energy company stock. DOT itself, in parallel public announcements, described this as intentionally 'slashing red tape' across FHWA, NHTSA, and FMCSA, and separately told the Washington Examiner it had removed more than 140,000 words from the Federal Register and saved a claimed $1.3 billion across 157 deregulatory actions.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy
primary_proponent.note: Publicly framed the effort as removing bureaucratic obstacles ('We want D.C. bureaucrats OUT of your trucks'); DOT's own press office promoted the same actions ProPublica's investigation scrutinized as a deliberate 'slashes red tape' initiative.

corporate_beneficiaries: Trucking industry (speed limiters, automatic emergency braking, and side underride guard rollbacks)
Pipeline operators (PHMSA penalty and reporting-threshold rollbacks; Deputy Administrator Ben Kochman is a former Interstate Natural Gas Association of America director)
Motorcycle industry (helmet safety mandate scrapped)

estimated_health_impact.summary: ProPublica's investigation aggregated the safety agencies' own prior modeling for five of the 30 targeted rules and found **they could together prevent up to 1,000 deaths and 40,000 injuries annually if kept in place** -- separate from the harder-to-quantify effect of the enforcement collapse (50-83% fewer investigations/cases across categories) on rules that remain on the books but are no longer meaningfully enforced. DOT's own $1.3 billion savings figure, by contrast, is a self-reported industry-compliance-cost estimate, not independently verified.

rule_name: Wheelchair Rule (Ensuring Safe Accommodations for Air Travelers With Disabilities Using Wheelchairs, 49 CFR Part 382, finalized December 2024)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed)
original_rule_summary: A Biden-era DOT rule, finalized December 17, 2024 under Secretary Pete Buttigieg, made mishandling of passengers' wheelchairs and scooters a violation of the Air Carrier Access Act. It required airlines to accept liability for damaged, delayed, lost, or stolen mobility devices; reimburse fare differences when a passenger's device could not fit on their booked flight; give passengers written notice of their rights when checking a device; and provide annual refresher training for staff who handle wheelchairs and assist disabled passengers.
what_changed: DOT announced on September 29, 2025 (Federal Register notice published September 30, 2025) that it will exercise enforcement discretion and not enforce several of the rule's provisions -- initially reported as covering airline liability for mishandled wheelchairs, fare-difference reimbursements, and written rights notifications, with a DOT spokesperson describing the agency as reevaluating whether those provisions 'adhere to statute or if they are redundant.' A later DOT filing extended the non-enforcement window (through April 30, 2027 for some provisions) and broadened it to five specific provisions, adding the rebuttable presumption for damaged checked wheelchairs and the annual refresher-training requirements for ground staff and flight attendants. DOT says it is pursuing a replacement rulemaking rather than a repeal. The move follows a February 14, 2025 petition to the Fifth Circuit by American, Delta, JetBlue, Southwest, and United, plus trade group Airlines for America, seeking to have the rule -- or specific provisions of it -- set aside as exceeding DOT's statutory authority.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation
primary_proponent.note: No DOT official is named on the record as personally deciding the enforcement pause; a DOT spokesperson speaking for the department, under Duffy, is the only on-record attribution found in sourcing. Duffy is included here as the accountable office-holder, per this tracker's institution-proxied-attribution convention, not because he personally signed or announced it.

rule_name: 2009 Endangerment Finding rescission
status: Fully Repealed
date_of_action: 2026-02-12 (finalized); published 2026-02-18; effective 2026-04-20
original_rule_summary: 2009 EPA scientific and legal finding, based on peer-reviewed climate research, that greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare -- this finding is the legal foundation obligating EPA to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and stationary sources under the Clean Air Act.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0500): on July 29, 2025 -- the same day Administrator Zeldin announced this rescission proposal -- the Department of Energy released a report attacking the scientific basis for climate regulation, authored by five longtime climate-science skeptics (Steve Koonin, John Christy, Ross McKitrick, Judith Curry, and Roy Spencer) convened as an internal DOE 'Climate Working Group.' The report was not peer-reviewed before release. Texas A&M climate scientist Andrew Dessler helped organize a volunteer effort by more than 85 international climate experts to produce a public, point-by-point rebuttal (a 439-page document, per CBS News), submitted to DOE during the public comment period that closed September 2, 2025. The Environmental Defense Fund and Union of Concerned Scientists separately sued, alleging the working group's formation violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act by not disclosing its existence for months and by selecting only members who would produce a one-sided argument. DOE dissolved the Climate Working Group by a letter from Energy Secretary Chris Wright dated September 3, 2025 (reported by CNN on September 10) but declined to withdraw the report itself. Despite this scientific groundwork, EPA's eventual final rule (below) dropped the climate-science-based rationale the DOE report was meant to support, resting the rescission purely on statutory interpretation and the major questions doctrine instead -- meaning the report's scientific claims were never actually tested in, or formally relied upon by, the final agency action, even as the administration continued to point to it publicly during the proposal phase. When EPA proposed the rescission on July 29, 2025, its announcement claimed the proposal would 'save more than $54 billion annually'; Reuters reported on July 30, 2025 that lawyers and trade groups warned the specific legal approach EPA was taking could backfire, creating regulatory uncertainty and litigation risk for companies that had already made multibillion-dollar compliance investments under the standards being repealed, and that the proposed repeal of vehicle standards was reportedly broader than industry anticipated, also covering air-conditioning efficiency testing and battery monitoring/durability requirements, not just tailpipe standards. Separately, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine released a consensus report on September 17, 2025 -- commissioned specifically in response to EPA's rescission proposal -- **concluding that the evidence for current and future harm to human health and welfare from human-caused greenhouse gas emissions is 'beyond scientific dispute,' and that the 2009 Endangerment Finding's original conclusion has been reinforced, not undermined, by evidence accumulated since 2009.** EPA finalized the rescission of the 2009 Endangerment Finding anyway, on February 12, 2026 (published Feb 18, effective April 20, 2026), removing the legal foundation for EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles under CAA Section 202(a). As part of the same final action, EPA also repealed all GHG emission standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles and engines (model years 2012 through 2027+), eliminating future measurement, control, and reporting obligations for manufacturers -- including retroactively for vehicles already manufactured. EPA's final rule notably dropped its earlier proposed climate-science-based rationale entirely, resting the rescission purely on statutory interpretation (that CAA Section 202(a) does not authorize regulation based on global climate change concerns) and the major questions doctrine. NOTE: this action substantially overlaps with the separately-tracked 'ldmv-ghg-standards-repeal-trump2' entry in this database -- both describe the same vehicle-standards repeal, which occurred as part of this single final rule rather than as two separate actions. Recommend merging or cross-referencing these two entries. Update: on April 8, 2026, Zeldin defended the rescission at a Heartland Institute conference -- a think tank that rejects mainstream climate science -- telling attendees to 'celebrate vindication' and framing the repeal as reversing decades of 'unthinking adherence to liberal politicians and environmental groups' on climate change; Heartland president James Taylor called Zeldin 'the greatest EPA administrator ever.' Environmental groups criticized the appearance as EPA's own administrator publicly aligning with climate-denial advocacy rather than the agency's own prior scientific findings. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0609): an E&E News (POLITICO) review published October 20, 2025 found that four of the report's five authors had spoken out against the endangerment finding and that at least three had ties to groups that have long criticized energy regulations and have collectively received millions of dollars in funding from fossil fuel industry groups or foundations that oppose regulations -- Roy Spencer affiliated with the Heartland Institute and Heritage Foundation, Ross McKitrick a fellow at Canada's Fraser Institute and affiliated with the Cato Institute, and Steve Koonin's prior work through the Hoover Institution focused specifically on opposing the endangerment finding. Industry-aligned advocacy groups (the Competitive Enterprise Institute, WattsUpWithThat) publicly disputed a separate Politico critique of the report's hurricane science as itself misleading, making the report's underlying scientific merit a genuinely contested question between advocacy groups on both sides, distinct from the funding-ties finding, which rests on E&E News's reporting of the authors' institutional affiliations rather than a scientific judgment. Update 2026-09-26: The final rule's Federal Register preamble (Feb 18, 2026) says EPA 'is no longer monetizing benefits from PM2.5 and ozone', and acknowledges that the agency had relied on the 2009 finding to extend greenhouse gas regulation to power plants under Clean Air Act section 111, although the rescission itself covers only the section 202(a) motor-vehicle program. EPA's economics fact sheet for the final rule says the 'over $1.3 trillion in savings' covers 2027 through 2055 and consists of about $1.1 trillion in reduced costs for new vehicles plus $200 billion in avoided costs of EV chargers and related equipment. FactCheck.org reported on March 17, 2026 that the $1.3 trillion 'is not a net total': it leaves out offsetting costs, primarily higher fuel and maintenance costs, and does not factor in any health or environmental benefits, and 'in no case is there a net savings of $1.3 trillion.' Per FactCheck.org, most of EPA's modeled scenarios still show a net savings, but in its scenario using the Energy Information Administration's reference fuel-price forecast, the repeal costs Americans $180 billion on net; only two of EPA's four scenarios at a 3% discount rate top $1.3 trillion in avoided costs, and at 7% they never exceed $870 billion. The same article quoted NYU's Jason Schwartz citing an Environmental Defense Fund analysis that estimated up to 58,000 more premature deaths and as many as 37 million more asthma attacks through 2055 from repealing the standards. On March 19, 2026, a coalition led by the attorneys general of New York, Massachusetts, California and Connecticut, joined by 24 states in all plus the District of Columbia and several cities and counties, petitioned the D.C. Circuit (No. 26-1061); the court consolidated it with American Public Health Association v. EPA (No. 26-1037). On Sept 17, 2026, EPA finalized a repeal of most provisions of the 2024 power-plant carbon standards, on what it called 'distinct legal and technical grounds', and in a concurrent supplemental proposal argued that section 111 'does not authorize the EPA to regulate emissions from power plants in response to global climate change concerns', which would rescind the 2015 power-plant findings and repeal all 2015 and 2024 power-plant GHG standards (comments due Nov 2, 2026).

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA itself described this as 'the single largest deregulatory action in U.S. history.' Trump directed EPA to evaluate the finding's legality via executive order on his first day in office (Jan 2025); Zeldin formally recommended reconsideration by March 2025.

corporate_beneficiaries: Fossil fuel producers and fossil-fuel-dependent power generators broadly, as the finding underlies multiple downstream emissions rules
Vehicle and engine manufacturers, who EPA states no longer have future GHG measurement/control/reporting obligations for any highway vehicle, including past model years

estimated_health_impact.summary: The rescission removes the legal foundation for EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles, and the same action repealed all vehicle GHG standards, even though the National Academies concluded that the evidence of current and future harm to human health from human-caused greenhouse gas emissions is 'beyond scientific dispute.' EPA says the rescission will save Americans over $1.3 trillion, but that is its claimed gross avoided cost for 2027-2055 (about $1.1 trillion in new-vehicle costs plus $200 billion in EV chargers and related equipment), not a net figure: EPA's analysis counts no health or environmental benefits, and its own scenarios show higher fuel and maintenance costs that partly or fully offset the savings (per FactCheck.org). FactCheck.org concluded that 'in no case is there a net savings of $1.3 trillion.' EPA's preamble says the agency had relied on the 2009 finding to extend greenhouse gas rules to power plants, but the rescission itself covers only the section 202(a) motor-vehicle program. Power plants are being handled in separate rulemakings: on Sept 17, 2026, EPA finalized a repeal of most provisions of the 2024 power-plant carbon standards on 'distinct legal and technical grounds' and proposed a parallel theory that Clean Air Act section 111 does not authorize regulating power-plant emissions 'in response to global climate change concerns.'

rule_name: 10-for-1 Regulatory Repeal Mandate (Executive Order 14192, "Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation")
agency: White House / OMB (governs all federal agencies)
status: Fully Enacted (in effect, ongoing)
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- this is a new process mandate. It revives and escalates the approach of the first Trump administration's 2017 EO 13771, which required a 2-for-1 repeal ratio and was revoked by President Biden's EO 13992 on January 20, 2021.
what_changed: Requires every federal agency to identify at least 10 existing regulations (broadly defined to include guidance documents, memoranda, and policy statements, not just formal APA rules) to repeal for every 1 new regulation proposed. Also requires that the total incremental cost of all new regulations in FY2025 be 'significantly less than zero,' effectively mandating net deregulation by volume and cost simultaneously. Exempts military, national security, homeland security, foreign affairs, and immigration-related regulations, agency organization and personnel rules, and categories the OMB Director exempts.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed personally on January 31, 2025, eleven days into his second term; builds on and escalates his own first-term EO 13771 (2-for-1), revoked in 2021.

corporate_beneficiaries: Regulated industries broadly across all sectors -- this is a cross-cutting structural mandate rather than a sector-specific rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Severe systemic/structural risk: by design, this EO prioritizes repeal volume and aggregate cost reduction over case-by-case risk assessment of which specific protections get cut, **creating pressure to eliminate rules based on their cost to industry rather than their public health or safety value**.

figures.value: About $211.8 billion in present and future regulatory costs (present value as of 2024; Treasury $128.6B, DHS $47.7B, HHS $19.3B of the total)
figures.source: OMB/OIRA, Final Accounting for Fiscal Year 2025 (Table 1)

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health impact figure exists for the EO itself, since it is a process mandate rather than a rule targeting a specific pollutant, product, or practice -- its harm is best argued structurally (the mechanism itself deprioritizes public-health benefit analysis) rather than with a body-count claim. Downstream rules repealed under its authority may have their own quantified figures (see other entries in this tracker). Outcome figures are the administration's own: OIRA's final accounting for fiscal year 2025 says agencies 'far exceeded the 10 for 1 requirement' in the administration's first eight months, issuing 646 deregulatory actions against 5 significant regulatory actions (129 to 1), and that regulations eliminated in 2025 will save about $211.8 billion in present and future costs. A March 2026 analysis by George Washington University's Regulatory Studies Center argues the ratio counts every deregulatory action (428 of them guidance and other non-CFR documents) against only significant new rules, and that the largest share of the savings comes from formally retiring items that were already obsolete, such as Treasury's IRS notices ($128.6 billion, 61% of the total); it concludes the results mostly reflect reduced regulatory output, while 'true deregulation remains elusive.'

confidence_note: This is one of the strongest 'process is the harm' entries in the tracker -- the EO's text itself, not a critic's characterization, establishes that repeal volume/cost savings are the stated goal, independent of the safety value of any given rule. Good for framing a systemic argument distinct from any single rollback. Re-verified 2026-10-05: the Federal Register text still carries the 10-for-1 rule, the 'significantly less than zero' FY2025 cost cap and the listed exemptions; OIRA's reginfo.gov page reports FY2025 results under the order and says FY2026 agency cost allowances are still to be released; no court challenge or revocation found.

rule_name: EPA's March 12, 2025 Announcement of 31 Simultaneous Deregulatory Actions -- 'The Greatest Day of Deregulation in Our Nation's History'
status: Announced (each of the 31 individual actions proceeded on its own separate rulemaking timeline afterward -- see the specific-rule entries this announcement launched)
original_rule_summary: Before this announcement, EPA administered dozens of separate Biden-era and earlier environmental regulations across air, water, and climate policy -- including the 2009 endangerment finding underpinning EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gases, power-plant and vehicle emissions standards, mercury and toxics limits, PFAS drinking-water standards, the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the Clean Air Act's interstate 'Good Neighbor' pollution provision, and the agency's practice of weighing health costs from storms, wildfires, and droughts in its own rulemaking.
what_changed: **On March 12, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced 31 deregulatory actions in a single day, calling it 'the greatest day of deregulation our nation has seen'** and stating the agency was 'driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion to drive down the cost of living.' The targeted list spanned the 2009 endangerment finding for greenhouse gases, vehicle emissions/fuel-economy standards, coal-fired power-plant carbon and mercury limits, oil-and-gas-sector methane rules, coal-plant wastewater discharge limits, the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the Clean Air Act's interstate 'Good Neighbor' provision, and EPA's practice of considering climate-linked health costs (from storms, wildfires, droughts) in its own cost-benefit rulemaking, among other targets. Framed as a single package, the announcement functioned as a roadmap rather than a set of completed actions -- each individual rule then proceeded on its own separate proposal/finalization timeline over the following year. The announcement itself, not any single rule within it, is documented here because of its scale, its status as the stated organizing framework for the administration's broader environmental deregulatory program, and the bipartisan condemnation it drew on its own terms.

primary_proponent.note: Personally announced all 31 actions in a single press event, framing them explicitly in ideological terms ('a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion') rather than as individually justified technical rulemakings.

corporate_beneficiaries: Fossil-fuel and coal-power-generation industries broadly, per EcoWatch's framing of the announcement as 'the day Trump's Big Oil megadonors paid for' -- a characterization from Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, not an EPA-sourced or independently quantified claim

rule_name: EPA's Decision to Stop Monetizing Public-Health Benefits in Air Pollution Rulemaking
status: Finalized -- adopted as part of a new final rule on power-plant emissions, with EPA stating it will apply the same non-monetization approach to future air-pollution rulemakings generally
original_rule_summary: For decades, EPA's cost-benefit analyses for air-pollution rules have assigned a dollar value to avoided deaths, illnesses, and hospitalizations from reduced ozone and fine-particulate (PM2.5) pollution, using an established methodology (the 'value of a statistical life' framework) to weigh regulatory costs against quantified public-health benefits -- these monetized health benefits have historically been the largest benefit category justifying stricter air-pollution standards.
what_changed: On January 12, 2026, EPA announced it would no longer assign an economic value to lives saved or health improved when justifying air-pollution rules, unveiling a final rule under the Clean Air Act that simultaneously revised (weakened) nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission limits for new gas-burning turbines at power plants and industrial facilities. EPA's new regulatory language stated the agency would stop monetizing public-health benefits from reduced ozone and fine-particulate pollution because, in EPA's words, its 'historical analytical practices often provided the public with false precision and confidence' -- **even while the agency's own rule acknowledged that these pollutants contribute to pulmonary disease, heart attacks, and premature death**. EPA characterized the change as applying beyond this single rule to its air-pollution rulemaking generally going forward, meaning future rules would be justified without counting the dollar value of avoided illness and death as a benefit, structurally shifting the cost-benefit balance toward looser standards across the agency's future air-pollution decisions.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA finalized the policy change under Zeldin's leadership as part of the same broader deregulatory program including the March 2025 31-rule announcement and the February 2026 endangerment-finding rescission.

corporate_beneficiaries: Power plant and industrial-facility operators facing future air-pollution rulemakings, whose compliance costs would no longer be weighed against a monetized health-benefit figure

estimated_health_impact.summary: This is a methodological change to how EPA justifies air-pollution rules, not a rule permitting a specific quantity of additional pollution -- but because monetized health benefits have historically been the dominant benefit category in EPA's cost-benefit analyses, removing them structurally weakens the case for stricter future air-pollution standards across the board, independent of any single rule's specific numbers.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed quantifies an aggregate future health impact from this methodological shift, since its effect depends on which specific future rules it is applied to and how; the entry documents the structural policy change itself, which multiple public-health and environmental-law observers (Human Rights Watch, EDF, the University of Chicago's Air Quality Life Index project) characterize as highly consequential precisely because of its generality.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across The Washington Post, NBC News, Human Rights Watch, OPB/GBH (NPR member stations), the Environmental Defense Fund, and the University of Chicago's Air Quality Life Index project, all reporting the same January 12, 2026 announcement and EPA's own quoted 'false precision and confidence' rationale.
