rule_name: EPA civil/criminal enforcement and compliance monitoring of environmental laws against polluters -- including Clean Water Act violations specifically (not a specific rule -- documents an enforcement-practice collapse achieved without formally repealing underlying statutes/rules)
agency: EPA / DOJ (DOJ files civil enforcement referrals on EPA's behalf)
status: Ongoing as of Sept. 2026: DOJ civil suits for EPA fell to a record-low 16 in Trump's first year back, and EPA now favors fine-free compliance orders under a Dec. 2025 "compliance first" policy. Congress rejected the proposed 54% FY2026 EPA budget cut, instead trimming it about 4%.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 to 2026-01-20 (first year of Trump's second term); Environmental Integrity Project report published 2026-02-05
original_rule_summary: Historically, DOJ files civil court complaints on EPA's behalf against companies found violating environmental laws (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and related statutes), a routine enforcement mechanism independent of any specific rule needing to change.
what_changed: On March 12, 2025, EPA's acting enforcement chief issued a memo requiring a political appointee's advance approval for any enforcement action that would "unduly burden or significantly disrupt" energy production or power generation, according to the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP). The administration's fiscal 2026 budget request, released in spring 2025, proposed cutting EPA's budget by about 54%, including a 30% cut to civil enforcement ($61.1 million cut from $201.3 million), a 49% cut to criminal enforcement ($29.6 million cut from $60 million), a 35% cut to compliance monitoring ($38 million from $107.1 million) and cuts of roughly 90% to the Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Funds, per a Holland & Knight analysis of the request. Congress later rejected the proposed overall cut; EIP reported in February 2026 that Congress had instead reduced EPA's fiscal 2026 budget by $325 million (about 4%) from fiscal 2025. The New York Times reported August 8, 2025, citing a six-month analysis by EIP, that DOJ filed just 11 civil lawsuits against major polluters in the first six full months of Trump's second term, compared with 30 in the same period under Biden, and reached only 18 settlements in such cases compared with 53. On December 5, 2025, acting enforcement chief Craig Pritzlaff issued a "compliance first" memo directing EPA staff to favor compliance assistance over formal enforcement, raising the bar for findings of violation, requiring political sign-off for most monitoring and third-party audit requirements, and ending supplemental environmental projects that benefit communities harmed by polluters (EIP said the memo prohibited them; Inside Climate News said it paused them). A February 2, 2026 report by the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative (EDGI) found that 14 of the 24 EPA enforcement measures it tracked were at their weakest or second-weakest level in 20 years in 2025, and that EPA launched fewer civil judicial cases in 2025 than under any administration in that span. EIP's February 5, 2026 report found DOJ filed just 16 civil complaints in EPA-referred cases in the 12 months after Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, a historic low: 76% below Biden's first year (67), 81% below Trump's first year in 2017 (86) and 87% below the first year of Obama's second term (127). Judicial settlements fell to 40, from 112 in Biden's first year and 186 in 2013. EPA's administrative case settlements rose compared with Biden's and Trump's first-term first years, driven mainly by Clean Air Act risk-management-plan and Safe Drinking Water Act cases, but only 50% of them carried a penalty, and administrative penalties assessed from Inauguration Day through September 30, 2025 totaled $41 million, about $8 million (16%) less than the same period of Biden's first year after adjusting for inflation. As of January 2026, 3,001 facilities were listed in "significant noncompliance" with the Clean Water Act for at least three years and 697 had unresolved high-priority air violations dating back more than 34 months, yet over the prior year only 12% of facilities with air-pollution violations and 2% with water-pollution violations received any federal or state enforcement action. NPR and Inside Climate News, citing an E&E News analysis, reported that at least a third of lawyers in DOJ's environment division had left in the past year. An EPA spokesperson called EIP's report "erroneous" and said EPA had concluded more cases in the first year of the Trump administration than the Biden administration had in its last year. In March 2026, EPA's fiscal 2025 enforcement results claimed 2,127 concluded civil cases, the most in nine years; that fiscal year included the last three and a half months of Biden's term. On March 18, 2026, Earthjustice's enforcement director countered that EPA's own data showed the fewest judicial case conclusions in at least a decade, and that of more than $650 million in civil penalties EPA touted, only $1.45 million (under 1%) came from judicial settlements filed and entered under Trump. In June 2026, DOJ renamed its Environment and Natural Resources Division, which had lost more than a quarter of its workforce, the Energy and Natural Resources Division, with a mission of "advancing U.S. energy dominance," Inside Climate News reported. An Inside Climate News analysis of EPA data published September 1, 2026 found that EPA had lost more than a quarter of its workforce by the end of June; that its administrative actions had flipped from roughly 60% penalty orders to mostly compliance orders that impose no fine; that the median total cost to offenders of an administrative action had fallen to its lowest since 2000; and that orders telling public water systems to inventory lead service lines made up more than a third of all administrative orders, at a median cost below $600. EPA responded that it had concluded more than 2,300 enforcement actions in the first year, a 10-year high. The decline was achieved through enforcement policy, staffing and case choices rather than formal rule repeal: the underlying standards remain on the books but are enforced far less.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA called the Environmental Integrity Project's report "erroneous"; its March 2026 fiscal 2025 enforcement results claimed 2,127 concluded civil cases, the most in nine years, a count critics say is built on administrative orders and Biden-era cases.

corporate_beneficiaries: Industrial polluters and regulated entities facing substantially reduced likelihood of federal civil enforcement action for Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and related violations

estimated_health_impact.summary: Companies breaking air and water pollution laws now face far less chance of being stopped or fined, which leaves nearby communities exposed to illegal pollution for longer. As of January 2026, 3,001 facilities had been in significant noncompliance with the Clean Water Act for at least three years, and over the prior year only 2% of facilities with water-pollution violations and 12% with air-pollution violations faced any federal or state enforcement. Court cases, which bring the largest penalties and court-backed cleanup orders, fell to a record-low 16 in Trump's first year back. Penalties shrank too: EPA now relies mostly on compliance orders with no fine, and the orders against water systems over lead-pipe inventories cost offenders a median of under $600. Polluters that skip compliance save money that law-abiding competitors spend. All of this weakens environmental protection without any rule repeal, public comment period or judicial review.

rule_name: Copper Rule (EPA emissions standards for primary copper smelters, finalized May 13, 2024 under Clean Air Act Section 112)
agency: EPA / White House (Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) presidential exemption authority)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- two-year compliance exemption, not a rule rescission
date_of_action: 2025-10-24 (proclamation reported; White House fact sheet same period)
original_rule_summary: EPA finalized the Copper Rule on May 13, 2024 under Clean Air Act Section 112, imposing stricter emissions limits on the only two primary copper smelters operating in the U.S. -- Freeport-McMoRan's Miami, Arizona smelter and Rio Tinto's Utah smelter -- covering toxic air pollutants including lead, arsenic, mercury, benzene, and dioxins.
what_changed: President Trump issued a proclamation under Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) -- a rarely-used provision letting the President exempt a stationary source from a Section 112 standard for up to two years if compliance technology is unavailable and exemption serves the national security interest -- granting Freeport-McMoRan's Arizona smelter a two-year exemption from the Copper Rule's compliance deadlines. The proclamation stated 'the technology to implement the Copper Rule is not available' in a 'commercially viable form' to meet the rule's deadlines, and that preserving domestic smelting capacity was essential to critical-minerals access in a crisis; the accompanying White House fact sheet said imposing the requirements on 'such a limited and already strained domestic industry risks accelerating further closures.' Freeport-McMoRan said the exemption 'provides needed time to assess and plan for appropriate regulatory reconsideration of the Copper Rule.' Rio Tinto's Utah smelter was not affected, as the company had already invested in emissions-capture equipment to comply. This is the same Section 112(i)(4) mechanism -- and, per ProPublica reporting, the same email-based exemption-request process EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin invited industry to use -- already documented in this tracker's epa-ethylene-oxide-sterilizer-emissions-rollback-2026.json entry, where it was applied to exempt 40 sterilization facilities (roughly 45% of that industry) from a different Section 112 rule; this is a second, independently-documented industry where the same national-security exemption authority was invoked to delay compliance with toxic-emissions standards.

rule_name: Ethylene Oxide Emissions Standards for Sterilization Facilities (NESHAP Residual Risk and Technology Review)
status: Delayed/Paused + Proposed Repeal -- a July 17, 2025 proclamation exempts 40 facilities (~45% of the industry) from the 2024 rule for two years; a D.D.C. challenge awaits a ruling on threshold dismissal issues. EPA's March 17, 2026 proposal to rescind much of the rule is not yet final.
date_of_action: 2025-07-17 (proclamation exempting 40 facilities, ~45% of industry, for two years); 2026-03-17 (broader repeal proposed) -- comment period on the broader proposal subsequently extended to 2026-05
original_rule_summary: A 2024 EPA rule tightened emissions standards for ethylene oxide (EtO) -- a chemical used to sterilize medical equipment and classified as a potent human carcinogen -- at commercial sterilization facilities nationwide. EPA projected the rule would cut annual EtO emissions from these facilities by roughly 90% by 2027, and it required larger sterilizers (those using at least 10 tons of EtO per year) to install stronger emissions-control technology and implement continuous monitoring.
what_changed: On March 17, 2026, EPA proposed rescinding significant portions of the 2024 EtO rule. The proposal argues EPA overstepped its legal authority under Clean Air Act Section 112(f)(2) when it performed a new residual-risk review as part of the 2024 rulemaking, and on that basis would rescind the tighter risk-based emissions standards the 2024 rule imposed. The proposal would additionally relax technology-based emissions standards specifically for facilities using at least 10 tons of EtO per year and rescind the requirement that larger chemical sterilizers implement continuous emissions monitoring. AP reported the 2024 rule had targeted nearly 90 commercial sterilization facilities across the country. EPA extended the public comment period on the proposal to May 15, 2026. Separately -- and preceding the March 2026 proposed rescission -- President Trump signed Proclamation 10959 on July 17, 2025 (published in the Federal Register July 23, 2025), invoking Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) national-security authority to exempt 40 sterilization facilities, roughly 45% of the industry, from the 2024 rule's compliance deadlines for two years. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin had invited companies to email the agency directly to request exemptions. The Southern Environmental Law Center and NRDC, representing environmental groups in North Carolina, Georgia, and Virginia, sued Trump, EPA, and Zeldin in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (filed late January 2026, per MedTech Dive reporting), arguing the Clean Air Act permits this kind of exemption only when compliance technology is unavailable or genuine national-security interests are at stake -- not as a general deregulatory tool. Added 2026-09-11: the same Section 112(i)(4) national-security exemption authority was separately invoked on Freeport-McMoRan's Arizona copper smelter in October 2025, tracked in its own entry on the copper smelter exemption -- a second, independently-documented industry where this mechanism delayed toxic-emissions compliance.

Sourcing reviewed did not separately identify a specific named official driving the March 2026 proposed rescission beyond the agency's own legal-authority rationale in that proposed rule -- the two actions are distinct and this note attributes each accordingly.

rule_name: Fenceline air-monitoring and emissions-reporting reform for coke ovens, chemical plants, and other high-risk industrial sources (multiple NESHAP rules requiring real monitors in place of industry self-estimated 'emission factors')
status: Trump granted U.S. Steel's Clairton Coke Works and other coking plants a two-year exemption from fenceline benzene-monitoring requirements; EPA separately halted planned permanent-monitor requirements at 130+ industrial plants nationwide and granted two-year exemptions to roughly 50 chemical plants, while beginning formal 'reconsideration' of three underlying fenceline-monitoring rules. No reversal of these actions had been identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry.
date_of_action: 2025 (exemptions and rule-reconsideration begin following Trump's January 2025 inauguration) through 2025-11-04 (ProPublica's investigation published)
original_rule_summary: For decades, EPA allowed industrial facilities -- including coke ovens, chemical plants, and other high-risk sources -- to estimate their own air-toxics emissions using standardized 'emission factors' rather than direct measurement, despite EPA itself acknowledging since 1990 that many of these factors, particularly for coke ovens, were 'poor' or 'below average' in accuracy. Biden-era NESHAP rules moved toward requiring real fenceline (perimeter) air monitors at the highest-risk facility types specifically to replace this self-reported 'honor system' with actual measured data and to trigger corrective action when measured concentrations exceeded action levels.
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation published November 4, 2025 found that when EPA required 20 industrial facilities to install temporary fenceline monitors in 2023, actual measured emissions exceeded company self-reported estimates in 97% of cases, often dramatically: benzene at U.S. Steel's Clairton Coke Works (Pittsburgh) measured 37 times higher than estimated; vinyl chloride at a Dow Chemical plant in Plaquemine, Louisiana measured 156 times higher, with ethylene dichloride at the same facility measuring 1,033 times higher; ethylene dichloride at a Formosa plant in Point Comfort, Texas measured 69 times higher; and ethylene oxide at an Indorama plant in Port Neches, Texas measured 7 times the EPA's own new standard. Following Trump's inauguration, EPA halted requirements for permanent fenceline monitors at more than 130 industrial plants nationwide, granted two-year compliance exemptions to roughly 50 chemical plants, and began formally 'reconsidering' three of the underlying fenceline-monitoring rules. U.S. Steel separately applied for its own exemption for the Clairton plant -- obtained by ProPublica via public-records request -- arguing the fenceline benzene-monitoring requirement was too stringent given 'many miles of piping and thousands of valves and flanges at a coke facility' that would be costly and complex to fully seal. President Trump subsequently granted Clairton and other coking plants nationwide a two-year exemption from the fenceline benzene-monitoring requirement specifically. **EPA's own modeling found the new monitoring-triggered standards would have reduced the number of people facing unacceptable cancer risk near larger chemical plants from roughly 90,000 to roughly 3,000, a 97% reduction** -- a reduction now delayed or at risk depending on the rules' ultimate 'reconsideration' outcome.

estimated_health_impact.summary: ProPublica reported more than 5 million people face increased cancer risk living near the affected facility types; EPA's own modeling found the monitoring-triggered standards this rollback delays would have cut the number of people facing unacceptable cancer risk near larger chemical plants from roughly 90,000 to roughly 3,000. Pittsburgh-area residents near Clairton Coke Works documented specific health effects: David Meckel (77) reported difficulty breathing and near-fainting during exertion; Cindy Meckel (66) was diagnosed with anemia and lost three dogs to cancer within eight years; Miriam Maletta (62), diagnosed with lymphoma (in remission), lost her father to gastric cancer after 20+ years working at the coke plant; and Qiyam Ansari (29) survived a near-fatal asthma attack as a teenager and maintains air purifiers throughout his home. The Meckels relocated away from the area in spring 2025, saying 'we're escaping with our lives because we gave it everything we could do and it didn't matter.'

rule_name: EPA's Formaldehyde Risk Assessment Under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA)
agency: EPA, Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention
status: Proposed -- public comment period ran through February 2, 2026; no final rule identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-12-03 (EPA released proposed revisions) through 2026-02-02 (public comment period closed)
original_rule_summary: Under the Biden administration, EPA's TSCA risk evaluation for formaldehyde used the 'linear' dose-response model -- the approach EPA has applied to potent carcinogens for nearly 40 years under administrations of both parties, which assumes even minimal chemical exposure carries some cancer risk with no fully 'safe' threshold. Applying that model, EPA found formaldehyde posed an 'unreasonable risk' in 58 specific worker and consumer exposure settings, including automotive-care products, crafting supplies, building materials, textiles, and leather goods.
what_changed: EPA, under Principal Deputy Assistant Administrator Nancy Beck and Deputy Assistant Administrator Lynn Dekleva -- both former officials of the American Chemistry Council, the chemical industry's main trade group -- proposed on December 3, 2025 to replace the linear model with a 'threshold' model for formaldehyde, which assumes the chemical poses no cancer risk below a specific exposure level. **The industry-preferred threshold approach nearly doubles the level of formaldehyde EPA would consider safe to inhale.** Dekleva had personally advocated for this same threshold approach in a 2022 letter to an EPA scientist, which the agency rejected at the time. Applying the new model, EPA's proposal reverses the prior 'unreasonable risk' finding in 5 of the 58 previously identified exposure settings, including wood-product manufacturing, while leaving the other roughly 53 settings' risk findings standing for now. Earthjustice attorney Jonathan Kalmuss-Katz said 'the science on formaldehyde hasn't changed'; former EPA scientist Tracey Woodruff warned the move would 'open the floodgates,' since 'chemical companies want every carcinogen to be considered a threshold carcinogen.' The proposal's public comment period closed February 2, 2026, after which EPA can move to finalize it.

rule_name: EPA's Proposed Elimination of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP)
status: Proposed Repeal (not yet finalized -- EPA extended the 2025 reporting deadline separately to October 30, 2026, and said it would finalize the broader elimination in one or more later actions)
date_of_action: 2025-09-12 (proposed)
original_rule_summary: The Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, established in 2009, has required roughly 8,000 large industrial facilities -- power plants, refineries, landfills, and other major emitters -- to measure and publicly report their greenhouse gas emissions to EPA annually, producing the U.S. government's primary facility-level emissions dataset used by regulators, researchers, states, and industry itself.
what_changed: On September 12, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin proposed effectively ending the GHGRP, removing reporting obligations for all source categories except petroleum and natural gas systems (those facilities would still report starting in 2034, tied to the separate methane emissions tax). EPA framed the proposal as cutting 'burdensome, costly' red tape, estimating it would save regulated companies up to $2.4 billion. The proposal drew unusually bipartisan pushback: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Kevin Cramer (R-ND) jointly urged EPA to withdraw it, warning that ending the program would harm American industrial competitiveness and specifically damage the domestic carbon-capture and LNG sectors, which rely on GHGRP data to verify emissions for federal tax credits (the Section 45Q carbon-sequestration credit and Section 45V clean-hydrogen credit). Rep. Sean Casten (D-IL) led a separate House Democratic letter arguing the elimination violated 'clear congressional directives.' EPA received more than 50,000 public comments by the November 3, 2025 deadline. As of early 2026, EPA had not finalized the core elimination; instead it finalized a narrower action extending the 2025 reporting-year deadline to October 30, 2026, stating it would address the rest of the reconsideration proposal in later, separate final actions.

rule_name: AIM Act Technology Transitions Rule -- HFC (hydrofluorocarbon) refrigerant phasedown compliance deadlines for supermarket, remote-condensing, industrial-chiller, and semiconductor refrigeration systems
status: Finalized -- EPA published a final rule May 26, 2026, effective July 27, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-12 (EPA announces reconsideration) through 2026-05-26 (final rule issued); effective 2026-07-27
original_rule_summary: The American Innovation and Manufacturing (AIM) Act of 2020 -- a bipartisan law Trump signed in his first term -- directed EPA to phase down high-global-warming-potential (GWP) hydrofluorocarbon refrigerants nationwide. EPA's October 2023 Technology Transitions Rule implemented that phasedown with specific GWP limits and compliance deadlines for different equipment sectors, including supermarket/remote-condensing refrigeration systems, industrial chillers, and semiconductor-manufacturing refrigeration, with several deadlines set for January 1, 2026 and January 1, 2028.
what_changed: On March 12, 2025 -- the same day EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced 31 simultaneous deregulatory actions -- EPA announced it would reconsider the 2023 Technology Transitions Rule. EPA released its formal reconsideration proposal on October 3, 2025, and closed the public comment period on November 21, 2025. EPA finalized the rule on May 26, 2026, effective July 27, 2026: the GWP threshold for remote condensing units and supermarket systems, originally set to drop to 150-300 on January 1, 2026, was instead raised to an interim 1,400 starting July 27, 2026, with the original 150/300 limit not taking effect until January 1, 2032 -- a six-year delay. Separately, compliance deadlines for industrial chillers and semiconductor-manufacturing refrigeration systems, originally January 1, 2026 and January 1, 2028 respectively, were both pushed to January 1, 2030. The final rule also removed a prohibition on installing R-410A (a higher-GWP refrigerant) systems. EPA and Trump justified the delay by citing 'stranded inventory' -- billions of dollars in already-manufactured equipment that would become illegal to install under the original deadlines -- and Trump said the change would save consumers $2.4 billion by reducing grocery and retail-store operating costs. Industry reaction was split rather than uniform: the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) and the Alliance for Responsible Atmospheric Policy -- representing manufacturers who had already invested in new compliant equipment, refrigerants, and production lines to meet the original deadlines Congress and the first Trump administration set -- opposed the delay, arguing it would keep demand for older high-GWP refrigerants elevated even as supply keeps falling under the AIM Act's separate production phasedown, pushing refrigerant prices higher for the very companies that complied on schedule. AHRI's Stephen Yurek said extending the deadline 'is maintaining and even increasing demand in the market for existing refrigerants while supply continues to fall,' and that 'refrigerant prices are likely to rise.' Other industry segments -- particularly grocery and retail-store operators represented by the Food Industry Association -- supported the delay for the cost relief it offered. Environmental groups including NRDC criticized the rule as undermining the AIM Act's climate goals.

primary_proponent.note: Announced and finalized the reconsideration and delay of the Technology Transitions Rule's compliance deadlines, framing the change around 'stranded inventory' relief; President Trump separately publicized the $2.4 billion consumer-savings estimate.

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Delaying the shift away from high-GWP refrigerants by up to six years extends the use and installation of chemicals with substantially greater heat-trapping potential than their low-GWP replacements, working against the AIM Act's bipartisan climate-mitigation goal**; the harm here is a climate/regulatory-durability one rather than a direct public-health-standard rollback, and industry itself is split on whether the delay is a net benefit (cost relief for late-adopting operators) or a net harm (price and stranded-investment risk for manufacturers who already complied on the original schedule).

rule_name: Methane emission rules for low-producing ('stripper') oil and gas wells
status: Proposed Repeal -- rulemaking process underway as of ProPublica's June 2026 reporting
date_of_action: 2026-06 (reporting on the rollback effort)
original_rule_summary: In 2024, the Biden administration issued the first-ever federal methane emission regulations targeting low-producing 'stripper' wells -- older wells that individually produce little oil or gas but, in aggregate, emit outsized quantities of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, relative to their energy output.
what_changed: The Trump EPA is engineering a rollback of the 2024 stripper-well methane rules. ProPublica reported the rulemaking effort is being led in significant part by Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for Hilcorp -- a privately held oil and gas company owned by Texas billionaire Jeffery Hildebrand -- whom Trump named to a top EPA post. Hilcorp specializes in buying up old, low-producing stripper wells and is one of the industry's largest methane emitters relative to its output. Hildebrand and his wife have donated more than $15 million to Trump and other Republican federal candidates since 2020, giving substantially more after the 2024 methane rule was issued. Separately, per the same June 2026 Source New Mexico reporting, Republican lawmakers have introduced legislation that would permanently exempt stripper wells from EPA methane regulation entirely -- a legislative track running alongside the administrative rollback effort.

rule_name: EPA's Fast-Tracked Approval of New PFAS ('Forever Chemical') Pesticides
status: Finalized (multiple approvals; additional PFAS pesticides reported pending)
date_of_action: 2025-11 (cyclobutrifluram and isocycloseram approved) through 2025-12 (broader reporting on the fast-tracked approval pattern)
original_rule_summary: EPA pesticide registration under FIFRA requires the agency to find that a new pesticide will not cause 'unreasonable adverse effects' on human health or the environment before approving it for use; PFAS-class pesticides -- built around carbon-fluorine bonds that make them extremely persistent and difficult to break down -- had previously been approved at a markedly slower pace.
what_changed: In early November 2025, EPA approved cyclobutrifluram, a fungicide for use on golf courses, lawns, cotton, soybeans, and lettuce, and known to break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), described by researchers as one of the most pervasive PFAS water contaminants in the world. Roughly two weeks later, EPA approved isocycloseram, an insecticide for golf courses, lawns, and food crops including oranges, tomatoes, almonds, peas, and oats; **among the health concerns cited by EWG and other reviewers were reduced testicle size, lower sperm count, and liver toxicity in animal studies**. Public-health and environmental groups (EWG, the Center for Biological Diversity) characterized both as part of a broader acceleration: in less than two years, EPA authorized five PFAS pesticides -- roughly quintupling the pace of the prior administration, which approved just one PFAS pesticide across four years. EPA and some agricultural-industry commentators pushed back on aspects of the PFAS characterization itself, with AGDAILY arguing environmental groups had 'stretched' the PFAS classification for some of the newly registered products.

primary_proponent.note: EPA's Office of Pesticide Programs, under Zeldin's leadership, approved both pesticides via the standard registration process; no source reviewed identified an individual official personally directing the accelerated pace beyond the administration's general deregulatory posture.

corporate_beneficiaries: Pesticide manufacturers of cyclobutrifluram and isocycloseram, and agricultural users of both products (named manufacturers not identified in sourcing reviewed)

rule_name: Risk Management Program 'Common Sense Approach' Rollback
agency: EPA (Office of Land and Emergency Management)
status: Proposed (comment period closed May 11, 2026; EPA has stated intent to finalize in late 2026)
date_of_action: 2026-02-24 (proposed rule published) -- final action pending
original_rule_summary: The 2024 Safer Communities by Chemical Accident Prevention (SCCAP) rule, finalized under the Biden EPA, strengthened Risk Management Program (RMP) requirements under Clean Air Act Section 112(r) for roughly 11,700-11,900 facilities handling extremely hazardous substances. Key provisions included mandatory Safer Technology and Alternatives Analyses (STAA) with implementation requirements for high-accident-rate sectors (chemical manufacturing, petroleum/coal products), third-party compliance audits, expanded public disclosure of chemical hazard information, natural-hazard and power-loss risk assessment requirements, worker protections including anonymous hazard reporting and stop-work authority, and enhanced community/emergency-responder notification systems.
what_changed: On February 24, 2026, EPA published a proposed rule, the 'Common Sense Approach to Chemical Accident Prevention,' that would rescind or substantially scale back most of the 2024 SCCAP requirements. Key rollbacks: eliminating STAA requirements for existing facilities in the two highest-risk sectors (chemical manufacturing and petroleum/coal products, NAICS 324/325), limiting STAA to newly built processes only; rescinding most third-party audit requirements (with a narrower option requiring audits only for facilities with 2+ accidents in 5 years); eliminating the requirement to share chemical hazard information directly with the public on request, relying instead on EPA's more limited online Data Tool; and rescinding several worker-protection provisions including anonymous reporting, stop-work authority, and mandatory workers' rights training. EPA frames the changes as realigning RMP with OSHA's existing Process Safety Management standard and removing 'duplicative' requirements. The proposal followed a March 2025 EPA announcement that it would reconsider the SCCAP rule, itself prompted by Executive Orders 14148 and 14154 directing agencies to rescind Biden-era regulatory actions. The public comment period closed May 11, 2026; as of this writing the rule remains a proposal, with EPA's own regulatory agenda indicating a target of finalizing it in late 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Announced on March 12, 2025 that EPA would reconsider the 2024 SCCAP rule; EPA under his leadership published the Common Sense Approach proposed rule in February 2026 and held the required public hearing in March 2026.

corporate_beneficiaries: Roughly 11,700-11,900 RMP-regulated facilities nationwide, concentrated in chemical manufacturing and petroleum/coal products refining -- sectors represented in commenting by the American Chemistry Council, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, American Petroleum Institute, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, all of which had petitioned against the 2024 rule before this rollback was proposed.

estimated_health_impact.summary: EPA's own 2024 SCCAP rulemaking found accidental releases from RMP facilities cost society more than $540 million annually and **cited a real-world case (the 2019 TPC Group explosion in Port Neches, TX) where the STAA and safeguard requirements being rolled back likely would have mitigated or prevented the accident**. EPA's own estimated population near RMP facilities is disproportionately exposed to accident risk.

rule_name: EPA's Attempt to Vacate the 2024 Soot (PM2.5) Air Quality Standard
status: Rejected by federal appeals court -- the 2024 standard remains in effect
date_of_action: 2025-11 (EPA moves to vacate) through 2026-06-26 (appeals court denies the motion)
original_rule_summary: In 2024, EPA under the Biden administration tightened the national ambient air quality standard for fine particulate matter (soot, PM2.5) from power plants, oil refineries, and other industrial sources, lowering the annual limit from 12 micrograms per cubic meter to 9 micrograms per cubic meter, to take full effect by 2032.
what_changed: Republican attorneys general from 24 states and an industry coalition sued in March 2024 arguing EPA lacked statutory authority to tighten the standard and that it was improperly influenced by 'environmental justice' considerations. **In November 2025, EPA under the Trump administration moved in that litigation to vacate its own 2024 rule, arguing the agency had exceeded its statutory authority and acted unreasonably by failing to adequately consider costs -- an unusual posture in which the agency defending a rule instead asked the court to strike it down.** On June 26, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals denied both the original petitions for review and EPA's own motion for vacatur, finding the challengers' arguments 'lack merit.' The 9 microgram/cubic meter standard remains legally in effect as a result.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Directed EPA to move to vacate its own predecessor's finalized rule rather than defend it in litigation -- part of the same broader deregulatory push as the March 2025 31-rule announcement.

corporate_beneficiaries: Power plant, oil refinery, and other industrial operators that would have faced a looser compliance standard had the vacatur motion succeeded

estimated_health_impact.summary: Had EPA's vacatur motion succeeded, the tighter 2024 soot standard -- which environmental and public-health groups credit with preventing pollution-related illness and premature death from fine particulate matter, a pollutant linked to heart attacks, asthma, and other cardiopulmonary harm -- would have reverted to the looser 12 microgram/cubic meter limit. The court's rejection means this harm did not materialize.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: Because the rollback attempt failed, no source reviewed quantifies a harm that was ultimately averted rather than realized; the entry documents the attempt and its rejection, not a realized health impact.

This is a rare instance in this database of a specific rollback attempt being fully defeated in court rather than finalized, delayed, or contested.

rule_name: Procedures for Chemical Risk Evaluation Under TSCA (2025 Framework Rule proposal)
agency: EPA (Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention)
status: Proposed (comment period closed November 7, 2025; EPA's regulatory agenda has targeted a final rule for mid-2026)
date_of_action: 2025-09-23 (proposed rule published) -- final action pending
original_rule_summary: The 2024 TSCA Risk Evaluation Framework Rule, finalized under the Biden EPA, required the agency to evaluate all conditions of use of a chemical and all exposure pathways (not a subset chosen by EPA) when determining whether it poses an "unreasonable risk" under Section 6 of the Toxic Substances Control Act, and barred EPA from assuming workers use personal protective equipment (PPE) correctly when estimating occupational exposure -- on the reasoning that assuming correct PPE use could understate real-world risk to workers. It also required a single, whole-chemical risk determination rather than separate determinations per condition of use.
what_changed: On September 23, 2025, EPA published a proposed rule amending the TSCA Risk Evaluation Framework for the third time since 2017 ("Take 3"). The proposal would reinstate an assumption that workers handling toxic chemicals use correct PPE and follow applicable engineering/administrative controls when EPA estimates occupational exposure -- reversing the 2024 rule's bar on that assumption. It would also require EPA to issue a separate unreasonable-risk determination for each condition of use of a chemical rather than one determination for the chemical as a whole, and would scale back manufacturer information-request obligations to what is "known to or reasonably ascertainable," reducing data requirements the 2024 rule had expanded. The public comment period closed November 7, 2025; EPA's own regulatory agenda has targeted finalizing the rule by mid-2026, though the exact date has been reported inconsistently (April vs. July 2026) across legal-industry trackers.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA under his leadership published the proposed rule in the Federal Register on September 23, 2025; no more specific individual is named on the record as having personally driven the proposal beyond the agency action itself.

corporate_beneficiaries: Chemical manufacturers subject to TSCA Section 6 risk evaluations -- reduced information-request obligations and a PPE-use assumption both narrow the scope of exposure EPA can find and the resulting regulatory burden per condition of use

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Reinstating the PPE-use assumption reverses the 2024 rule's explicit finding that assuming correct PPE use can understate real-world worker exposure to toxic chemicals**; splitting risk determinations by condition of use, rather than evaluating the chemical as a whole, narrows the scope of exposure captured in any single EPA risk finding.

Revisit if EPA publishes a regulatory impact analysis with the final rule.

rule_name: Elimination of the Endangered Species Act's "blanket" Section 4(d) rule, plus a new economic/national-security exclusion for critical habitat designations under Section 4(b)(2)
agency: Department of the Interior (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) and Department of Commerce (NOAA/NMFS)
status: Finalized -- announced July 17, 2026; published in the Federal Register; effective August 20, 2026 (blanket-rule change applies prospectively only, to species newly listed or reclassified as threatened after that date, not to species already listed as threatened)
date_of_action: 2025-11-20 (proposed) through 2026-08-20 (effective)
original_rule_summary: Since the 1970s, FWS's 'blanket' Section 4(d) rule automatically extended the same protections against killing, harassment, and harm that endangered species receive to any species newly listed or reclassified as 'threatened' (the less-imperiled of the ESA's two protected categories), while the agency worked out a tailored, species-specific rule. Separately, Section 4(b)(2) previously allowed only limited consideration of economic impact when the agency designated a species' 'critical habitat.'
what_changed: On November 20, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, FWS, and NOAA/NMFS jointly proposed eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule and revising the critical-habitat-exclusion standard under Section 4(b)(2) to allow agencies to weigh economic impact and national security more heavily when deciding whether to exclude land from a critical habitat designation. The package was finalized July 17, 2026. Under the new regime, newly listed or reclassified threatened species no longer receive automatic protection against killing or harm the moment they are listed -- **FWS must instead draft an individual, species-specific 4(d) rule for each one, a process advocacy groups warn is 'far more time-consuming and resource-intensive' and will create gaps in protection while individual rules are drafted**. The change applies prospectively only, to species listed or reclassified after August 20, 2026; it does not strip protections already in place for currently-listed threatened species. FWS Director Brian Nesvik framed the change as enabling 'a more cooperative relationship with the American people'; Burgum said the ESA had been 'weaponized to stop almost any new project in America, driving up costs for families, weakening our competitiveness, and undermining our national security,' and separately that nearly 97% of species ever listed under the ESA remain listed today, citing that as evidence the law has not succeeded at its stated recovery goal. The same November 20, 2025 announcement also proposed the separate rescission of the ESA's habitat-modification 'harm' definition -- that rule followed its own, earlier timeline (proposed April 2025, finalized July 11, 2026) and rests on a different statutory provision (the definition of 'take'/'harm' under Sections 3 and 9), but both actions were promoted together as one package and finalized within days of each other in July 2026. Named species cited by reporting as illustrative of what is at stake under a weakened listing regime include the monarch butterfly, Florida manatee, California spotted owl, North American wolverine, and Yarrow's spiny lizard (for which a separate listing petition was filed the same week as the November 2025 announcement). The Property and Environment Research Center and Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation had already sued Interior in March 2026 arguing the (then-still-proposed) blanket rule was illegal on separate, pro-deregulation grounds (that FWS lacked authority to have created the blanket rule in the first place); Earthjustice, Humane World for Animals, and Humane World Action Fund oppose the rollback, with Humane World Action Fund president Sara Amundson calling the decision 'a profound failure by Interior Secretary Burgum and his department.'

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Announced and finalized the change jointly with FWS Director Brian Nesvik and NOAA/NMFS; publicly framed the ESA as 'weaponized' against development and cited the 97%-not-delisted figure as justification.

corporate_beneficiaries: Logging, mining, oil and gas, and other development interests seeking faster permitting for projects affecting newly threatened-listed species' habitat

estimated_health_impact.summary: This is an ecological/species-conservation rollback rather than a direct human-health standard. The concrete risk critics identify is a protection gap for newly listed threatened species during the time FWS takes to draft individual species-specific rules -- previously bridged automatically by the blanket rule -- with named species (monarch butterfly, Florida manatee, California spotted owl, North American wolverine, Yarrow's spiny lizard) cited as illustrative of what could be affected by future listings. No sourcing reviewed provided a quantified extinction-risk or species-count estimate specific to this rule change.

rule_name: Rescission of the Endangered Species Act's regulatory definition of "harm" to include habitat destruction (50 C.F.R. § 17.3)
agency: Department of the Interior (Fish and Wildlife Service) and Department of Commerce (NOAA/NMFS)
status: In effect since September 14, 2026 (final rule published July 14, 2026). Challenged by environmental groups and two tribes (suits filed July 14) and 21 attorneys general (Sept. 9); no court ruling reported as of mid-September 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-04-17 (rule first proposed) through 2026-09-14 (effective date)
original_rule_summary: Since 1975 (revised 1981), federal regulations defined 'harm' to a protected species under the Endangered Species Act to include 'significant habitat modification or degradation where it actually kills or injures wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioral patterns, including breeding, feeding, or sheltering.' This definition meant that destroying or significantly degrading a species' critical habitat -- not just directly killing or injuring an individual animal -- could itself violate the ESA's prohibition on 'take' of a listed species, and was the legal basis on which courts and agencies had evaluated development, logging, mining, and drilling proposals in critical habitat for nearly five decades.
what_changed: On April 17, 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service jointly proposed rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm' under the Endangered Species Act (90 FR 16102), with a comment period that closed May 19, 2025 and drew approximately 358,000 public comments. In November 2025, while that proposal was still pending, the administration proposed a separate package of ESA rollbacks, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the administration was 'restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent' while respecting 'the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.' On July 10, 2026, the Departments of the Interior and Commerce announced they were **rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm' that had included significant habitat modification or degradation, eliminating that language entirely from the operative regulation**. Burgum said federal agencies had 'abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses,' and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said 'President Trump is rescinding overly broad and burdensome regulations that have restrained our fishermen for too long.' The final rule was published in the Federal Register on July 14, 2026 (91 FR 43300) and took effect September 14, 2026; the agencies said permits and incidental take statements finalized before that date will not be reevaluated. With the definition gone, the agencies rely on the statute's bare text, which, in their reading, means that development activities that destroy or degrade a protected species' habitat would no longer, on their own, constitute unlawful 'harm' to that species -- only actions that directly kill or injure individual animals would qualify. In the final rule, the agencies summarized commenters' estimates that about $483 million had already been spent on species habitat under the old framework, that the proposal alone had chilled another $300 million in planned investment, and that habitat restoration broadly approaches $10 billion in economic impact and supports more than 53,000 jobs; the agencies called the magnitude of such effects uncertain and dismissed those markets as 'regulatory rents.' Challengers sued on July 14, 2026. Earthjustice and the Conservation Law Foundation, representing the Center for Biological Diversity, Sierra Club, Conservation Law Foundation and six other groups, filed in federal court in Seattle, with Earthjustice attorney Kristen Boyles saying the repeal 'violates the core purpose of the statute and decades of legal precedent'; the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community and Squaxin Island Tribe sued in the same court, warning of harm to threatened Skagit River Chinook salmon that remain at about 20% of their recovery levels; and the Environmental Protection Information Center and allied groups sued in the Northern District of California. Defenders of Wildlife sent a notice of intent to sue, with senior attorney Jane Davenport saying 'destroying the habitat -- the home -- of endangered wildlife harms that species ...' On September 9, 2026, a coalition of 21 attorneys general sued to challenge the rescission alongside other ESA rollbacks.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Interior, jointly with the Department of Commerce, announced and finalized the rescission of the habitat-modification language from the ESA 'harm' definition.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Logging, mining, and oil and gas development interests operating in or near critical habitat for listed species
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Development projects that significantly degrade protected species' habitat -- without directly killing or injuring individual animals -- would no longer require the same level of ESA review or mitigation that the habitat-modification definition had required for nearly 50 years.

estimated_health_impact.summary: The rescission removes habitat destruction from what counts as unlawful 'harm' to endangered and threatened species, so projects that degrade habitat without directly killing or injuring animals no longer violate that ESA prohibition. The human harm documented is indirect: the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, suing with the Squaxin Island Tribe, warns of fewer treaty-reserved Skagit River Chinook salmon, already at about 20% of recovery levels, to feed its members, and its fisheries manager, Tandy Wilbur, said: "I fear for the health of our people." Financially, commenters told the agencies that the habitat mitigation and restoration market built under the old rule (about $483 million spent, $300 million in planned investment already chilled, more than 53,000 restoration jobs broadly) stands to lose demand.

rule_name: FCC Net Neutrality Repeal ("Restoring Internet Freedom Order")
status: Fully Repealed
original_rule_summary: 2015 FCC Open Internet Order reclassified broadband internet access as a Title II common-carrier telecommunications service, banning internet service providers from blocking, throttling, or paid-prioritizing web traffic based on source, destination, or content.
what_changed: The FCC voted 3-2 along party lines to reclassify broadband back to a lightly-regulated Title I 'information service,' **eliminating the common-carrier blocking/throttling/prioritization bans**. ISPs remain subject only to a transparency (disclosure) requirement.

primary_proponent.name: Ajit Pai
primary_proponent.note: Led the repeal vote; had dissented against the original 2015 rules and argued net neutrality regulation was solving a problem that didn't exist ('the Internet wasn't broken in 2015').

estimated_health_impact.caveat: This is fundamentally a digital-access/market-structure issue, not a health rollback in the sense of the environmental or labor entries in this tracker -- use the telehealth-throttling angle cautiously as a theoretical risk, not a documented realized harm.

rule_name: Rescission of the FCC's Section 105 telecom network-security rule (the 'Salt Typhoon rule')
status: Finalized -- FCC voted to rescind in November 2025
date_of_action: 2025-01 (rule adopted) through 2025-11-20 (rescission vote)
original_rule_summary: In January 2025, in the final days of the Biden administration, the FCC adopted a rule under Section 105 of the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act (CALEA) requiring telecommunications carriers to affirmatively secure their networks against unauthorized access, in direct response to the Salt Typhoon intrusion -- **a China-linked state-sponsored hacking campaign that had infiltrated at least eight major U.S. telecom carriers, geolocating millions of Americans and intercepting call and text data, in one of the largest telecom breaches in U.S. history**.
what_changed: On November 20, 2025, the FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, voted along party lines to rescind the Section 105 network-security rule adopted less than a year earlier in direct response to Salt Typhoon. Carr argued the rule 'exceeded the agency's authority' and 'did not present an effective or agile response to the relevant cybersecurity threats,' framing it as a rushed, ineffective, last-minute Biden-era action. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), the Senate Commerce Committee's ranking member, publicly opposed the rollback, sending a formal letter to Carr in November 2025 and noting the reversal came after direct lobbying from the same telecom carriers whose networks had been breached by the Salt Typhoon hackers the rule was written to guard against.

primary_proponent.name: Brendan Carr
primary_proponent.note: Led the party-line vote to rescind the rule, characterizing it as exceeding FCC authority and ineffective, rather than defending it as insufficiently protective against the threat it was written to address.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Major telecom carriers subject to the rescinded security mandate
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: The same carriers whose networks Salt Typhoon had breached lobbied the FCC to rescind the mandatory network-security rule adopted in response to that breach, per Sen. Cantwell's public letter.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Not a direct public-health rollback; the harm alleged is to U.S. communications-infrastructure security and consumer privacy/surveillance risk, given the rule was adopted specifically in response to a documented foreign state-actor breach that intercepted Americans' calls and location data.

figures.source: Federal News Network, Cybersecurity Dive, November 2025 reporting on the rescission vote

estimated_health_impact.caveat: The FCC's stated rationale (that the rule exceeded statutory authority and was an ineffective, rushed response) is a genuine legal and policy argument, not addressed here as pretextual; the timing relative to industry lobbying, documented by Sen. Cantwell's letter, is presented as a relevant fact for evaluating the rescission, not proof of improper motive.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the rescission vote, Carr's stated rationale, and Cantwell's opposition letter and lobbying allegation are corroborated across Federal News Network, Bloomberg, Cybersecurity Dive, and the Senate Commerce Committee's own published letter. This entry is closely related to, but distinct from, this tracker's Government Service Redirection entry on CISA workforce cuts ([[cisa-cyber-workforce-cuts-trump2]]), which documents the separate story of CISA's own staffing losses rather than this FCC regulatory rollback.

rule_name: FDA Consumer Warning Webpage Against Chlorine Dioxide and Other Unproven Autism 'Treatments'
status: Fully Repealed (webpage removed, not republished)
date_of_action: 2025-05 (webpage first found removed, per Wired) through late 2025 (HHS's own stated removal timing)
original_rule_summary: FDA maintained a consumer-facing warning page, unchanged since 2019, advising against chlorine dioxide (marketed as 'Miracle Mineral Solution'/MMS), raw camel milk, and other unproven products promoted online as cures or treatments for autism -- part of FDA's ordinary consumer-protection messaging, not a binding regulation, but the agency's clearest public statement that ingesting chlorine dioxide is dangerous and not an approved treatment for anything.
what_changed: By June 2025, Wired reported the FDA's chlorine dioxide/autism-treatments warning page had quietly disappeared from the agency's website, coinciding with a surge in online chlorine dioxide/MMS promotion following remarks HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made about the substance during his confirmation process, and with previously prosecuted or investigated 'bleach cure' promoters re-emerging and connecting with Trump-aligned figures, including at events at Trump's Doral resort. A more thorough investigation by ProPublica, published roughly eight months later, confirmed the page's removal and obtained HHS's own explanation: the department said it had retired the page 'during a routine clean up of dated content at the end of 2025,' framing it as content-maintenance rather than a policy reversal. The page has not been restored or replaced with updated guidance as of the most recent reporting reviewed. Chlorine dioxide/MMS advocates interpreted the removal as a positive signal, with one telling ProPublica they hoped the new administration, with Kennedy at HHS, might now allow chlorine dioxide to be studied as a legitimate therapeutic.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services (FDA's parent department)
primary_proponent.note: No specific HHS or FDA official is named on record as personally ordering the page's removal; HHS's own institutional statement attributed it to 'routine clean up.' Kennedy is included as the department's accountable head and because his own public chlorine-dioxide-adjacent remarks during confirmation are documented by Wired as contemporaneous context for the surge in advocacy the removal coincided with -- see confidence_note for this attribution's limits.

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Chlorine dioxide/MMS ingestion has documented, FDA-recorded harms including severe vomiting, severe diarrhea, life-threatening dehydration-induced low blood pressure, acute liver failure, and death**; removing FDA's own consumer warning removes a specific, checkable public deterrent against a product with a known toxicity record, at a moment reporting found renewed promotional activity around it.

figures.value: At least 2 documented (a 56-year-old woman, 2009; a 48-year-old woman, 2013), plus additional hospitalizations for liver failure, hemorrhaging, intestinal perforation, and heart attack
figures.source: FDA adverse-event reports, cited in consumer-health reporting

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No dollar cost/savings figure applies to this specific webpage removal -- unlike a rule repeal with an industry compliance-cost or agency-budget dimension, this is a content-maintenance action with no identified monetary figure on either side of the ledger in sourcing reviewed; the health-harm figures above predate this specific 2025 removal and describe chlorine dioxide's known toxicity generally, not deaths attributable to the removal itself, since the removal is too recent for its own downstream health effects to yet be documented in available sourcing.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts: the page's removal is independently confirmed by both Wired (May/June 2025) and ProPublica (roughly eight months later, with HHS's own on-record explanation obtained directly). MODERATE confidence on the causal link to Kennedy personally -- no source identifies a specific HHS or FDA official who ordered the removal, and HHS's own stated reason (routine content cleanup) is a genuinely available alternative explanation, not merely a pretext asserted by this entry. The contemporaneous surge in chlorine dioxide advocacy activity, and one advocate's on-record hope that Kennedy's HHS might permit further study of the substance, are presented as documented context suggesting the removal's political salience, not as proof the removal was ordered for that purpose.
pull_quote: HHS said it retired the warning page “during a routine clean up of dated content” -- as one chlorine dioxide advocate told ProPublica they hoped Kennedy’s HHS might now allow the substance to be studied as a legitimate therapeutic.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: FDA's own records already link the substance to at least two deaths and serious organ damage, independent of this specific removal.

rule_name: FDA premarket tobacco product authorization standard for flavored e-cigarettes (informal reversal of the agency's longstanding practice of denying most flavored vape authorizations, including fruit and mint flavors, on youth-appeal grounds)
status: Finalized: FDA issued marketing orders on May 5, 2026 for four Glas pods, two fruit-flavored and two menthol. Ten senators asked the acting commissioner to rescind them; no rescission has been reported. Makary, who had opposed the move, resigned May 12.
original_rule_summary: Under FDA's premarket tobacco product application standard, the agency had for years denied the large majority of applications for flavored e-cigarette products -- including fruit and mint flavors -- on the grounds that their appeal to youth outweighed any public-health benefit to adult smokers switching from combustible cigarettes, banning most flavored vaping products from the market.
what_changed: FDA authorized the marketing of fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for the first time in the agency's history, approving pods including 'Gold' (mango) and 'Sapphire' (blueberry) flavors manufactured by Glas, Inc., alongside menthol variants. The decision followed a Wall Street Journal report that Trump had personally rebuked FDA Commissioner Marty Makary over the weekend for not approving flavored vapes more quickly, consistent with a 2024 campaign promise to 'save' vaping. The Vapor Technology Association and other industry groups had met with administration officials in the preceding weeks calling for more action on flavors. FDA's stated safeguard is a digital age-verification system requiring users to verify age via government ID and pair the device to their phone via Bluetooth before use. Makary had initially opposed the authorization despite career staff signing off on it, the Wall Street Journal reported; he resigned on May 12, and the New York Times reported he had told confidants his conscience would not allow him to approve the vapes because of their appeal to young people. Within two weeks of the authorization, FDA also issued guidance allowing unauthorized vapes with pending applications to stay on the market, and ten senators led by Richard Blumenthal and Jeff Merkley asked Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas to rescind the Glas authorization. In September, the Wall Street Journal reported the administration planned to make marketing authorization easier and faster for e-cigarettes, nicotine pouches and other products; on September 28, FDA announced it intends to evaluate changes to its 2021 premarket application rule, including new rulemaking to replace that framework.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Per Wall Street Journal reporting, personally pressured FDA Commissioner Makary to approve flavored vapes faster, consistent with his 2024 campaign pledge to 'save' vaping; the approval followed direct meetings between the Vapor Technology Association and administration officials.

corporate_beneficiaries: Glas, Inc. -- the specific manufacturer whose fruit- and menthol-flavored pods received the first-ever FDA authorization
Vapor Technology Association and the broader e-cigarette/vaping industry, which lobbied administration officials directly for the policy change

estimated_health_impact.summary: Public health and parent advocacy groups warn **the authorization of fruit-flavored vapes -- a category FDA had specifically excluded for years due to documented youth appeal -- risks reversing progress made in reducing underage vaping**, notwithstanding the digital age-verification safeguard FDA cited.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified projection of youth-uptake impact from this specific 2026 authorization was found in reporting reviewed; health groups' warnings are qualitative, based on the well-documented general pattern that flavored products appeal disproportionately to minors, not a modeled figure specific to this authorization.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the facts of the authorization, Trump's personal pressure on Makary, and industry lobbying -- corroborated across many independent outlets (CNBC, CBS News, NPR, STAT News, Scientific American, Fox Business). No quantified health-harm projection specific to this action was identified, so the health-impact framing should stay qualitative rather than citing a specific figure. Re-verified 2026-10-06: CNBC, STAT News and NPR still support the authorization facts; FDA issued the Glas marketing orders on May 5, 2026, not May 6; Makary's May 12 resignation, the senators' rescission demand, the reported overhaul of the premarket review rule and FDA's September 28 announcement that it intends to evaluate replacing that rule were added; no rescission of the Glas orders was found.

rule_name: FDA Marketing Restriction on Ingestible Fluoride Supplement Products for Children
status: Finalized (marketing-restriction action taken; FDA stopped short of a formal product ban)
date_of_action: 2025-03-10 (Utah becomes first state to ban water fluoridation, RFK Jr. publicly signals a coordinated federal push) through 2025-10-31 (FDA announces fluoride-supplement marketing restriction)
original_rule_summary: Ingestible fluoride supplements (drops and tablets) have been available, without a formal FDA approval process, as a decades-old preventive dental-health option recommended by dentists and pediatricians for children -- particularly those under 3 and those at higher cavity risk -- who lack access to fluoridated drinking water, most often in rural areas or private-well communities. The American Dental Association and American Academy of Pediatrics have long supported graduated fluoride supplementation for high-risk children starting at six months of age as safe and effective cavity prevention.
what_changed: As newly installed HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly pushed to eliminate water fluoridation nationwide -- posting that the administration would 'advise all U.S. water systems to remove fluoride from public water' -- Utah's legislature moved first: Republican Gov. Spencer Cox announced on March 10, 2025 that he would sign, and signed by March 28, 2025, a law making Utah the first state to ban fluoride from public drinking water systems, over opposition from dentists and the American Dental Association. With water fluoridation itself outside FDA's direct authority, the agency instead targeted the alternative lawmakers and advocates had pointed to for communities without fluoridated water: on October 31, 2025, the FDA announced it was moving to restrict the sale of ingestible fluoride supplement products for children, sending notices to four manufacturers about marketing supplements to children under 3 and to older children with low or moderate cavity risk, along with warning letters to healthcare professionals who prescribe them. The FDA stopped short of an outright ban on the products. Separately, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton opened investigations into Colgate-Palmolive and Procter & Gamble over children's fluoride toothpaste marketing; both companies settled by agreeing to depict pea-sized amounts rather than larger swirls in promotional imagery, while maintaining their products already complied with FDA requirements.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced the administration's intent to move against water fluoridation nationally and has repeatedly claimed fluoride causes 'profound IQ loss' and other health harms; the FDA action against ingestible supplements followed under his HHS oversight after the water-fluoridation push itself proved outside FDA's direct regulatory reach.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Fluoride is one of the most effective, low-cost tools for preventing tooth decay, particularly for children without access to fluoridated water. **The American Dental Association and American Academy of Pediatrics both opposed the FDA's restriction, warning it removes a supported option for exactly the population -- children in non-fluoridated, often lower-income rural communities -- who benefit most, and that restricting supply will likely raise cavity rates in those areas.** The National Institutes of Health has said toxic fluoride overdoses are rare accidents, not a risk from standard supplement or water-fluoridation dosing, cutting against the safety rationale cited for the restriction.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No independently quantified national estimate of cavity-rate increase or dollar cost attributable specifically to this restriction was identified in sourcing reviewed; the harm case here rests on the established dental-health consensus (ADA, AAP, NIH) that fluoride supplementation is a safe, effective, and until now clinically recommended prevention tool being narrowed on disputed scientific grounds, rather than on a modeled figure.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of events (Utah's law, RFK Jr.'s public statements, the FDA's October 31, 2025 marketing-restriction action, and ADA/AAP opposition), corroborated by CNN, NBC News, STAT News, and ProPublica's detailed reporting on the FDA action and Paxton's parallel toothpaste-marketing investigations. MODERATE confidence on classifying this as a Corporate Deregulation consumer_safety rollback rather than a Government Services Redirection entry -- Utah's own ban is a state action outside this tracker's federal scope and is included here only as context for the coordinated national campaign RFK Jr. publicly announced; the entry's tracked action is anchored specifically to the FDA's federal marketing restriction.

rule_name: FDA's Category 2 restricted-compounding list for peptide drugs (BPC-157, TB-500, and related unapproved peptides)
status: Partially loosened, outcome unresolved -- FDA removed BPC-157 and 11 other peptides from the restricted Category 2 list in April 2026 without adding them to the permitted Category 1 list, leaving a regulatory gray zone; a July 2026 advisory panel narrowly recommended Category 1 addition for BPC-157 tied to one specific indication, but FDA has proposed NOT adding it to the compounding bulks list, with no final resolution expected before late 2026 at the earliest
date_of_action: 2023 (FDA's original Category 2 restriction, citing cancer/liver/kidney/heart risks) through 2026-07 (PCAC advisory vote); ongoing
original_rule_summary: In 2023, under the Biden administration, FDA placed nearly 20 peptide substances -- including BPC-157 (marketed for injury healing/inflammation) and TB-500 (banned by international sports authorities) -- on its Category 2 list of substances compounding pharmacies should not produce, based on a determination that these peptides 'present significant safety risks' given a near-total lack of human clinical testing, most safety data coming only from animal studies, and specific concerns about cancer and liver, kidney, and heart problems.
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a self-described peptide user who told Joe Rogan 'I'm a big fan of peptides ... I've used them myself and with really good effect on a couple of injuries,' repeatedly pledged throughout 2025 to loosen FDA restrictions on peptides even while acknowledging gray-market safety risks ('With the gray market you have no idea if you're getting a good product'). Unapproved peptides had already become popular among wellness influencers and 'Make America Healthy Again' (MAHA) supporters -- including longevity influencer Gary Brecka, who sells peptide formulas directly through his own website -- despite the FDA's existing restriction and repeated public warnings about contamination, allergic reactions, and quality-control risks given the near-total absence of human safety data. On February 27, 2026, Kennedy announced that approximately 14 of the 19 restricted peptides would be moved from Category 2 back to Category 1 (the list of substances permitted for compounding). FDA followed on April 15, 2026 by removing BPC-157 and eleven other peptides from Category 2 entirely -- but without adding them to Category 1, leaving them in a regulatory gray zone, neither explicitly prohibited nor affirmatively authorized for compounding. FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) then met July 23-24, 2026 and voted narrowly, 8-6, to recommend adding BPC-157 to Category 1 -- but only tied to a specific proposed ulcerative-colitis indication, not a blanket recommendation, and over continued objections from FDA's own scientists about the absence of human clinical data. As of this entry, FDA has proposed NOT adding BPC-157 to the formal 503A compounding bulks list despite the panel's recommendation, and a final compounding pathway is not expected to be resolved before late 2026 at the earliest, if ever.

rule_name: FDA's longstanding requirement that new drugs be supported by two independent clinical studies before approval
status: Finalized (policy change announced)
date_of_action: 2026-02-18 (announcement, per AP reporting)
original_rule_summary: FDA has long applied a default expectation that new drug approvals be supported by two independent, adequate, and well-controlled clinical studies -- a standard intended to guard against a single trial's results being a statistical fluke, methodological artifact, or site-specific anomaly, and to provide independent replication of a drug's safety and efficacy findings before it reaches the market.
what_changed: This policy had an internal antecedent conflict that predates its formal announcement. Dr. Richard Pazdur -- a 26-year FDA veteran Makary had personally recruited to lead the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) on November 11, 2025, reportedly with promises of autonomy -- publicly and internally raised legal and safety objections within days of taking the role, telling colleagues the plan to reduce the standard evidentiary bar to a single clinical trial in many cases 'is not sufficiently transparent and could be illegal,' and separately raised similar concerns about Makary's National Priority Voucher program, which aimed to compress drug review timelines from 10-12 months to 1-2 months. The dispute came to a head when Pazdur was handed a prepared press release containing a quotation attributed to himself endorsing the reduced trial requirements and was told, in his own words, to 'just agree to it' -- which he characterized as breaching 'this wall between the commissioner's office and the review staff.' Pazdur filed his retirement on December 2, 2025, barely three weeks into the CDER director role, and left by the end of that month; HHS defended the underlying changes as necessary reform and characterized Pazdur himself as indecisive. FDA announced it will end its longstanding two-independent-study requirement for new drug approvals, moving to a default standard of a single trial, with the stated goal of accelerating drug approvals. The change was led by FDA Commissioner Marty Makary and vaccine/biologics official Dr. Vinay Prasad -- the same official whose office separately refused to even review Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine application over trial-design objections (see fda-moderna-mrna-flu-vaccine-refusal-2026.json), creating an apparent tension between accelerating approval standards for new drugs generally while applying an unusually strict, refusal-to-file standard in that specific vaccine case. Days later, Commissioner Makary announced a related acceleration measure: a pilot 'Reviewer Recognition and Excellence' program offering quarterly cash bonuses (starting around August 2026) to drug reviewers who complete evaluations ahead of schedule, tied to 'weighted time savings' and work-quality/complexity metrics. Makary told FDA staff the payments were meant to 'recognize and reward staff who find ways to be more efficient,' and that securing approval for the bonuses took 'some wrangling.'

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Marty Makary / Dr. Vinay Prasad
primary_proponent.role: FDA Commissioner / FDA vaccine and biologics official
primary_proponent.note: The administration's stated rationale is accelerating the pace of drug approvals and reducing development costs and timelines for pharmaceutical companies.

corporate_beneficiaries: Pharmaceutical companies seeking faster, lower-cost paths to drug approval, since a single required trial substantially reduces development time and cost compared to two independent studies

estimated_health_impact.summary: Replication across independent studies has historically served as a safeguard against approving drugs based on results that don't hold up under a second trial -- **a single-trial default standard increases the risk that approved drugs' safety/efficacy profiles rest on findings that would not have replicated**, a tradeoff FDA is making explicitly in favor of faster approval timelines.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: FDA retains discretion to require additional studies for specific drugs under the new default policy; this entry documents the announced change in the default standard, not a claim that every future approval under it will prove unsafe or ineffective.

status: Finalized (guidance permanently rescinded and replaced)
