rule_name: Public-lands oil, gas, and coal extraction rules -- bonding requirements and methane venting/flaring standards
status: Proposed Repeal -- rulemaking announced June 2026
date_of_action: 2026-06 (Interior's proposal announced)
original_rule_summary: Biden-era Interior Department rules required oil and gas companies drilling on public lands to post financial bonds of up to $500,000 to guarantee funds are available to clean up and plug wells after extraction ends, and required companies to detail plans to limit methane emissions -- including restrictions on venting and flaring, both of which release methane, a potent greenhouse gas -- when applying for drilling permits.
what_changed: The Interior Department, under Secretary Doug Burgum, proposed rolling back regulations for oil, gas, and coal extraction on public lands. The proposal would cut the bonding amount companies must post to guarantee well cleanup from $500,000 to $25,000 -- a 95% reduction -- weaken environmental reporting obligations, and eliminate the requirement that companies detail methane-limiting plans when applying for drilling permits, while revising the definitions governing when venting and flaring are authorized. Burgum characterized the changes as advancing 'energy dominance' by cutting red tape that has 'historically deterred investment.' Re-verified 2026-08-16: the proposal's bond cuts apply at two levels -- the statewide bond drops from $500,000 to $25,000 (a 95% reduction, as above) and the individual per-lease bond drops from $150,000 to $10,000 (a ~93% reduction), per Center for Western Priorities' detailed review of the proposed rule text. The same rulemaking package separately proposes shrinking public comment periods for oil and gas lease sales from 90 days to 10 days, by eliminating both 30-day scoping and 30-day draft-document comment periods. The proposal's own public comment period remains open through August 24, 2026; no final rule has been published. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the proposal was formally published in the Federal Register on June 24, 2026 as "Oil and Gas Leasing" (BLM-2025-0037, FR doc. 2026-12734), confirming this is now the operative proposed-rule text rather than only a June announcement. Its public comment period is scheduled to close August 24, 2026 -- still open as of this recheck, two days out -- with no final rule published. Update 2026-08-30: the proposal's public comment period closed as scheduled on August 24, 2026. Coverage of the closure (North Dakota Monitor, Aug. 24, 2026) documented landowner and environmental-group opposition specifically to the split-estate notice/comment-period provisions -- New Mexico landowner Don Schreiber, speaking at a press conference organized by the Western Organization of Resource Councils, summarized the concern as 'No notice, no voice, no future.' No final rule has been published as of this update.

Re-verified 2026-08-16: the proposal's bond cuts apply at two levels -- the statewide bond drops from $500,000 to $25,000 (a 95% reduction, as above) and the individual per-lease bond drops from $150,000 to $10,000 (a ~93% reduction), per Center for Western Priorities' detailed review of the proposed rule text. The same rulemaking package separately proposes shrinking public comment periods for oil and gas lease sales from 90 days to 10 days, by eliminating both 30-day scoping and 30-day draft-document comment periods. The proposal's own public comment period remains open through August 24, 2026; no final rule has been published. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the proposal was formally published in the Federal Register on June 24, 2026 as "Oil and Gas Leasing" (BLM-2025-0037, FR doc. 2026-12734), confirming this is now the operative proposed-rule text rather than only a June announcement. rule_name: 5% Cost Safe Harbor for Establishing 'Beginning of Construction' on Wind and Solar Projects (IRC Sections 45Y/48E Clean Electricity Tax Credits)
status: Weakened, then vacated by a federal court -- IRS Notice 2025-42 (Aug. 15, 2025) eliminated the safe harbor; the U.S. District Court for D.D.C. vacated the notice in its entirety on June 6, 2026, finding it arbitrary and capricious, and remanded to the IRS
date_of_action: 2025-08-15 (Notice 2025-42 issued) through 2026-06-06 (vacated by federal court)
original_rule_summary: Before this action, developers of wind and most solar projects could establish that construction had 'begun' for purposes of qualifying for the Clean Electricity Production Credit (IRC Section 45Y) and Clean Electricity Investment Credit (IRC Section 48E) either by satisfying a physical-work test or by incurring at least 5% of a project's total cost before a deadline -- the '5% Safe Harbor,' a longstanding IRS administrative rule that let projects lock in credit eligibility years before construction was physically underway, which developers, financiers, and utilities had relied on for planning and financing large-scale projects.
what_changed: On August 15, 2025, Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2025-42, implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's (signed July 4, 2025) phase-out of wind and solar tax credits pursuant to Executive Order 14315 (July 7, 2025). The notice eliminated the 5% Safe Harbor for wind projects and for solar projects exceeding 1.5 megawatts that had not already established beginning-of-construction status under prior guidance by September 1, 2025 -- leaving the stricter 'physical work of a significant nature' test as the only way such projects could qualify. Industry groups said this would harm projects that had been in planning, design, and financing for months or years while relying on the 5% Safe Harbor's availability. The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) said political attacks on solar and storage -- including this notice, the broader OBBBA tax-credit phase-out, and other executive/agency actions -- threatened more than 500 planned projects totaling nearly 116 gigawatts, over half of all U.S. power capacity planned to be built through 2030, and could cut previously projected 2025-2030 solar installations (up to 330 GW) by as much as 38%. Industry groups and Democratic lawmakers contrasted this with China, which added more than 430 gigawatts of new wind and solar capacity in 2025 alone -- more than the U.S. and the rest of the world combined in the first half of the year -- arguing the U.S. rollback would cede clean-energy manufacturing and deployment leadership. A coalition led by the Oregon Environmental Council sued, and **on June 6, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Oregon Environmental Council v. IRS, No. CV-25-4400) vacated Notice 2025-42 in its entirety, ruling the IRS had acted arbitrarily and capriciously under the Administrative Procedure Act by eliminating the Safe Harbor without adequately addressing extensive industry comments documenting substantial reliance on it, and remanded the matter back to the IRS**. The ruling restored the 5% Safe Harbor, at least pending any further IRS action or appeal.

rule_name: Joint-Employer Standard Narrowing (NLRB)
administration: Trump II (2025-present) -- corrected from an earlier draft that misdated this as a First Term action
status: Fully Repealed (2023 rule withdrawn; 2020 standard reinstated)
date_of_action: 2026-02-25 (final rule); effective 2026-02-27
original_rule_summary: The NLRB's joint-employer standard determines when two companies (e.g. a franchisor and franchisee, or a company and its staffing agency) can both be held liable for labor law violations and both required to bargain collectively with the same workers. A 2023 Biden-era rule broadened the standard to include 'indirect' or 'reserved' (even unexercised) control over terms like wages, work rules, or health and safety -- making it easier to hold parent companies/franchisors jointly liable.
what_changed: The 2023 rule was vacated by a federal court in March 2024 as 'arbitrary and capricious.' **The NLRB (with its quorum restored) formally withdrew the 2023 rule and reinstated the narrower 2020 first-Trump-term standard: an entity is now a joint employer only if it 'possesses and exercises substantial direct and immediate control' over essential terms of employment (wages, benefits, hours, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, direction). Indirect or unexercised control no longer counts.**

primary_proponent.name: National Labor Relations Board (agency-level action)
primary_proponent.note: No single named Board member or Chairman was clearly identified as the primary individual driver in sourcing found this session -- the NLRB characterized the rulemaking as 'ministerial,' implementing the court's vacatur rather than a new policy choice by named leadership. Flag attribution as agency-level, not individual, until further verified.

corporate_beneficiaries: Franchisors, staffing agencies, and businesses using subcontractors -- explicitly named as beneficiaries in legal analysis of the rule

estimated_health_impact.summary: Minimal direct physical health impact. The harm is corporate accountability: narrowing joint-employer liability limits the ability to hold parent companies/franchisors responsible for labor violations (including workplace safety violations) occurring at a franchisee's or contractor's site, since the parent company is less likely to be considered a joint employer absent direct, exercised control.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health/safety figure exists for this rule -- it is a liability-allocation rule, not a safety standard itself. The health-relevant argument is indirect: reduced accountability for the entity best positioned to enforce safety standards across a franchise/contractor network.

Two things to flag: (1) this is a Trump II action from Feb. 2026, not Trump I as an earlier version of this tracker listed -- the 2020 rule referenced here was Trump I, but the specific rollback being tracked (reversing the 2023 expansion) happened this year; (2) no individual proponent is clearly named in sourcing, unlike most other entries in this tracker. rule_name: Light- and Medium-Duty Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Standards (Model Year 2027+)
status: Fully Repealed, effective 2026-04-20. Challenges by a 40-member coalition of states, cities and counties, and by health and environmental groups, are pending together in the D.C. Circuit (No. 26-1037). As of 2026-09-18, petitioners' July motion to pause the case was undecided; no merits ruling.
date_of_action: 2025 (Executive Order 14,154, 'Unleashing American Energy', directed the review); EPA's final rule rescinding the underlying 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and eliminating GHG emission standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles/engines was finalized 2026-02-12 (published in the Federal Register 2026-02-18), effective 2026-04-20
original_rule_summary: EPA tailpipe emissions standards for new light- and medium-duty vehicles beginning model year 2027, designed to cut vehicle greenhouse gas emissions and accelerate the market shift toward more efficient and electric vehicles; also produced fuel-cost savings for individual drivers.
what_changed: EPA fully repealed the standards, citing Executive Order 14,154. The repeal removes both the emissions limits and the associated fuel-economy-driven consumer savings that came with them. EPA's Feb. 12, 2026 final rule went further than a standalone repeal of this one rule: **it rescinded the 2009 Endangerment Finding itself, the underlying legal finding that GHG emissions from motor vehicles endanger public health, on the theory that Clean Air Act Section 202(a)(1) does not authorize EPA to set vehicle emission standards in response to global climate change concerns, and that the standards would not materially affect the health and welfare risks the 2009 finding identified** -- eliminating not just the light/medium-duty MY2027+ standards this entry tracks, but GHG standards for heavy-duty vehicles/engines as well. The rule was published in the Federal Register on Feb. 18, 2026 and took effect April 20, 2026. EPA said it does not affect its separate criteria-pollutant (soot- and smog-forming) vehicle standards or NHTSA's fuel-economy rules. Health, environmental and public-interest groups led by the American Public Health Association petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review on Feb. 18, 2026 (American Public Health Association v. EPA, No. 26-1037). On March 19, 2026 a 40-member coalition of 23 states, the District of Columbia, the U.S. Virgin Islands, nine cities, five counties and Pennsylvania's environmental agency, co-led by the attorneys general of New York, Massachusetts, California and Connecticut, filed its own petition, which the court is hearing alongside the groups' case. On July 29, 2026 the health groups, the state coalition and most other petitioners moved to hold the case in abeyance; EPA and 24 states intervening on its side opposed the motion on Aug. 10, 2026. As of the docket's Sept. 18, 2026 entries, the court had not ruled on that motion or on the merits.

primary_proponent.note: Signed the February 2026 final rule. On March 12, 2025 he announced the 31-action deregulatory package that launched the reconsideration, which EPA billed as the 'Biggest Deregulatory Action in U.S. History.'

estimated_health_impact.summary: The repealed standards were projected by EPA's own 2024 analysis to prevent about 2,577 premature deaths from fine-particle and ozone pollution in the year 2055, with fine-particle health benefits valued at about $10.9 billion a year. Drivers stand to lose about $11.4 billion a year in net consumer savings (fuel, maintenance and repair savings minus higher vehicle costs). Counting about $78.7 billion a year in climate benefits and netting out compliance costs, NYU's Institute for Policy Integrity puts $101.9 billion a year in net benefits at risk, the largest of any rollback in its tracker.

original_rule_summary: Consumers Energy had planned to retire the J.H. Campbell coal plant on May 31, 2025 and DTE Energy's Monroe plant faced similar planned closure, consistent with Michigan's own clean-energy transition plans and the utilities' own long-term resource planning, which had determined the aging coal plants -- among the dirtiest in the U.S. -- were no longer economically or environmentally justified to keep operating.
what_changed: On May 23, 2025, the Trump administration's Department of Energy declared an electrical-supply 'national energy emergency' and issued an emergency order forcing Consumers Energy to keep the J.H. Campbell coal plant operating past its planned May 31, 2025 retirement date, overriding the utility's own retirement plan and Michigan's clean-energy planning. DTE Energy's Monroe plant faced a similar forced-extension order. DOE issued repeated additional emergency orders extending the forced operation: a second and third order continued the extensions through 2025, a fourth order in February 2026 extended operation an additional 90 days (to May 18, 2026), for a cumulative extension of 270+ days past the original planned retirement. Environmental and public-interest groups, state attorneys general, and even the utilities themselves challenged the orders in court as an illegal use of emergency authority to override routine utility retirement decisions absent an actual demonstrated grid emergency.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: DOE, under Secretary Wright, issued each of the successive emergency orders forcing the plants to remain operational.

corporate_beneficiaries: Coal-mining and coal-transport industry suppliers to the affected plants

estimated_health_impact.summary: **The J.H. Campbell and Monroe plants are among the highest-emitting coal facilities in the U.S., together producing nearly half of Michigan's power-sector greenhouse gas emissions and releasing pollutants including arsenic and heavy metals into local water**; forcing continued operation past their planned retirement extends these environmental and public-health exposures beyond what state and utility planning had already determined was no longer justified.

rule_name: MSHA silica exposure rule reconsideration/pause and NIOSH functional elimination
agency: Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Dept. of Labor and HHS respectively
status: Indefinitely stayed pending judicial review (8th Circuit stay, originally granted April 11, 2025, formally extended to the MNM conforming amendments via an April 6, 2026 Federal Register notice; the litigation abeyance itself was further extended by at least two more months on August 10, 2026) -- a stronger, clearer status than 'delayed/paused, escalating toward reconsideration,' since the entire rule including the MNM compliance deadline is now confirmed covered by the same court-ordered stay, and the abeyance period MSHA and industry petitioners are using to negotiate has now been running, with court approval, for over a year; Weakened to point of functional elimination (NIOSH)
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (initial enforcement pause); litigation and reconsideration process ongoing as of mid-2025 through at least Oct 2025
original_rule_summary: A new MSHA silica exposure rule (finalized April 18, 2024 under the Biden administration; effective June 17, 2024) would halve the allowable exposure limit to respirable crystalline silica dust (to 50 micrograms/cubic meter) for coal and metal/nonmetal (MNM) miners, requiring enhanced monitoring, medical surveillance, and respiratory protection, targeting silicosis, black lung disease, and other respiratory illness. Separately, NIOSH is the federal agency that conducts the injury/fatality research and certifies respiratory protection equipment underlying OSHA and MSHA rulemaking.
what_changed: MSHA announced an enforcement pause for coal mine operators on April 8, 2025 (initially through Aug 18, 2025), citing 'unforeseen NIOSH restructuring' affecting the supply of certified respirators and dust monitors. Separately and significantly, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted industry groups (National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association; National Mining Association) a temporary stay of the rule on April 4, 2025, before MSHA's own pause was announced. By around October 2025, MSHA announced it would 'engage in limited rulemaking to reconsider' portions of the rule under ongoing litigation -- a materially stronger action than an administrative enforcement pause, since it signals MSHA intends to substantively rewrite parts of the rule, not just delay its start date. The metal/nonmetal (MNM) compliance deadline of April 8, 2026 has now passed as of this entry's last verification; this entry's sourcing does not confirm whether that deadline was met, further paused, or is itself subject to the same reconsideration process -- flag for follow-up. Separately, the administration's restructuring eliminated significant NIOSH research capacity (reported layoffs of 870+ NIOSH employees) and closed 11 OSHA field offices in states with the highest workplace fatality rates, plus 34 MSHA offices. Update: this entry previously flagged the passed April 8, 2026 MNM compliance deadline as needing follow-up. That's now resolved -- on April 6, 2026, MSHA published a Federal Register notice formally delaying the effective date of the MNM conforming amendments, confirming the deadline is covered by the same 8th Circuit stay (originally granted April 11, 2025) that paused the coal-sector provisions, rather than having separately taken effect or lapsed unaddressed. MSHA continues enforcing the pre-2024-rule standards in the interim and states it will publish a further Federal Register notice once the judicial stay is terminated. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the rule's status -- the 8th Circuit has granted the parties' request to hold the litigation in abeyance while they attempt to resolve the challenge through negotiation, rather than proceeding to a ruling; MSHA reiterated its intent to pursue limited reconsideration rulemaking in a January 2026 status update to the court, consistent with what this entry already documents. Re-verified 2026-08-22: on August 10, 2026, the 8th Circuit granted MSHA's request to extend the litigation abeyance by at least another two months, per West Virginia Gazette-Mail reporting -- MSHA itself asked the court to keep the rule in legal limbo rather than the industry petitioners driving this extension, continuing the negotiated-resolution posture already documented rather than moving toward a ruling or a reconsideration proposal.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Labor leadership under the Trump II administration
primary_proponent.role: MSHA and OSHA are both housed under DOL
primary_proponent.note: Reporting on the specific individual driving the NIOSH cuts ties them to the administration's broader federal workforce restructuring effort (DOGE-linked); a single named proponent for this specific action was not clearly identified in available sourcing -- flag as lower-confidence on attribution and verify before using in debate. The litigation itself was initiated by industry petitioners (NSSGA, National Mining Association), not the administration, though MSHA's subsequent reconsideration rulemaking is an administration action responding to that litigation.

corporate_beneficiaries: Coal and metal/nonmetal mining operators subject to the paused/reconsidered stricter silica exposure limit
National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association and National Mining Association member companies specifically, as the litigants who obtained the initial stay

estimated_health_impact.summary: The Department of Labor's own prior estimate for the silica rule (before the pause/reconsideration) projected substantial prevented deaths and illness -- pausing enforcement and reconsidering the rule puts those prevented cases at risk. Notably, a bipartisan-leaning congressional signal exists on the other side: the Senate Appropriations Committee approved report language (July 31, 2025) directing MSHA to 'fully and effectively enforce' the rule and not use funds to weaken it -- worth citing as a counterpoint showing this is contested even within Congress, not a uniformly one-sided rollback. This is no longer purely a modeled/projected risk: **black lung clinics across Appalachia report a real, observed surge in cases, including younger miners (in their 30s and 40s) developing severe and often fatal forms of the disease, driven in part by deeper mining through silica-rich rock as easily accessible coal seams are depleted** -- a materializing harm alongside DOL's original prevented-case estimate, not a replacement for it. As of November 2025, AP reported NIOSH's own screening data (11,500 central Appalachian miners' X-rays, mid-2020 through mid-2025) showing 55% of screened miners with some form of black lung and a 62% rate among those screened in just the most recent year -- while NIOSH's own screening and mobile-testing staff were themselves being cut and partially reinstated during the same period documented below, and MSHA's silica-rule enforcement remained paused.

Primary proponent attribution remains the weak point, unchanged. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to report; the abeyance-for-negotiation detail is corroborated by Conn Maciel Carey's MSHA Defense Report. Re-verified 2026-07-28: Appalachian Voices, Undark, and Yale E360 corroborate an observed rise in severe black-lung cases among younger miners, giving this entry both a modeled DOL estimate and real-world clinical evidence of the harm the paused rule was meant to prevent. Re-verified 2026-08-14: added AP's November 2025 reporting of NIOSH's own screening-data figures (55%/62% prevalence), a third independent data point alongside DOL's modeled estimate and the Undark/Yale E360 clinical account -- also notes NIOSH's black-lung screening staff were themselves cut and partially reinstated during the same window, tying this entry's staffing-cut and health-outcome threads together directly. Re-verified 2026-08-22: corroborated via West Virginia Gazette-Mail that the 8th Circuit granted at least a further two-month abeyance extension on August 10, 2026, at MSHA's own request. Primary proponent attribution remains unresolved -- no current MSHA leadership was named in this or prior searches as personally driving the agency's position; continue flagging this as the entry's weak point rather than treating it as settled. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- the 8th Circuit abeyance (extended at least two more months on August 10, 2026) remains in effect; no ruling or new reconsideration proposal identified. Primary proponent attribution remains unresolved.

rule_name: PFAS ('Forever Chemical') Restrictions on Military Firefighting Foam and Base Cleanup, FY2026 NDAA
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- mixed final outcome, distinct from the original committee-stage rollback
date_of_action: 2025-08 (committee-stage provisions first reported) through 2025-12-18 (President Trump signed the final FY2026 NDAA, P.L. 119-60)
original_rule_summary: A 2020-2023 statutory framework (building on earlier NDAAs) required DOD to stop purchasing PFAS-based aqueous film-forming firefighting foam (AFFF) by October 2023 and stop using it by October 2024, paused open burning/incineration of PFAS-contaminated foam and waste pending safer disposal methods, and restricted DOD's purchase of everyday PFAS-treated products (cookware, carpets, etc.).
what_changed: Committee-stage House and Senate FY2026 NDAA text (reported August-September 2025 by the Guardian, The Hill, and Environmental Working Group) would have delayed the firefighting-foam phaseout, repealed the incineration/open-burning pause, rescinded the everyday-PFAS-product purchase restrictions, and cut PFAS-site cleanup funding versus FY2024 levels. The final, enacted NDAA (signed December 18, 2025) is a mixed outcome, not a straight rollback as first reported: it extends DOD's authority to purchase PFAS-based firefighting foam through 2026 and use existing stockpiles through 2028 (rather than the 2023/2024 phaseout deadlines), and grants DOD authority to destroy PFAS waste using 'innovative technologies' approved by federal or state regulators -- softer than the committee-stage full repeal of the incineration pause, but still a loosening of the prior blanket moratorium. The final bill did NOT add new restrictions on PFAS-treated firefighter turnout gear, a gap several outlets flagged as a missed opportunity. Separately, and cutting the other direction, the final NDAA also created a new, first-ever high-level DOD Coordinator position dedicated to PFAS-impacted defense communities, which Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), who pushed the provision, called 'the strongest federal reform yet for PFAS-impacted defense communities.' Independent of the NDAA itself, Senate Democrats separately pressed the Pentagon in November 2025 over an administrative decision to delay some PFAS site cleanups.

primary_proponent.name: Roger Wicker
primary_proponent.note: Senate Armed Services Committee text carried the most aggressive PFAS rollback provisions (including full repeal of the incineration/open-burning pause, later softened in the final conference outcome); House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers (R-AL) also a central figure in the joint bill's development.

corporate_beneficiaries: PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam manufacturers and defense contractors reliant on existing PFAS-based foam stockpiles
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce publicly lobbied to retain the rollback provisions in the NDAA text

estimated_health_impact.summary: **PFAS ('forever chemicals') from firefighting foam have contaminated drinking water and groundwater at hundreds of military installations, with exposure linked to certain cancers, thyroid disruption, immune effects, and other health harms.** The rollback provisions extend the window in which DOD may keep purchasing and using PFAS-based foam rather than accelerating the phaseout already in law; the cleanup-funding-cut figure reported at the committee stage was not confirmed against the final enacted bill's own text or appropriations figures.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: The committee-stage $186.4-200M cleanup-funding-cut figure comes from August-September 2025 reporting on House/Senate committee bill text, before conference and final passage; this entry could not confirm that figure against the enacted NDAA's own final funding tables or a subsequent appropriations bill, and it should be presented as the reported committee-stage figure, not a confirmed final cut, until re-verified. The 600,000+ exposed-servicemembers and installation-count figures are pre-existing background scale (from 2022-2023 DOD/EWG data), included for context on what's at stake generally, not as a measurement of this specific rollback's marginal health effect.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the enacted foam purchase/use-deadline extension and the destruction-technology authority replacing the committee-stage full incineration-pause repeal, corroborated across The Hill and Holland & Knight's FY2026 NDAA legal analysis. HIGH confidence the final bill also added a new DOD PFAS-communities Coordinator role, per Rep. Fitzpatrick's own press release. MODERATE-LOW confidence on the cleanup-funding-cut dollar figure, which comes from committee-stage reporting (Guardian/EWG, August-September 2025) and was not independently confirmed against the final enacted bill's own funding tables. This entry corrects an earlier framing (a straight 'PFAS rollback' based on August-September 2025 committee-stage reporting) to reflect the mixed final outcome actually signed into law December 18, 2025.

short_summary: Extended DOD's PFAS firefighting-foam use through 2028 and eased the incineration pause, while also adding a new PFAS-communities coordinator role.

rule_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Rescission of the Neighborhood Access and Equity Transportation Grant Program
agency: Congress / Department of Transportation (Federal Highway Administration)
status: Fully Repealed -- all unobligated program funds rescinded by statute
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed, rescinding unobligated funds)
original_rule_summary: The Neighborhood Access and Equity program, created by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 with $3.2 billion in funding and administered by the Federal Highway Administration, funded local projects to reconnect communities divided by highways, improve walkability and pedestrian/cyclist safety, and build transportation infrastructure in disadvantaged areas -- both Democratic- and Republican-represented districts received awards.
what_changed: As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Congress rescinded all unobligated funds awarded under the Neighborhood Access and Equity program. Transportation for America found that only about $777 million of the program's $3.2 billion had actually been obligated (contractually committed) by the time of rescission, leaving roughly $2.4 billion in already-awarded but not-yet-obligated grants clawed back -- reported elsewhere as approximately $2.2-3.1 billion depending on the specific accounting window and whether the full program authorization or only the awarded-but-unobligated portion is counted. The cuts hit projects in both parties' districts: in Jacksonville, Florida, a $147 million award (the largest federal grant in the city's history, developed with the Jacksonville Transportation Authority and nonprofit Groundwork Jacksonville) to build new links between urban neighborhoods was rescinded; in St. George, Utah, an $87 million award to build two underpasses relieving chronic traffic congestion caused by an interstate highway dividing the city was rescinded; a $75 million highway-rebuild project in Montana and infrastructure fixes in Kentucky's Bowling Green and rural Maryland were also affected, among 55 total projects nationwide, 19 of them in Republican-held districts. Congressional Republicans and the administration framed the rescission as part of a broader effort to eliminate federal programs using the terms 'equity' or 'DEI,' consistent with Trump's stated initiative against what he called 'radical and wasteful government D.E.I. programs' -- even though the underlying projects were physical road, sidewalk, and underpass infrastructure, not diversity training or personnel programs.

primary_proponent.name: House and Senate Republicans (OBBBA reconciliation bill)
primary_proponent.role: Passed the rescission as part of the broader FY2025 reconciliation act
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing this specific rescission; it was adopted as part of the broader OBBBA reconciliation package targeting programs framed as 'equity' initiatives.

estimated_health_impact.summary: **The rescinded projects were pedestrian, cyclist, and traffic-safety infrastructure (underpasses to separate pedestrians from highway traffic, walkability improvements) whose loss removes documented safety and mobility improvements from the affected communities**, though no source reviewed quantifies a specific injury or mortality impact.

rule_name: Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) Standards, Model Years 2022-2031 ("SAFE Vehicles Rule III")
agency: NHTSA (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration), Department of Transportation
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- final rule signed by NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison September 25, 2026 and released September 28; effective 60 days after Federal Register publication. Projected 2031 fleet average cut to about 34.9 mpg from about 50.4 mpg.
date_of_action: 2025-12-02 (proposed); 2026-09-25 (final rule signed, released 2026-09-28)
original_rule_summary: Biden-era CAFE fuel economy standards for passenger cars and light trucks required the industry fleet average to reach roughly 49.1 mpg by model year 2026, rising to roughly 50.4 mpg by model year 2031.
what_changed:
NHTSA's SAFE Vehicles Rule III, proposed December 2, 2025, would cut those requirements to roughly 30.4 mpg (MY2026) and 34.5 mpg (MY2031) -- an approximately 18.7 mpg reduction by 2031 relative to the existing standards -- while also retroactively resetting the MY2022 baseline to 36 mpg for passenger cars and 27.7 mpg for light trucks, excluding the outsized fuel-economy credit electric vehicles previously received; **DLA Piper's legal analysis called this an 'unprecedented retroactive change to standards for completed model years' 2022 through 2025, since those vehicles were already manufactured under the old baseline.** The proposal also eliminates the inter-manufacturer credit-trading system and revises the light-duty vehicle fleet classification system. Trump announced the proposal at a White House event on December 3, 2025, flanked by Detroit and global automaker executives; Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said the company 'appreciates the Trump Administration's actions to re-align the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards with real world market conditions.' DOT's own projections claim the changes would cut the average new-vehicle sticker price by about $900 by 2031 and save $109 billion in total over five years. Democratic lawmakers opposing the rollback cited estimates of more than 450 additional premature deaths and nearly 14,000 additional asthma exacerbations nationally if finalized, per The Hill's reporting on their public statement; the specific underlying study behind that figure was not independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed for this entry. Two related-but-legally-distinct actions were bundled into contemporaneous coverage of the administration's broader anti-EV push, but are NOT part of this NHTSA rulemaking and don't yet have their own dedicated entries in this tracker: Congress eliminated the federal EV purchase tax credit and moved up the end date of the home EV-charger installation credit via the 2025 reconciliation bill (a legislative action), and separately voted via the Congressional Review Act to revoke the Clean Air Act waivers that had let California set its own zero-emission-vehicle sales mandates.

Update 2026-09-29: NHTSA finalized the rule. Administrator Jonathan Morrison signed it September 25, 2026, and DOT released it September 28. NHTSA projects the final standards at a fleet average of about 34.9 mpg in model year 2031, against about 49.3 mpg under the 2024 rule (which NHTSA projected at about 50.4 mpg when it issued that rule), and the final rule still revises the standards for model years 2022-2026, fleets NHTSA says manufacturers have already produced in whole or in part. It ends inter-manufacturer trading of credits earned from model year 2028 and changes which vehicles count as light trucks from model year 2030. The 2025 reconciliation law (Pub. L. 119-21) had already set the civil penalty for missing CAFE standards at $0 starting with model year 2022. **NHTSA's own analysis projects 4.6% more gasoline use through 2050, $219.3 billion in fuel savings lost to drivers and $3.9 billion in lost health benefits from added fine-particle pollution (calendar years 2024-2050, 3% discount rate)**, against about $1,289 in up-front savings per model-year-2031 vehicle if manufacturers pass them on; it valued changes in greenhouse-gas and other non-criteria emissions at zero. Duffy said the standards are "making the American dream affordable again."

rule_name: Nuclear waste 'dilute and dispose' policy and spent-fuel reprocessing/recycling framework
status: Signed and in effect; implementation underway
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order signed) through 2026-02 (initial DOE recycling-technology grants awarded)
original_rule_summary: Since the Cold War era, the U.S. has generally pursued a 'dilute and dispose' policy for surplus weapons-grade plutonium -- diluting it with inert material and burying it, rather than reprocessing/recycling it -- specifically to avoid separating out plutonium in a form that could be diverted for weapons use, a nonproliferation safeguard. Commercial spent nuclear fuel from light-water reactors has similarly not been reprocessed domestically for decades, for the same proliferation-risk reasons that led the U.S. to abandon reprocessing in the 1970s.
what_changed: On May 23, 2025, as part of a broader package of nuclear-energy executive orders (including 'Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base'), Trump signed an order directing DOE to halt the surplus-plutonium 'dilute and dispose' program and instead establish a program to process surplus plutonium and make it available for industrial and reactor-fuel use, including for advanced reactor designs and power for AI data centers. The order also directs DOE to develop mechanisms to transfer spent nuclear fuel from commercial light-water reactors to a government-owned, privately operated reprocessing and recycling facility, and to evaluate reprocessing/recycling of DOE- and DoD-managed reactor fuel. On nuclear regulatory structure, the order directs the Secretary of Energy, in consultation with the NRC Chair and OMB Director, to develop a plan to expand domestic uranium conversion and enrichment capacity -- a framework critics say shifts influence over nuclear fuel-cycle decisions toward DOE and the White House relative to the historically independent NRC's safety-focused regulatory role. Implementation proceeded through 2025-2026: DOE issued an RFA in October 2025 to establish a surplus-plutonium industrial-use program, and awarded $19 million in February 2026 to five companies for spent-fuel recycling technology research.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed the executive order directing DOE to reverse the dilute-and-dispose policy and pursue reprocessing/recycling; Energy Secretary Chris Wright's department is responsible for implementation.

corporate_beneficiaries: Advanced nuclear reactor developers and AI data-center operators seeking domestic fuel-cycle capacity
Nuclear fuel recycling/reprocessing technology companies (five awarded DOE R&D funding in February 2026)

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Nuclear nonproliferation experts warn that reprocessing spent fuel and reclaiming plutonium for industrial/reactor use, reversing decades of U.S. policy specifically adopted to avoid creating separated, weapons-usable plutonium stockpiles, increases proliferation risk domestically and could weaken the international nonproliferation norm the U.S. has long promoted by example.** Critics also raise safety concerns about shifting nuclear fuel-cycle oversight structures relative to the NRC's traditionally independent safety-review role.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified figure for increased proliferation risk, radiological exposure risk, or a specific safety-incident probability was identified in sourcing reviewed -- the estimated impact described by experts is a risk/policy-reversal characterization, not a measured outcome, since implementation (actual reprocessing facilities) was still in early R&D/RFA stages as of this entry's creation.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the executive order's existence, date, and specific directives, corroborated by DOE's own fact sheets, the Federal Register notice, and K&L Gates' and CSIS's independent legal/policy analyses. MODERATE confidence on the proliferation-risk characterization, which is expert/advocacy framing rather than a government-commissioned risk assessment finding; should be cited as expert concern, not an established quantified risk.

rule_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Accelerated Wind/Solar Tax-Credit Phase-Out, Plus USDA's Cancellation of Farmland Solar/Wind Funding
agency: Congress / Department of the Treasury (tax-credit phase-out); Department of Agriculture (farmland funding cancellation)
status: Enacted: wind/solar credits end for projects not begun by July 4, 2026 (now passed) unless in service by end of 2027. USDA farmland solar/wind limits imposed Aug. 2025; REAP grant applications halted Mar. 31, 2026 pending new rules.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (H.R. 1 signed) through 2025-08-19 (USDA farmland funding announcement)
original_rule_summary: The Inflation Reduction Act's clean-energy tax credits (for wind and solar generation, among other technologies) allowed projects placed in service on a multi-year timeline to qualify for federal tax credits, supporting project financing industry-wide. Separately, USDA's Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) had provided over $2 billion for renewable energy projects such as solar and wind, according to the agency's website as cited by Reuters (Canary Media counts about $1.2 billion in grants and $2.5 billion in loan guarantees for rural solar since 2014), and USDA's Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan program had been open to wind and solar projects.
what_changed: The House passed its version of H.R. 1, the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' (OBBBA), on May 22, 2025. As the House passed it, The Guardian reported, tax credits for cleaner cars would end in 2025, incentives for wind, solar and even nuclear projects would be scaled down and eliminated by 2032, and home energy-efficiency subsidies would end after 2025. As the Senate neared its vote, AP reported (June 30, 2025) on the stakes for Cartersville, Georgia, in Bartow County, which backed Trump with 75% of the vote all three times he appeared on the ballot: **Cartersville is home to a $5 billion Hyundai Motor Group/SK On battery factory under construction and a $2.3 billion Qcells solar-panel plant, an investment that federal subsidies helped land, with both plants pledging thousands of jobs at average wages of $53,000 a year**. The bill would end the $7,500 EV tax credit and the 40% federal credit that buyers of Qcells panels receive; a Republican county commissioner called the cuts 'a little concerning,' and the mayor said he hoped agreements already in place would be carried out to fulfillment. The Senate rewrote several of the House provisions, passed the bill on July 1, the House passed the Senate version on July 3, and Trump signed it into law on July 4, 2025. The enacted law ends the EV credit after September 30, 2025 and the home energy-efficiency and residential clean-energy credits after 2025, and lets nuclear, hydropower, geothermal and storage keep a longer runway than wind and solar, with their credits phasing down for projects that begin construction after 2033. Wind and solar are cut much sooner: a wind or solar facility loses the clean-electricity production and investment credits unless it begins construction by July 4, 2026 or is placed in service by the end of 2027. A newly added 2.5% production credit for metallurgical coal used in steelmaking covers 2026 through 2029. Reuters called the Senate bill a big blow to renewable energy, and community-solar developers warned it would strand thousands of projects already under development. Other provisions of the same law expanded federal oil, gas and coal leasing, cut oil and gas royalty rates, cut the federal coal royalty rate from 12.5% to no more than 7% through September 2034, and postponed the Inflation Reduction Act's methane waste-emissions charge until 2034. On July 7, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14315 directing the Treasury to strictly enforce the wind and solar termination. Treasury and the IRS followed with Notice 2025-42, which, for projects not begun before September 2, 2025, took away the long-used 5% cost safe harbor for showing that construction had begun (except for solar facilities of 1.5 megawatts or less), leaving the physical-work test. On Monday, August 18, 2025, at an event in Lebanon, Tennessee, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced USDA would no longer fund solar and wind projects on productive farmland; USDA's press release followed on August 19. Effective immediately, wind and solar projects became ineligible for Rural Development's Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan program, and ground-mount solar systems larger than 50kW, or unable to document historical energy usage, became ineligible for the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) guaranteed-loan program and no longer receive priority points for REAP grants. An internal USDA memo, reported by Agri-Pulse and Canary Media, also denied REAP loan guarantees to projects on land the Farm Service Agency certifies as cropland and to systems with any component made in a country named as a foreign adversary, which Canary Media noted covers almost all solar panels; the memo cited Trump's July 7 executive order and carried an August 31, 2026 expiration date. Rollins justified the change by saying 'our prime farmland should not be wasted and replaced with green new deal subsidized solar panels,' and wrote on X that 'millions of acres of prime farmland is left unusable' and that 'this destruction of our farms and prime soil is taking away the futures of the next generation of farmers.' USDA's own research undercuts the scale of that claim: a 2024 USDA Economic Research Service study, summarized in its Amber Waves magazine in September 2024, found wind turbines and solar farms directly affected about 424,000 acres of rural land in 2020, less than 0.05% of the roughly 897 million acres used for farmland, and that agricultural land near solar and wind projects usually remained in agricultural production after development. On March 31, 2026, USDA halted REAP grant applications, saying there would be no further REAP grants until it rewrote the program's regulations to comply with the same executive order; REAP guaranteed-loan applications stayed open, and DTN reported that USDA had awarded no new REAP grants since the administration took office.

primary_proponent.role: Trump signed the OBBBA tax-credit phase-out into law; Rollins announced and directed the USDA farmland-funding cancellation
primary_proponent.note: Trump signed H.R. 1 on July 4, 2025 and signed Executive Order 14315 on July 7 directing strict enforcement of the wind/solar termination; Rollins announced the REAP/loan-program changes at an August 18, 2025 event in Lebanon, Tennessee, and USDA's August 19 press release announced and justified them.

corporate_beneficiaries: Coal producers supplying metallurgical coal for steelmaking (new 2.5% production tax credit, 2026-2029)
Oil and gas leaseholders (expanded federal leasing and lower royalty rates under the same law)

estimated_health_impact.summary: The entry documents financial harm with human effects rather than a sourced health toll. The law cuts off wind and solar tax credits for projects not begun by July 4, 2026 unless they are in service by the end of 2027, and Energy Innovation's model of the final law's energy provisions projects 760,000 lost jobs by 2030, household energy costs about $170 a year higher by 2035, and consumer electricity rates 9-18% higher by 2035. USDA's curbs take away loan and grant support that farmers and rural businesses had used to install solar and cut their energy bills, even though USDA's own research found wind and solar directly affected less than 0.05% of U.S. farmland. DTN reported that USDA had awarded no new REAP grants since the administration took office, and on March 31, 2026 USDA halted REAP grant applications until it rewrites the program's rules.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: The job, energy-cost and rate figures are one think tank's model (Energy Innovation's Energy Policy Simulator) of all the final law's energy provisions, including oil and gas leasing and other credit repeals, not the wind/solar deadlines alone; they are projections, not observed outcomes. Energy Innovation's earlier model of the House-passed bill projected 430 additional premature deaths a year by 2030 and 930 by 2035 from higher air pollution, but that model assumed the House text and a repeal of vehicle emission rules, and its final-law summary gives no health figure, so no health toll is claimed here. The REAP dollar figures measure past support, not a measured loss; the entry has no count of farm projects cancelled by USDA's changes. The 424,000-acre figure is USDA's own research and cuts against Secretary Rollins's rationale; USDA has not reconciled the two in sourcing reviewed.

The OBBBA's wind/solar deadlines are stated in the IRS's own Notice 2025-42 and in law-firm analyses of the enacted text (Sidley Austin, Kirkland & Ellis); the USDA changes are stated in USDA's own August 19, 2025 press release and corroborated by Reuters, DTN/Progressive Farmer and pv magazine USA. The 424,000-acre/0.05% figure comes from USDA's own Economic Research Service research, not an advocacy estimate. The May 22, 2025 House-passage details rest on The Guardian's reporting; the Cartersville example rests on AP's June 30, 2025 reporting, widely republished (GPB, WABE, 11Alive, Fortune), so the copies are not independent corroboration. The job and energy-cost projections are Energy Innovation's modeling, not an agency estimate.

rule_name: Federal buyouts to cancel offshore wind leases; DOE Section 202(c) emergency orders forcing aging coal plants to stay online
agency: Department of the Interior (offshore wind leasing); Department of Energy (Section 202(c) emergency orders); Department of the Treasury (buyout payments)
status: Ongoing -- the administration has agreed to pay $3.9B+ to buy back 12 offshore wind lease areas, and nine states are suing over several of the deals; the D.C. Circuit vacated DOE's first Michigan coal-plant order Sept. 11, 2026, but DOE keeps issuing emergency orders, including for that plant.
date_of_action: 2025-05 (first DOE Section 202(c) coal emergency orders) through 2026-09 (Aug 6 RWE lease buyout; continued coal-plant orders after a Sept 11 court loss)
original_rule_summary: Offshore wind leases had been awarded and projects were underway (including by TotalEnergies off New York and North Carolina) under normal federal leasing and permitting processes established under prior administrations; separately, aging coal plant operators had scheduled retirements through normal grid-planning and utility-commission processes, coordinated with regional grid operators to ensure adequate replacement capacity.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09: the buyout strategy below was the administration's second approach, not its first. In an earlier, more direct phase, Trump officials told a federal court on August 25, 2025 that they would move, no later than September 12, 2025, to remand and vacate the approval for US Wind's Maryland offshore project (designed to power an estimated 718,000 homes), following an already-imposed suspension of offshore leasing and a stop-work order on a Rhode Island wind farm. By late September 2025, the administration had also banned new solar and wind development on federal land and in federal waters and publicly called clean energy a 'scam.' It was these direct-action attempts that federal courts went on to block, prompting the shift to the buyout strategy described below. After federal courts blocked Trump's attempts to halt offshore wind development through direct executive action, the administration shifted to a buyout strategy: paying developers to voluntarily forfeit already-awarded offshore wind leases. By late June 2026, buyout agreements covered nine offshore wind lease areas on the East and West coasts at a cost of roughly $2.7 billion in taxpayer funds. French energy company TotalEnergies forfeited its leases for New York and North Carolina offshore wind projects in exchange for $928 million reimbursing its original lease expenditures -- money TotalEnergies has said it will reinvest into oil and gas projects, including a liquefied natural gas export facility in Texas. Separately, starting in May 2025, the Department of Energy began issuing 90-day emergency orders under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to prevent the retirement of aging coal-fired power plants, overriding operators' own retirement schedules; DOE had used this authority on five coal plants in Colorado, Indiana, Michigan and Washington state by March 2026 (Stateline), including preventing Colorado's Craig Station Unit 1 from retiring one day before its scheduled date, and DOE's order list shows a sixth, Florida's Stanton Energy Center Unit 1, first ordered in June 2026, with all six orders renewed in August-September 2026. Straight Arrow News reported in May 2026 that the cost of keeping these plants open had exceeded $200 million, though the exact amount is unknown, and cited a 2025 Grid Strategies report estimating that total annual ratepayer costs could top $3 billion if more plants scheduled to retire before 2028 were ordered to stay open (Stateline, citing the same firm, reported that as many as 90 aging plants could face such orders, at $3 billion to $6 billion a year); Mother Jones separately reported the administration has directed roughly $1.1 billion specifically toward extending coal plant life, alongside lowered federal coal royalty rates and expanded coal leasing. Added 2026-09-10: the specific figures behind that royalty/leasing action were reported September 29, 2025 -- the administration said it would open 13 million acres of federal land for coal mining, and the Department of Energy, under Energy Secretary Chris Wright, announced $625 million to recommission or modernize coal-fired power plants; separately, the Republican tax bill Trump signed cut the federal coal royalty rate from 12.5% to 7%. At the Interior Department news conference that day, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum described 'mine, baby, mine' as another Trump initiative, framing it alongside the 'drill baby, drill' oil-and-gas push. Added 2026-09-09: the direct-action track this entry documents did not end when the buyout strategy began -- it continued in parallel. The Rhode Island stop-work order referenced above targeted Revolution Wind specifically: an Orsted-owned, $6.2 billion, 704-megawatt project 80% complete (all offshore foundations installed, 45 of 65 turbines up) that would have powered 350,000 homes across Rhode Island and Connecticut, halted by an August 22, 2025 Bureau of Ocean Energy Management order citing unspecified national-security concerns. On December 22, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum expanded this into a broader freeze, pausing five East Coast offshore wind projects -- Vineyard Wind 1 (Massachusetts), Revolution Wind (Rhode Island), Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind/CVOW (Dominion Energy), Sunrise Wind (New York), and Empire Wind 1 (New York) -- citing classified Defense Department reports on 'emerging national security risks.' Burgum later specified the concern publicly: turbine blades and reflective towers allegedly create radar 'clutter' that could obscure detection of 'drone swarms' approaching the East Coast, particularly around New York. Developers and states sued: Dominion Energy filed first, on December 23, 2025, over the Virginia project, followed by Orsted (Revolution Wind) and Equinor (Empire Wind 1) on January 1-2, 2026; Connecticut and Rhode Island joined as plaintiffs, arguing the freeze was arbitrary and unconstitutional given the projects' multi-billion-dollar sunk investment. As in the entry's earlier direct-action phase, courts again ruled against the administration: federal judges granted preliminary injunctions allowing Revolution Wind, Empire Wind 1, and the Dominion Virginia project to resume construction while the underlying lawsuits proceeded. Revolution Wind itself came online, delivering power to the New England grid, by March 13, 2026. Update 2026-09-26: In the five-project freeze litigation, Judge Royce Lamberth ruled for Revolution Wind on January 12, 2026; the federal court in Washington, D.C. granted Empire Wind a preliminary injunction on January 15; the Eastern District of Virginia granted Dominion's CVOW injunction on January 16; Judge Brian Murphy granted Vineyard Wind relief from the stop-work order on January 27; and Lamberth granted Sunrise Wind a preliminary injunction on February 2. Electrek reported that all five projects had secured injunctions and that Burgum allowed the final appeal deadline to lapse. The Interior Department's March 23, 2026 release set TotalEnergies' reimbursement at $133,333,333 for its Carolina Long Bay lease and $795,000,000 for its New York Bight lease. Utility Dive reported on June 30, 2026 that the administration had agreed to buy back nine lease areas for more than $2.6 billion. The Maritime Executive reported that on August 6, 2026 the administration agreed to pay RWE $1.22 billion to give up three U.S. offshore wind leases, its fifth such deal, after earlier deals totaling approximately $2.7 billion, bringing committed reimbursements to more than $3.9 billion; added to the nine lease areas Utility Dive had counted, the RWE deal brought the total to 12 lease areas. Update 2026-10-06: On September 11, 2026, a unanimous D.C. Circuit panel vacated DOE's original May 23, 2025 order keeping Michigan's J.H. Campbell coal plant open, ruling it an unlawful use of Section 202(c); the ruling did not reach DOE's later renewals, and a sixth order still requires the plant to run until November 14, 2026. Michigan's attorney general said Consumers Energy has reported $295 million in Campbell costs from May 2025 to June 30, 2026. DOE kept issuing orders anyway: Al Jazeera/AP reported that Wright ordered a Centralia, Washington coal plant to keep running hours after the ruling, and DOE extended the Colorado Craig unit order a fourth time, to December 25, 2026. On the wind side, Canary Media reported that New York and six other states sued over the TotalEnergies New York lease buyout, and California became the eighth state to sue in late August 2026, over a $120 million Golden State Wind buyout. On September 22, 2026, New York led eight eastern states in two more suits over the Bluepoint Wind and Invenergy deals ($1.4 billion for four leases), and California sued separately over Invenergy's Morro Bay lease, bringing the number of states suing to nine (The Maritime Executive).

rule_name: OSHA 'Improve Tracking of Workplace Injuries and Illnesses' rule — electronic reporting rollback
status: Weakened (partially repealed)
original_rule_summary: 2016 Obama-era OSHA rule requiring employers with 250+ workers at an establishment to electronically submit detailed, itemized workplace injury and illness data (Forms 300, 301, 300A) to OSHA annually, making injury patterns easier for regulators, researchers, and the public to identify.
what_changed: OSHA finalized a rule eliminating the requirement to submit the detailed itemized logs (Forms 300 and 301), leaving only the aggregated summary form (300A). The final rule was published during the 2018-2019 government shutdown. Anti-retaliation protections for injury reporting were left in place.

primary_proponent.name: Alexander Acosta
primary_proponent.note: Department of Labor under Acosta finalized and published the rule; OSHA is a sub-agency of DOL.

corporate_beneficiaries: Large employers (250+ workers) previously subject to detailed injury-log disclosure, particularly in construction and manufacturing

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Labor advocates and unions argued the rollback makes it significantly harder for OSHA, researchers, and the public to detect workplace-injury patterns and target enforcement, since only aggregate (not itemized, establishment-level) data remains available -- an effect on detection and prevention capacity rather than a directly modeled mortality/injury count.**

figures.metric: U.S. workplace deaths per year (context figure, not rollback-specific)
figures.source: Economic Policy Institute, citing BLS data

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No agency or independent body has published a quantified estimate of additional deaths/injuries directly attributable to this specific reporting rollback -- the harm argument is about degraded detection/prevention capacity, not a modeled body count. Present it that way rather than implying a specific casualty figure.

confidence_note: Frame as a transparency/detection-capacity rollback, not a body-count claim -- this is the more defensible, harder-to-rebut version of the argument. Unions (IBEW) and NELP are the sourced critics; note them as advocacy voices, not neutral analysts. Update: 2026-09-06 recheck sweep surfaced a July 21, 2026 Fifth Circuit ruling vacating an OSHA rule requiring mental-health-illness logging on OSHA 300 forms -- verified this concerns a separate OSHA rule, not the 2019 Forms 300/301 electronic-submission rollback tracked here. No development found specific to this entry's own tracked rule.
pull_quote: Roughly 5,000 U.S. workers died on the job in 2016, the baseline year before this rollback — context for what detection capacity injury-log data is meant to support, not a rollback-specific death count.

section_summaries.what_changed: OSHA dropped the requirement to submit detailed injury logs, leaving only aggregated summary data; anti-retaliation protections stayed in place.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: The harm here is blindness, not body count -- regulators lose the itemized data needed to spot injury patterns and aim enforcement.
section_summaries.confidence_note: The stronger, harder-to-rebut argument is reduced injury-detection capacity, not a death count -- and unions/NELP are advocacy sources, not neutral analysts.

rule_name: OSHA workplace-safety inspection and enforcement activity (not a specific rule repeal -- documents an enforcement-practice decline achieved without formally changing underlying safety standards)
agency: Occupational Safety and Health Administration / Department of Labor
status: Completed comparison-period figure (April-September 2025 vs. the same months of 2024); senators asked DOL to answer by March 4, 2026, and no public DOL reply has been reported. OSHA head David Keeling said in September 2026 that OSHA had hired more than 120 new inspectors since May.
date_of_action: April-September 2025 (comparison period), data released 2026-02-18
original_rule_summary: OSHA conducts workplace inspections and issues violation findings -- including 'willful' violation findings, reserved for the most serious, knowing violations of safety standards -- as its primary enforcement mechanism for existing workplace-safety rules, independent of any specific rule needing to change.
what_changed: OSHA statistics provided confidentially to Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office, and released by Warren and five other Democratic senators in a February 18, 2026 letter to the Labor Department, showed OSHA conducted 20% fewer workplace inspections in April through September 2025 than in the same months of 2024, alongside a 42% drop in findings of 'willful' violations -- the most serious enforcement category, reserved for violations OSHA determines were committed with plain indifference to or intentional disregard for employee safety. As with this tracker's separately documented collapse in EPA civil enforcement, this decline was achieved through reduced enforcement activity rather than any formal repeal of the underlying workplace-safety standards, meaning the rules remain on the books but are being enforced against far fewer violators.

estimated_health_impact.summary: **A 42% drop in 'willful' violation findings -- OSHA's most serious enforcement category -- alongside a 20% drop in inspections overall suggests reduced deterrence against the most serious, knowing workplace-safety violations, at a time when the underlying safety standards remain formally in place but are being enforced against fewer employers.**

Warren's office's data release characterizing OSHA's own enforcement statistics; a single comparison period can be affected by staffing transitions and other administrative factors, though the specific and simultaneous decline in both inspection volume and the most serious violation-finding category suggests more than ordinary year-to-year variance.

rule_name: PFAS Drinking Water Rule Rollback (Compliance Extension + Partial Rescission)
status: Proposed Repeal (two linked proposed rules, comment period closed 2026-07-20, public hearing 2026-07-07, not yet finalized)
date_of_action: 2026-05-18 (proposed); intent announced 2025-05-14
original_rule_summary: April 2024 EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation -- the first-ever federal limits on PFAS ('forever chemicals') in drinking water -- set legally enforceable Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for six PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA/GenX, and Hazard Index mixtures), with compliance required by 2029. EPA's own analysis projected the rule would prevent PFAS exposure for approximately 100 million people and prevent thousands of deaths and tens of thousands of serious illnesses over time.
what_changed: EPA proposed two linked rules: (1) rescinding enforceable limits entirely for four of the six regulated PFAS (PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA/GenX, and the Hazard Index mixture), while keeping the PFOA/PFOS limits (4 ppt) technically in place; and (2) extending the PFOA/PFOS compliance deadline by two years, from 2029 to 2031, via a federal exemption framework. Net effect: of the six PFAS regulated in 2024, only two retain enforceable limits, and even those get a longer compliance runway.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the plan in April/May 2025; EPA frames the rescission as correcting a procedural 'failure to follow the clear statutory requirements' of the Safe Drinking Water Act rather than a substantive health disagreement, and states it is 'not seeking comment on... any information about health risks associated with PFAS.'

corporate_beneficiaries: Water utilities facing compliance costs
PFAS manufacturers and industrial users of the four PFAS losing enforceable limits

estimated_health_impact.summary: **EPA's own original 2024 rule projected the full six-PFAS rule would prevent PFAS exposure for ~100 million people and prevent thousands of deaths and tens of thousands of serious illnesses over time -- this is the benefit now partially being unwound by removing 4 of 6 chemicals from enforceable limits and delaying compliance on the remaining 2 by two years.** PFAS exposure is linked by CDC/ATSDR research to certain cancers, thyroid disruption, immune effects in children, reproductive difficulties, and elevated cholesterol.

rule_name: Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Standards (Clean Air Act Section 111 EGU Standards)
status: Repealed -- finalized and announced September 14, 2026, alongside a separate proposed rule intended to prevent future administrations from reinstating power-sector GHG standards. More than a dozen environmental and health organizations have already sued EPA Administrator Zeldin and the agency over the rollback.
date_of_action: 2025-06-11 (proposed); sent to OMB/OIRA for final review 2026-05-14; finalized 2026-09-14
original_rule_summary: EPA carbon dioxide emissions standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants (coal and new gas), issued under Clean Air Act Section 111, requiring plants to install carbon capture or otherwise limit CO2 output. Finalized by the Biden administration May 9, 2024.
what_changed: EPA proposed repealing the standards entirely on June 11, 2025, citing Executive Order 14,154 and arguing GHG emissions from fossil-fuel-fired power plants do not 'contribute significantly' to dangerous air pollution. As of May 14, 2026, EPA sent a final rule to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review -- the last procedural step before publication in the Federal Register. OMB reviews can take up to 90 days, meaning publication could occur any time through roughly mid-August 2026. This is a status escalation from the prior 'proposed, no further movement noted' state -- the rule is now genuinely close to finalization, though not yet finalized as of this entry's last verification. Update 2026-08-30: A second, broader draft entered White House/OMB review on August 25, 2026 -- rather than simply repealing the 2024 Section 111 standards, this supplemental proposal would go further and assert that the Clean Air Act gives EPA no authority to regulate greenhouse gases from the power sector at all, a more sweeping legal theory than the original repeal's 'does not contribute significantly' framing. E&E News/POLITICO reporting indicates EPA may time the rule's release around the Supreme Court's October 5, 2026 oral arguments in Suncor Energy v. Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County, a climate-liability case in which the government and oil industry are separately arguing the Clean Air Act makes EPA the 'primary regulator' of industrial GHG emissions -- a position in tension with the no-authority theory in this new proposal. Update 2026-09-14: **EPA finalized the repeal, formally asserting that greenhouse gas emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants 'do not contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution' and calling those emissions 'a small and decreasing part of global emissions' -- a characterization in tension with EPA's own 2023 data showing the power sector produced 31% of U.S. carbon emissions from fossil-fuel burning, the second-highest of any industry.** Alongside the repeal, EPA proposed a separate rule that, per reporting on people familiar with the proposal, could prevent future administrations from regulating power-plant greenhouse gas emissions at all -- functionally an attempt to lock in the rollback beyond this administration. Industry analysts project the rollback could increase coal use for power generation more than tenfold; the repealed standards were separately estimated to have prevented roughly 30,000 deaths and $275 billion in health and climate costs annually. More than a dozen environmental and public-health organizations filed suit against Zeldin and EPA over the rollback the same week.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Part of the same broader deregulatory package targeting power plant pollution rules and the endangerment finding. The related Endangerment Finding rescission (see separate entry) finalized Feb 12, 2026 and rests on the same 'does not contribute significantly' legal theory being applied here.

Fossil-gas-fired power plant developers

estimated_health_impact.summary: Second-largest single rollback in the current-term tracker by dollar value (per Institute for Policy Integrity), with the majority of monetized benefits coming from avoided climate damages, but with a substantial monetized public-health component from reduced particulate and other co-pollutant exposure near power plants. Separately, EPA's own regulatory text for the underlying proposal estimates compliance-cost savings alone (not the broader net-benefit figure below) at $19 billion (3% discount rate) or $9.6 billion (7% discount rate) in present value over the 2026-2047 period -- a narrower, agency-originated figure worth citing alongside the broader Policy Integrity estimate.

rule_name: Aggregate mortality projection for the combined effect of Trump's 2025 climate/energy rollbacks -- not a single rule; this entry's subject is the cross-cutting analysis itself
agency: Multiple (EPA's March 2025 deregulatory announcement; OBBBA's clean-energy tax-credit repeal; expanded federal oil/gas/mining leasing; reversed methane-emission efforts)
status: N/A for this entry -- it documents an aggregate mortality analysis spanning several already-tracked actions, not the repeal status of any one rule; see the cross-referenced entries below for each underlying action's own status
date_of_action: 2025 (analysis published November 19, 2025; projects mortality through roughly 2115)
original_rule_summary: Not applicable in the single-rule sense -- this entry aggregates the projected mortality effect of several distinct 2025 actions, each separately tracked: EPA's March 12, 2025 omnibus deregulatory announcement (see propublica-climate-rollback-heat-death-projection-2025's cross-reference to epa-31-rule-deregulation-announcement-2025.json), the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's repeal of clean-electricity/EV/manufacturing tax credits, easing of coal-plant pollution restrictions, weakened vehicle fuel standards, and expanded oil/gas/mining leasing on federal lands.
what_changed: A ProPublica/Guardian joint analysis (published Nov. 19, 2025) estimated that the combined effect of the above 2025 actions will cause approximately 1.3 million additional heat-related deaths globally between now and roughly 2115. The analysis used Rhodium Group's midrange estimate of 5.7 billion additional metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions attributable to the policies through 2035, applied to the peer-reviewed 'mortality cost of carbon' metric (developed by economist R. Daniel Bressler), under which each roughly 4,434 metric tons of CO2 emitted causes one additional temperature-related death over an 80-year window. The analysis found the burden falls overwhelmingly on poorer, hotter countries that contributed little to historical emissions: the U.S. has produced about 20% of the world's cumulative greenhouse gases with 4% of its population, but is projected to bear only up to about 1% of the temperature-related deaths these specific additional emissions cause. Each individual policy this analysis aggregates over -- the EPA announcement, the OBBBA tax-credit repeal, the vehicle-standards rollback, the drilling/mining expansion -- is tracked in this database's own separate entries; this entry exists specifically to hold the combined, cross-policy mortality estimate the individual entries note has not otherwise been produced (see epa-31-rule-deregulation-announcement-2025.json's own estimated_health_impact caveat, written before this analysis was published).

primary_proponent.role: The aggregate policy program this analysis measures spans EPA rulemaking, congressional legislation, and executive land-leasing decisions -- no single named individual drove all of it

rule_name: SEC Climate-Related Disclosure Rules (adopted March 2024)
status: Proposed Repeal (public comment period closed August 3, 2026; a final commission vote is still required and had not occurred as of this entry's last verification, with rescission unlikely before late 2026 or early 2027)
date_of_action: 2026-05-07 (SEC tells the Eighth Circuit it will no longer defend the rules in pending litigation) through 2026-05-29 (formal rescission proposal published)
original_rule_summary: Adopted by the SEC in March 2024, the rules required public companies to disclose climate-related risks material to their business, strategy, or financial outlook, along with certain greenhouse-gas emissions data (Scope 1 and 2 for larger filers) and the financial impact of severe weather events and other climate-related costs -- giving investors a standardized way to assess companies' exposure to climate-related financial risk.
what_changed: In a May 7, 2026 letter to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (where the rules had been under legal challenge since adoption), the SEC advised the court it 'does not intend to renew its defense of the Rules.' On May 29, 2026, the Commission formally proposed to rescind the climate-disclosure regime in its entirety, opening a 60-day public comment period. SEC Chair Paul Atkins framed the move as part of a broader return to a 'materiality-focused' approach to securities regulation, rolling back disclosure requirements for U.S.-listed companies more generally. rule_name: Revocation of SEC Enforcement Division's Delegated Authority to Issue Formal Orders of Investigation and Subpoenas
status: Fully Repealed (the 2009 delegation of authority itself)
original_rule_summary: Since 2009 -- adopted after the financial crisis, specifically to speed up fraud investigations -- the SEC had delegated authority to the Director of the Division of Enforcement to issue formal orders of investigation and the subpoenas that come with them, letting enforcement staff open investigations and compel documents/testimony without a Commission vote for each case.
what_changed: On March 10, 2025, the SEC's Republican majority -- then-Acting Chairman Mark Uyeda and Commissioner Hester Peirce -- voted to revoke the Enforcement Division's delegated authority to issue formal orders of investigation and subpoenas, over the objection of the sole Democratic commissioner, Caroline Crenshaw. The rule returns the SEC to its pre-2009 process, in which a majority of sitting Commissioners must personally approve the opening of any formal investigation and any subpoena issued in connection with it. Law-firm client alerts (Ballard Spahr, Arnold & Porter, Latham) characterized the change as likely to slow the pace and reduce the volume of SEC investigations by adding a bureaucratic approval step to every case. The rule took effect roughly six weeks before Paul Atkins was confirmed and sworn in as SEC Chairman (April 2025); **its practical effect became publicly visible a year later when Enforcement Division Director Margaret Ryan abruptly resigned in March 2026 after reportedly being blocked from pursuing fraud charges against Trump- and Musk-linked figures (Justin Sun, Elon Musk)** -- see the separate `sec-enforcement-chief-ryan-resignation-2026.json` entry for that downstream episode, which this rule's Commission-approval requirement structurally enabled.
