rule_name: Swine and Poultry Inspection Line Speed Deregulation
administration: Trump I (2017-2021), revived and expanded Trump II (2025-present)
status: Proposed Repeal -- FSIS proposed two rules in February 2026 to drop the swine line speed cap and raise poultry caps; neither is final. Waivers extended during the rulemaking let some plants run faster meanwhile. The 2019 rule's swine cap removal was vacated in 2021.
date_of_action: 2019-10-01 (First Term final rule); 2025-03-17 (Second Term announcement); 2026-02-19 (proposed rules published)
original_rule_summary: Federal meat inspection regulations cap processing line speeds (e.g. 1,106 head/hour for swine, 140 birds/minute for young chicken) and require federal FSIS inspectors -- not company employees -- to perform carcass-by-carcass safety inspection, on the theory that faster lines and non-federal inspection increase contamination and worker injury risk.
what_changed: The 2019 New Swine Slaughter Inspection System (NSIS) rule eliminated the swine line speed cap entirely and shifted carcass-sorting duties to company employees; a federal judge vacated its line speed provision in 2021 after a UFCW union lawsuit, finding the agency failed to properly consider public comments on worker safety, while the rest of the system stayed in effect. Under the second Trump administration, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced on March 17, 2025 plans to make faster line speeds a permanent federal standard for both pork and poultry, extended the plants' line speed waivers, and ended ongoing worker-safety data collection at modernized plants, calling it 'redundant.' In February 2026 FSIS proposed two rules that would let NSIS pork plants set their own line speeds, raise poultry caps to 175 birds/minute (chicken) and 60/minute (turkey), and drop the annual worker-safety attestations plants must file; the comment period closed April 20, 2026.

primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the 2025 plan to make faster line speeds permanent, four weeks after taking office. The original 2019 rule was a USDA/FSIS action without one clearly identified individual driver.

rule_name: 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule ('Roadless Rule')
status: Proposed Repeal (rulemaking in progress; final rule and record of decision expected late 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-06-23 (rescission announced) through 2026-08 (Forest Service formally files proposed repeal; rulemaking ongoing)
original_rule_summary: Finalized in 2001 under the Clinton administration, the Roadless Rule prohibited road construction, road reconstruction, and most timber harvest across roughly 58.5 million acres (nearly a third) of National Forest System land -- the largest single block of federal land-management protection outside the wilderness system -- to preserve undeveloped forest, protect watersheds and wildlife habitat, and limit human-caused wildfire ignition sources associated with roads.
what_changed: On June 23, 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced USDA's intent to rescind the Roadless Rule entirely, opening nearly 59 million acres of national forest to road construction, logging, and mining, framing the repeal as removing an 'impediment to responsible forest management' and citing wildfire-prevention goals. A public comment period on the initial proposal closed in September 2025, drawing 625,957 comments; the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities' review found more than 99% opposed repeal. USDA and the Forest Service continued the rulemaking through 2026: a formal proposed rule and draft environmental review followed, with the Forest Service filing the formal proposed repeal (covering an updated figure of roughly 44.7 million acres in some subsequent framing) in August 2026, opening a further comment period; a final rule and record of decision are expected in late 2026. Notably, the Forest Service's own internal fire analysis -- surfaced during the rulemaking process -- found that wildfire-ignition probability, frequency, and number all increase with road density, and that roadless areas see FEWER wildfire starts than roaded national forest land, directly undercutting the administration's stated fire-prevention rationale for the repeal; the agency's own scientists separately found the repeal could degrade drinking water quality for an estimated 25 million Americans who depend on national-forest watersheds. Firefighters and fire-policy experts, including FUSEE executive director Timothy Ingalsbee, publicly disputed the wildfire-prevention rationale, noting logging roads are built for resource extraction rather than fire suppression and that existing Forest Service road maintenance is already critically underfunded.

rule_name: VA fiduciary-based NICS reporting of veterans and related mental-illness gun restrictions, amid a 34-rule DOJ/ATF rollback
status: In effect (VA fiduciary NICS-reporting policy, effective February 17, 2026; not a Federal Register rule) / Rolling proposed and final actions (DOJ/ATF 34-rule package under Executive Order 14206, released April 29, 2026; ATF's mental-health definitions rule, RIN 1140-AB04, still proposed)
date_of_action: 2026-02-17 (VA fiduciary NICS-reporting policy change); 2026-04-29 (DOJ/ATF 34-rule package announced, including ATF's proposed mental-health definitions rule published 2026-05-08)
original_rule_summary: For about three decades, VA reported veterans it rated unable to manage their VA benefits and assigned a fiduciary to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) as prohibited firearm purchasers, relying on ATF's 1997 regulatory definition of "adjudicated as a mental defective," which covers determinations by a "court, board, commission, or other lawful authority." Beginning in 2024, Congress barred VA from using appropriated funds to report such veterans without a court ruling that they are a danger to themselves or others, and has continued that bar at least through September 30, 2026.
what_changed: **On February 17, 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs announced that, effective immediately, it would stop reporting veterans to NICS as prohibited firearm purchasers solely because they need a fiduciary to manage their VA benefits, and would work with the FBI to remove past fiduciary-only records, so background checks will no longer block gun purchases by veterans VA has found unable to manage their own financial affairs.** It was part of a broader administration effort under Executive Order 14206 (signed February 7, 2025): Attorney General Pamela Bondi said in VA's February 17 announcement that she was directing ATF to review its regulations and propose changes, and DOJ and ATF later announced 34 final and proposed rulemakings ("nearly three dozen," per the Washington Post) -- including rollbacks of rules restricting sales to people with documented mental illness and, per The New York Times, loosened oversight of private weapons transactions. In June 2025, the Washington Post had reported that DOGE sent staff into ATF with a mandate to revise or eliminate more than 50 rules and gun restrictions by July 4, 2025. Senior DOJ officials described the changes collectively as cutting 'unnecessary government bureaucracy without risking public safety'; gun-safety groups objected specifically to the mental-illness and fiduciary-status rollbacks as removing an existing, narrowly targeted safeguard. Re-verified 2026-08-16: DOJ and ATF's broader package has since been more precisely documented -- released April 29, 2026 under Executive Order 14206 as a 34-rule reform package, published in the Federal Register on May 6 and 8, 2026 and proceeding through individual notice-and-comment rulemakings on rolling timelines. Related DOJ/ATF actions outside the April 29 release include repeal of the Biden-era 'zero tolerance' dealer-penalty policy, a narrowed 'unlawful user of or addicted to controlled substance' definition (Federal Register, January 22, 2026), a gun-rights restoration (relief from disabilities) final rule published August 20, 2026 and effective September 21, 2026, and a proposal reducing fingerprinting requirements on certain firearms applications (Federal Register, July 6, 2026, comment through October 5, 2026). The package itself is documented in DOJ's release and the Federal Register, though this entry's original focus -- the mental-illness and private-transfer provisions specifically -- was not independently re-confirmed at that time beyond the original Washington Post reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the mental-illness provision within the broader DOJ/ATF package -- flagged in the prior recheck as not independently re-confirmed beyond the original Washington Post reporting -- is now specifically documented. ATF published a proposed rule on May 8, 2026 (RIN 1140-AB04) revising the regulatory definitions of "adjudicated as a mental defective" and "committed to a mental institution," the two categories that trigger a federal firearm-purchase prohibition on mental-health grounds. The proposal would narrow both definitions to require a formal legal adjudication or commitment process (notice, hearing, counsel, opportunity to contest) rather than an emergency hold, clinical judgment, or administrative form alone. Its comment period closed August 6, 2026; gun-violence-prevention groups Giffords and Brady submitted a joint opposition comment, and the rule had not been finalized as of this recheck. Update 2026-09-27: ATF's May 8, 2026 proposed rule states that VA had independently concluded that fiduciary incompetency determinations are not lawful adjudications under the federal gun ban and had directed removal of fiduciary-only records from NICS, and that the proposal would formalize the same distinction; it cites testimony that VA reported about 13,000 people to NICS in the year before the 2024 appropriations rider and only three in 2024, and says VA has reported over 250,000 veterans to NICS since its inception, and uses about 74,000 individuals in the accumulated set of VA records submitted to NICS in its illustrative estimate. ATF's own analysis of its proposal says the public-safety risk "may be minimal, or may be considerably greater (up to and including potential mass casualty events)." Giffords and Brady's August 6, 2026 comment argued that the rider did not restore any veteran's right to possess a firearm, so a VA-rated incompetent beneficiary remains a prohibited person under federal law; citing VA's 2025 National Veteran Suicide Prevention Annual Report, it said 6,389 veterans died by suicide in 2023 and that 73% of veteran suicides involved a firearm, compared with 53% of non-veteran suicides, and it cited Duke psychiatry professor Jeffrey Swanson's congressional testimony that fiduciary status is significantly correlated with suicide risk and violence.

what_changed.base: **On February 17, 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs announced that, effective immediately, it would stop reporting veterans to NICS as prohibited firearm purchasers solely because they need a fiduciary to manage their VA benefits, and would work with the FBI to remove past fiduciary-only records, so background checks will no longer block gun purchases by veterans VA has found unable to manage their own financial affairs.** It was part of a broader administration effort under Executive Order 14206 (signed February 7, 2025): Attorney General Pamela Bondi said in VA's February 17 announcement that she was directing ATF to review its regulations and propose changes, and DOJ and ATF later announced 34 final and proposed rulemakings ("nearly three dozen," per the Washington Post) -- including rollbacks of rules restricting sales to people with documented mental illness and, per The New York Times, loosened oversight of private weapons transactions. In June 2025, the Washington Post had reported that DOGE sent staff into ATF with a mandate to revise or eliminate more than 50 rules and gun restrictions by July 4, 2025. Senior DOJ officials described the changes collectively as cutting 'unnecessary government bureaucracy without risking public safety'; gun-safety groups objected specifically to the mental-illness and fiduciary-status rollbacks as removing an existing, narrowly targeted safeguard. Re-verified 2026-08-16: DOJ and ATF's broader package has since been more precisely documented -- released April 29, 2026 under Executive Order 14206 as a 34-rule reform package, published in the Federal Register on May 6 and 8, 2026 and proceeding through individual notice-and-comment rulemakings on rolling timelines. Related DOJ/ATF actions outside the April 29 release include repeal of the Biden-era 'zero tolerance' dealer-penalty policy, a narrowed 'unlawful user of or addicted to controlled substance' definition (Federal Register, January 22, 2026), a gun-rights restoration (relief from disabilities) final rule published August 20, 2026 and effective September 21, 2026, and a proposal reducing fingerprinting requirements on certain firearms applications (Federal Register, July 6, 2026, comment through October 5, 2026). The package itself is documented in DOJ's release and the Federal Register, though this entry's original focus -- the mental-illness and private-transfer provisions specifically -- was not independently re-confirmed at that time beyond the original Washington Post reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the mental-illness provision within the broader DOJ/ATF package -- flagged in the prior recheck as not independently re-confirmed beyond the original Washington Post reporting -- is now specifically documented. ATF published a proposed rule on May 8, 2026 (RIN 1140-AB04) revising the regulatory definitions of "adjudicated as a mental defective" and "committed to a mental institution," the two categories that trigger a federal firearm-purchase prohibition on mental-health grounds. The proposal would narrow both definitions to require a formal legal adjudication or commitment process (notice, hearing, counsel, opportunity to contest) rather than an emergency hold, clinical judgment, or administrative form alone. Its comment period closed August 6, 2026; gun-violence-prevention groups Giffords and Brady submitted a joint opposition comment, and the rule had not been finalized as of this recheck.

rule_name: Waters of the United States (WOTUS) Narrowing — Post-Sackett Redefinition
status: Proposed Repeal (comment period on original Nov. 2025 proposal closed 2026-01-05; EPA has since sent a supplemental proposed rule to OMB for review as of late June 2026, reopening comment on revised aspects rather than proceeding to finalize -- not yet finalized)
date_of_action: 2025-11-17 (proposed)
original_rule_summary: The 'waters of the United States' (WOTUS) definition determines which streams, wetlands, and other water bodies are protected under the Clean Water Act. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 Sackett v. EPA decision, the Biden administration issued a 2023 rule conforming WOTUS to Sackett's narrower 'relatively permanent' and 'continuous surface connection' standards.
what_changed: EPA and the Army Corps proposed a further narrowing of the 2023 rule -- the sixth WOTUS redefinition in a decade -- including removing 'interstate waters' from the definition entirely and tightening the definitions of 'continuous surface connection' and 'relatively permanent waters.' The stated aim is to end a split implementation (the 2023 rule is currently enjoined in 26 states) and further reduce federal permitting jurisdiction. Re-verified 2026-08-16: rather than proceeding to finalize the November 2025 proposal after its January 5, 2026 comment period closed, EPA sent a second, supplemental proposed rule to OMB for interagency review around June 30, 2026, revising unspecified aspects of the original proposal and seeking renewed public comment -- an unusual procedural step per InsideEPA.com and E&E News/POLITICO coverage. This substantially delays the final rule beyond the 'roughly mid-2026' timeline legal analysts had previously projected; no publication date for the supplemental proposal in the Federal Register was found as of this update.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA and the Army jointly proposed the rule; Zeldin is the named agency head across the broader 2025-2026 EPA deregulatory push.

corporate_beneficiaries: Developers, agricultural operations, and industries seeking reduced Clean Water Act Section 404/402 permitting obligations

estimated_health_impact.summary: **Narrower federal jurisdiction over wetlands and intermittent streams reduces natural filtration of agricultural and industrial runoff before it reaches drinking water sources -- a structural/general risk rather than a quantified rule-specific mortality or illness figure.**
